Spurs are getting things moving in the right direction under Roberto De Zerbi - but there's a missing piece to the puzzle

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tottenham Hotspur’s resurgence under Roberto De Zerbi has breathed fresh life into the club after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

There is one clear deficiency in their current make-up that threatens to limit what they can achieve in 2026/27, though - they can't finish.

Despite sitting comfortably in the top half after 12 games, Spurs’ underlying attacking numbers tell the story of a side creating plenty and squandering too much of it.

Tottenham have rattled off 170 shots in the Premier League this season - the fifth-highest tally in the division - while only Liverpool and Manchester City have registered more efforts from inside the penalty area than Spurs’ 109.

But, when it comes to actually hitting the target, De Zerbi’s side slump to 14th across the top flight.

There's also an issue with their ball-striking. According to Gradient Sports’ analysts, just six of Spurs’ 170 league attempts have been graded as ‘unsaveable’ - a figure bettered by every team in the Premier League bar Everton (5).

For context, high-flying Brighton have racked up 20 unsaveable efforts, while Erling Haaland has managed seven on his own. At 3.5 per cent, Tottenham boast the lowest proportion of unsaveable shots in the entire division.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

A glance at De Zerbi’s attacking options explains why to some extent. Richarlison has been frozen out entirely and is angling for a January move, Dominic Solanke has managed just two league goals, and big-money summer arrival Omar Marmoush is yet to hit the ground running in north London.

Centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is the team's joint-top Premier League goalscorer with two goals after 12 matches: Spurs need a centre-forward in January.

Enter Real Sociedad’s 22-year-old Icelandic international Orri Oskarsson.

Oskarsson is by no means LaLiga’s most prolific frontman, having netted four times in the Spanish top flight this term but his underlying metrics point towards a striker ready to thrive in a possession-heavy, attack-minded system.

Unlike De Zerbi’s Spurs, Real Sociedad do not dominate the ball as often, leaving their striker without service for large periods of matches. Oskarsson, though, is making every second count when his team are in possession, averaging a goal every 64 minutes that La Real actually have the ball this season.

In total, he has scored nine times across his last 13 appearances for club and country.

What makes Oskarsson particularly suited to Tottenham is how intelligently he moves to receive the ball. Gradient Sports’ data shows the Icelandic forward receives line-breaking passes 45 per cent of the time, placing him among LaLiga’s best at peeling off defenders and making himself available to creative midfielders.

That off-the-ball awareness is reinforced by the fact he has received the ball in a clear shooting position 10 times in the league this season - a tally bettered only by Barcelona’s Raphinha (13) and Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (11).

Once the ball arrives at his feet, Oskarsson has the penalty-box nous Tottenham lack. Ninety-two per cent of his LaLiga shots this season have been taken from inside the box, which aligns nicely with the 109 close-range openings Spurs have already generated this term. Even more impressive, out of the 25 shots he has taken in LaLiga, five have been graded as unsaveable by Gradient's analysts - just one fewer than Tottenham’s entire squad combined.

Gradient have also flagged just one occasion all season where Oskarsson opted to shoot when passing to a better-placed teammate was the superior option, highlighting good judgement under pressure and decision-making that is rare for a 22-year-old.

Meanwhile, his Expected Goals (xG) ranks sixth-highest in LaLiga - a decent return given Real Sociedad’s modest share of possession and chance creation.

And best of all, a winter deal is entirely plausible. For a Tottenham side creating plenty of penalty-box opportunities but with nobody reliable to tuck them away, Oskarsson could be one of the more shrewd January investments the market has to offer.

#854. How Liverpool finally unlocked Alexander Isak to solve big problem

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

After a nightmarish first season at Anfield, Isak heads into Sunday’s Merseyside derby enjoying a superb second year thanks to Andoni Iraola’s tactical tweaks

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As Liverpool prepare to make their shortest journey of the season, Alexander Isak has come a long way in a few months. The fact he is leaving Anfield, even if it is only about two-and-a-half miles to Hill Dickinson Stadium, for Sunday’s Merseyside derby against Everton may bode well for an increasingly impressive traveller – the misfit who has become a mainstay.

Since his unhappy return to Newcastle in the season opener, when Isak was barracked by the supporters who used to adore him, the Swedish striker has played in six away games and scored in each; indeed, of his 10 goals under Andoni Iraola, only two have come at Anfield.

There may be some significance in the identity of the last Liverpool player to score in six straight away matches: Mohamed Salah, and if Isak is not a direct replacement for a right winger in one respect, he has been charged with taking on the Egyptian’s mantle as Liverpool’s scorer in chief.

Even in Isak’s decidedly difficult debut year at Anfield, Liverpool may note two-thirds of his meagre tally of three league goals came away. Since Iraola took the reins, however, Isak has become his king of the road. The head coach admitted he is unsure why.

“I don’t have any clear reason, honestly,” he said. “I think the way we play is the same whether away or at home. We know we have to go for the games either way. So I think it is just a coincidence. I don’t think there is a big difference in performance away or at home.”

There may, however, be a difference in the context, when opponents open up and allow a side with Liverpool’s counter-attacking pace – wingers as speedy as Bradley Barcola, Victor Munoz and Rio Ngumoha, and a striker as quick as Isak – to break.

“Normally you will find more spaces when you play away because teams are normally more brave and they usually press you more,” said Iraola. “Then you will find more spaces.” He has always caveated his comments about Liverpool’s excellent away form this season with reminders that he prefers to play at home.

Does Isak? Much as St James’ Park loved him, explaining the sense of betrayal when he went on strike to force his exit, he was almost as potent away. In his first season at Newcastle, 2022-23, he scored five times at home, five away. In the following year, there were 15 goals on Tyneside, 10 elsewhere. In his final campaign, he scored 14 times at home, 12 away and a Carabao Cup final goal against Liverpool at neutral Wembley.

In 2024, he reached double figures for the campaign on Boxing Day. The following year, he got there on 21 December. Isak has reached 10 in November now. Viewed that way, he is on course to beat his personal best of 27 goals in a campaign. Not that Iraola has set any targets.

“I know how No 9s are, they are very focused on scoring goals,” he said. “But not from my side. It is not going to be the main thing. I will value him and rate him not because of his goals probably. I will focus in other areas which I think need improving and I think are very good for the team.”

That can be the Iraola way: to look at the collective. Florian Wirtz has found goalscoring form of late, too, but his manager insisted: “For me, it is not just about Florian or Alex, it is about if we play well, someone will score a goal, someone will give the assist, someone will make the numbers.”

At the moment, two players are and it’s the two signed for big numbers – the £125m Isak and the £116m Wirtz. It took time, amid the centre-forward’s injury-hit first year, but a connection is being forged. The German has found the Swede with a pass 29 times in the Premier League this season, and a further 10 in Wednesday’s Champions League win against Club Brugge.

That said, the assists for Isak have tended to come from others: four from Cody Gakpo, two from Barcola, even one from goalkeeper Alisson against Brugge. If that has a rarity value, he nevertheless has a fine supply line, while Iraola has channelled the striker’s speed. Isak has made the most runs in behind opposition defences this season; one led to Leny Yoro’s red card for Manchester United last week, and Dominik Szoboszlai’s opening goal from the resulting free-kick.

Perhaps it is typical that much of Iraola’s emphasis has been on regaining possession. Isak leads the line, and also the press.

“He has definitely improved a lot on the ball and without the ball,” said his manager. “He is understanding better the press and the better he understands the press the less he has to run also. Also, on the ball we are using him much better in possession, he is linking up play very well. Technically he is a very nice player.”

That technique has been apparent in the quality of some of Isak’s goals. But the most important element – if not for Iraola – may be the quantity, with 10 so far, and eight on the road.

Panini have launched their latest WSL sticker collection at event with ex-Lioness Rachel Daly

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Panini have launched their latest Barclays Women's Super League sticker collection, featuring teams from WSL and WSL 2 for a second year running.

This is only the fourth edition of the book for the top women’s league in this country, and Rachel Daly believes the culture of sticker collecting can play its part in growing the women’s game.

As the latest collection was launched in London this week, the ex-Lioness spoke to FourFourTwo about the rise of the women's game.

Speaking at the launch, Daly reflected on her own childhood memories of collecting Panini stickers.

"For me, it goes back to my childhood,” Daly told FourFourTwo. “I collected them with my brother. We used to, every Saturday morning, go and get the stickers.

"You'd get your piles and you'd trade them and swap them at school. Just that whole feeling of sitting down and putting stickers in.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I'm a Leeds fan, so I always wanted to get the whole Leeds team immediately when I was younger.

"I would literally swap any of my stickers, even if I'd already got the Leeds player, just to have more.”

While Daly grew up collecting men’s players, this WSL collection offers an opportunity to introduce more fans to the women's game, something Daly believes is particularly important as the league continues to grow.

The latest album has 545 stickers across all 26 WSL and WSL2 clubs, giving fans access to collect stickers of their favourite players from across the top two tiers of English women’s football.

"The visibility of the game is massive," she added.

"For the fact that it's WSL 1 and 2, I think it's equally as important. Those players in the WSL 2 deserve the same recognition as us.

"Being able to see kids being exposed to seeing the women's game as well, it's exciting."

Daly was speaking at the launch of the Panini Barclays Women's Super League Official Sticker Collection 2027 in London. The collection is available now at retailers nationwide and online via Panini.co.uk.

#852. How Singapore has turned a nation into a smart-city testing ground

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sandy Ong is a freelance writer based in Singapore.

As a city state, Singapore can often implement digital infrastructure projects more quickly than cities in much larger countries.Credit: Roslan Rahman/AFP via Getty Images

Singapore is one of the world’s smallest countries by land area, spanning roughly 744 km2. Yet as a technologically advanced city, it consistently punches above its weight. Earlier this year, Singapore placed ninth in the IMD Smart City Index 2026 — the highest-ranked city in Asia — noted for the strong trust its residents had in the government’s use of digital technologies. The index, published by IMD, a Swiss research institute, uses citizen surveys to evaluate cities’ physical and digital infrastructure across areas such as health and safety, governance and mobility.

The centralized government of Singapore, as a city-state, allows it to coordinate nationwide digital infrastructure projects with a speed and consistency that would be difficult in larger, more fragmented countries, says Orlando Woods, director of Singapore Management University’s Urban Institute, which studies urban growth and governance. “It has a single layer of government,” says Woods. “To make decisions and implement things is just so much easier.”

Singapore was among the earliest countries to digitize public services and integrate technological advancement across multiple government sectors, including health care, public services, transport and urban planning. In 2014, it announced these strategies as part of its ‘Smart Nation’ initiative, a major part of which is Virtual Singapore — one of the world’s first national-scale ‘digital twins’.

A dynamic, 3D replica of Singapore, the Virtual Singapore model encompasses everything from real-time air-quality statistics to population data and traffic flow. Comprising more than 100 TB of data collected from aerial photography, remote-sensing technologies and the thousands of sensors installed across the island, it is continually updated with new geospatial, environmental and infrastructure data.

Local authorities use Virtual Singapore to inform urban-planning decisions, such as identifying the best rooftops for solar panels. It is also used in planning public-safety measures, including modelling flood impacts, drafting disaster-response plans and pinpointing potential risk areas for disease outbreaks, such as dengue fever. Some features and data sets are freely available to researchers, businesses and residents.

#850. Tonda Eckert removes box of tissues as Southampton taunt Middlesbrough over Spygate

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Eckert distanced himself from a series of incidents between the Spygate rivals, including Finn Azaz running the length of the pitch to make a ‘crying’ gesture at the Boro fans

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert removed a box of tissues from the post-match press conference table and said he wanted to face Middlesbrough with “class” after a series of incidents between the teams resurfaced the tensions of ‘Spygate’ from last season.

Southampton hosted Middlesbrough on Friday night for the first time since they were kicked out of the Championship play-offs last season for breaking EFL rules by sending an analyst to their semi-final opponent’s training ground.

Finn Azaz ran the length of the pitch to celebrate his clinching goal in the 2-0 win front of the Middlesbrough fans, while also making a ‘crying’ gesture towards them, sparking a brawl between the opposing teams.

Southampton played the Oasis song ‘Stop Crying Your Heart Out’ at full-time while the club also posted a video onto social media taunting Middlesbrough by showing Oli McBurnie’s winner for Hull in last season’s play-off final at Wembley.

“I hope everyone who came here from Boro knows these things don’t come from me,” said Eckert, who removed the box of tissues from the press conference table before his Boro counterpart, Kim Hellberg, had arrived.

“I try to come from class. I don’t know if I have been able to do that but I hope there is an appreciation it doesn’t come from me.

“I think it was one of the best matches the Championship has had to offer this year. It was two very good teams facing each other.“I had hoped these games are remembered for the football.”

Former Boro player Azaz provoked the visitors even further by running the length of the pitch, Emmanuel Adebayor style, to celebrate in front of the travelling fans. He then made crying motions towards them.

Azaz explained the reason for his celebration by saying: “They sang about my family home and away last season, so I was just waiting for my moment to get one back.”

Before adding: “None whatsoever,” when asked if he had any regrets over his unsavoury antics.

Eckert was less impressed and said: “I will talk to him.”

Hellberg, who spoke to Azaz at the final whistle, said: “I told Finn that there are things he has to do better. I know there are a lot of emotions and emotions can get the better of you, but you have to be better than that.”

#849. Borussia Dortmund bows to fan pressure and end Rheinmetall deal

Borussia Dortmund has reluctantly ended its association with a major sponsor after long-term fan protests. They are not the first Bundesliga club to u-turn, as commercial interests clash with politics and fan culture.

Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.

The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season. Dortmund chairman Carsten Cramer confirmed the news on the club's website ahead of its AGM on Sunday, which may have proved a potential flashpoint. He acknowledged that "our partnership has been controversial from the outset" but lamented the loss of income.

"It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre. We will have to reprioritize planned investments and carefully examine how we can find viable solutions."

Though he welcomed the news, one of the leaders of the fan revolt against the partnership, Michael Schulze von Glaser, warned this is likely not the end of the road.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"I think in the end it was a victory for the fans. But I'm also a bit skeptical about what the future will bring us," the Dortmund fan and former head of the German Peace Society told DW. "Football fans in Germany always must be skeptical and always must watch what the club is doing.”

Many Dortmund fans have opposed the deal — which has seen Rheinmetall's logo on advertising boards and other surfaces at locations such as Dortmund's 83,000-capacity Westfalenstadion — from its beginnings in 2024. It was estimated to be worth between €7 ($7.68 million) and €9 million per year.

At the club's AGM that year, 556 of 855 members present voted against the deal in a non-binding vote. There were 247 votes in favour, with 52 abstentions. This, said Cramer, informed the eventual outcome.

Rheinmetall sells arms mostly to Germany, Ukraine and NATO but fans and critics feel that platforming any arms manufacturer goes against the club's statement of its core values. In that, Dortmund states its desire for "a club and a society that operate free of racism, anti-Semitism, LGBTQIA+ hostility, sexism, violence and discrimination."

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

It has always been clear, said Schulze von Glaser, that this deal did not chime with that.

"In the end, they kill people. They are for war," he said of Rheinmetall. "The slogan of Borussia Dortmund is true love (Echte Liebe). But for me and many others, our love ends there…. I know some fans who have put fan merchandise in the trash because they were so shocked.”

In the Q and A on the club's website, Cramer said he was still a "personal advocate" of the deal but that Dortmund's commitment to the 50+1 model, which means German clubs are majority controlled by the members, meant they had to listen to fan voices. But he also warned that Rheinmetall must be an "absolute exception and an isolated case."

That set off some alarm bells for Schulze von Glaser.

"It's a bit concerning that there are constantly these attacks on professional football — a new sponsorship, investment deals," he said.

Indeed, Dortmund's climbdown is not the first of its kind in Germany's top flight. Last year, after fan and media pressure, Bayern Munich ended its commercial deal with the tourism arm of the Rwandan government before its conclusion.

Fans had objected to the promotion of Rwanda, which many felt sought to divert attention from its poor human rights record and actions in the war with DR Congo, through sporting partnerships. Two years earlier, Bayern withdrew from a similarly controversial deal with Qatar Airways.

Elsewhere in the league, Werder Bremen fans objected to their long time shirt sponsor, Wiesenhof. Many supporters took issue with the factory farming practices of Germany's largest poultry producer. Though it was not given as a direct reason for the end of a shirt sponsorship deal in 2023, it likely played a part.

Union Berlin fans have also made their voices heard. When the club signed a new shirt-sponsorship deal with Luxembourg real estate company, Aroundtown, upon promotion to the top flight in 2019, many fans were frustrated at the tie up in a city where rent prices were skyrocketing.

"It's a problem for a lot of people," fan Sven Dobberstein told DW at the time.

"We have to try to find a way between commercialization and what we have at the moment. It isn't easy."

Striking that balance can often be a source of tension for Bundesliga clubs. 50+1 ensures fans have a voice, preventing rich owners, or nation states, from taking control as they do in England's lucrative Premier League or in France or Spain. Indeed fan protests have also stopped the league signing a €1billion private equity partner and seen Monday night matches scrapped. For Schulze von Glaser, this needs to be protected.

"In Germany, the fan culture has an impact," he said.

”If there is something bad or terrible happening in your club and in the Bundesliga, there are the organized fans and they can have an impact if they want, if they stand together and, yes, they can stop the Rheinmetall deal."

The parallels between the Hammers and the Foxes are impossible to ignore as Scott Parker’s team slide down the Championship table

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.

It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer plan and greater purpose.

Sometimes, though, relegation is just the start. If it is not taken seriously, relegation might not be rock-bottom, but a trapdoor that sends a club spiralling to new lows.

Leicester City know all about that trapdoor. The Foxes were Premier League champions in 2016, FA Cup winners in 2021 and Conference League semi-finalists in 2021/22, but are now in League One after a series of relegations.

They were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware, but years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy saw them fall into the second tier and beyond.

West Ham United were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware - the Conference League in 2023 - but dropped out of the Premier League last season after years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Hammers had been in the division since 2012 and finished as high as sixth in 2020/21, ending the campaign a place and a point behind Leicester. In 2024/25, the season before they went down, they generated the 20th-highest revenue in world football, according to the Deloitte Money League. Leicester were 17th in the Money League in 2021/22, the campaign before the first of their two recent relegations from the Premier League.

Both clubs boast facilities that are out of place in their division. West Ham’s 62,500-seater London Stadium has almost double the capacity of the next biggest Championship ground, while Leicester’s training complex is one of the best in the country, let alone League One.

The parallels do not end there. Like Leicester 12 months ago, West Ham were one of the pre-season Championship promotion favourites and started the campaign well, but those results papered over the cracks.

Since climbing to second with a 1-0 victory at then-leaders Swansea City on October 17, the Hammers have gone six games without a win and sacked manager Nuno Espirito Santo, replacing him with Scott Parker. They are 13th ahead of today’s visit of second-place Stoke City, with 24 points from 17 matches.

It is eerily similar to Leicester’s start to last season. Looking to make an immediate return to the Premier League, the Foxes were third on October 17. But like West Ham, results started to slide. Like West Ham, they had 24 points after 17 games.

Of course, Leicester’s season ended with relegation, and the Hammers are by no means destined for the drop. Right now, though, the parallels are impossible to ignore.

In terms of individual quality, both clubs began their respective seasons with one of the most talented squads in the league. Leicester had the likes of Abdul Fatawu, Jordan James and Stephy Mavididi, while West Ham can call on Jarrod Bowen, Konstantinos Mavropanos and Manor Solomon, among others.

However, both squads bore the hallmarks of years of poor recruitment. Leicester’s group included several big-money signings that had failed to deliver, including Patson Daka, Oliver Skipp and Jannik Vestergaard, and they did not pay a single transfer fee in the summer 2025 window to try to balance the books.

Meanwhile, West Ham have a top-heavy squad filled with attacking quality but light on defensive cover. The Hammers spent almost £40million this summer - including paying an EFL-record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic - yet failed to address some glaring gaps in the squad.

With all those attackers, West Ham need a manager who wants to dominate games. But Nuno prefers to let the opponents have the ball and attack quickly in transition, which was ill-suited to his squad. The Hammers have now appointed Parker, a Championship promotion specialist having previously taken Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley up.

Once again, it is strikingly similar to Leicester, who sacked Marti Cifuentes in January and turned to Gary Rowett, a Championship survival specialist. However, his pragmatic style did not get the best out of his players and the Foxes continued to slide.

This runs deeper than the managers, though. Any head coach at Leicester would have struggled to reinvigorate a group of players who had either lost belief or did not want to be at the club anymore.

That showed in their reaction to going behind. After November 8 last year, Leicester did not win a single Championship game in which they conceded first. If heads drop when you suffer a setback, it points to a lack of confidence, fight or both, and form will suffer.

This season, West Ham are yet to win in the league after going 1-0 down, drawing five times and suffering five defeats. They have conceded first in every game of their six-match winless run. This is the biggest red flag of the Hammers’ season so far. Having quality players means nothing if they do not have the right mentality, as Leicester found out last term.

It remains very unlikely that West Ham follow the Foxes into League One. But their recent transfer business does not suggest they will recruit smartly in January and if they miss out on promotion, you would expect some of their better players to leave next summer - sparking a transition period and potentially an extended spell outside of the top flight.

Even if Parker turns it around and wins promotion, is he the right man to lead them in the Premier League? The Hammers manager is yet to succeed in a top-flight job and if he is sacked in 12 months time, you would not back the club’s hierarchy to identify the right replacement based on their track record.

That was another feature of Leicester’s decline. The Foxes won promotion at the first attempt in 2023/24 but made poor managerial choices in Steve Cooper and then Ruud van Nistelrooy, and were relegated immediately.

Five years ago, West Ham fans would have dreamed of being the ‘next Leicester City’. Right now, it is the nightmare scenario.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#846. Xabi Alonso responds as Chelsea fans tell Wesley Fofana ‘you’re not welcome here’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Chelsea fans turned their anger towards Fofana after an ill-timed, unauthorised interview was published following the 4-1 defeat at Leeds

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Xabi Alonso defended under-fire Wesley Fofana as Chelsea fans directed chants of “f--- off” and “you’re not welcome here” towards him during the 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest.

It came after the centre-back gave an unauthorised interview to a French YouTuber this week, where he appeared to laugh off his penalty miss in the Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool last month.

The 25-year-old apologised for the interview and Alonso said on Thursday that the matter was closed, but the defender was singled out by the away fans after he gave away a penalty and was substituted during the Premier League defeat at the City Ground.

Fofana’s form had also come under the microscope following the 4-1 home defeat by Leeds last weekend, with his interview with YouTuber Zack Nani appearing online just days later.

“Well, we have to stick together, and everyone that is in the changing room, everyone in the team is needed,” Alonso said after the club’s third consecutive Premier League defeat.

“We need to help, and we need to go through these tough moments all together, and we don’t leave anyone apart. We need to support everyone. That is because we need everyone, and we need the fans.

“We need all the players. We need to stick together because if not, things will get more complicated, and that’s what we want to do.”

Chelsea trailed Forest after a brilliant volley from Igor Jesus in the opening minutes before Fofana conceded a penalty for fouling former Blues striker Liam Delap in the box, in which Morgan Gibbs-White scored to double the hosts’ lead.

Fofana was then replaced in the 56th minute by Levi Colwill and Alonso was asked after the game if it would be difficult to select the centre-back again moving forward, with Chelsea facing a short turnaround before they host Crystal Palace on Wednesday.

Alonso said: “Well, I’m thinking right after the game and for the next games, we will see.”

Former Leicester defending Fofana had also received backlash for stating that he considered retiring from football during his lengthy injury lay-off, only to be discouraged by his agent because “you’ve still got so many years left on your contract, and so much money to earn” - insinuating he was motivated to sit on his current lucrative deal at Stamford Bridge.

Alonso was pressed about the interview before Friday’s trip to Nottingham Forest, revealing in his news conference that Fofana had tried to make amends with the club.

“Absolutely, we have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate,” Alonso said.

“He apologised, he knows it was not right the moment, it was not right the content, we are here to take things seriously and he said that it's not going to be repeated and we know that it's something that we don't want, these kind of things and they are not going to be repeated for sure.”

Asked whether Fofana would face any further sanction, such as be dropped from the squad, or if the case was closed, Alonso replied: “Closed.”

#844. Poch suffers nightmare Old Trafford debut as brilliant Brentford pile on misery

Manchester United vs Brentford. Premier League.

Old TraffordAttendance: Attendance74,026.

Report and free match highlights as Brentford win at Old Trafford for the very first time to condemn Mauricio Pochettino to nightmare home debut as manager; Callum Wilson scored twice, with goals in the second half from Kristoffer Ajer and Kevin Schade; United could finish weekend bottom

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Manchester United sank to another frightening low in Mauricio Pochettino's first home game in charge, thrashed 4-0 by Champions League-chasing Brentford at Old Trafford.

United have now lost half of their 12 Premier League games this season, and as a result, are consigned to another week in the relegation zone. They could conceivably be bottom by the end of the weekend.

If Pochettino did not know or understand the scale of the task in front of him, this latest non-performance captured the chaos perfectly.

Harry Maguire kissed the crossbar with a header early on and Patrick Dorgu missed a sitter, but the difference in final third quality was striking. Callum Wilson scored twice in a miserable first half for Pochettino, whose presence on the touchline did little to improve how submissive his players were in and out of possession.

Amad was robbed for the opener before Senne Lammens allowed Wilson's strike to flash through his fingers. The 34-year-old's second was easier still, rounding off a quick break fashioned by a cutting Mikkel Damsgaard pass and a smart run from Dango Ouattara.

Defensive frailties continue to plague a team devoid of any confidence and the second half offered no respite. Leny Yoro, sent off at Liverpool last week before the decision was overturned, was lucky not to concede a penalty when Kevin Schade went racing through on goal. The substitute could have added a third moments later as gaps got larger and legs tired of chasing shadows.

Man Utd are the first side in Premier League history to concede at least twice in six successive halves of football. After conceding two in both halves against Brentford, their tally now stands at seven.

But the visitors had plenty more opportunities to improve the scoreline and took two of them. Kristoffer Ajer netted an easy third from a corner and Schade made good on his earlier threat by chipping Lammens for a stylish fourth.

United have lost successive league games by at least four goals for the first time since Boxing Day 1963. Just three games into his tenure, the outlook for Pochettino already looks bleak.

11: CHANCE! Fernandes meets Dalot's precise cross and heads wide of the mark.

17: HUGE CHANCE! Amad sends an in-swinger to the back post but Dorgu guides a poor effort wide.

19: GOAL! Amad loses the ball and Wilson glides between the static Maguire and Yoro to blast beyond Lammens.

31: GOAL! Damsgaard fizzes a fine pass through to Ouattara on the run and he feeds Wilson for a tap in.

54: SHOT! Dorgu fires straight at Caoimhin Kelleher after neat build-up play.

61: ESCAPE! Yoro's clumsy coming together with Schade in the box goes unpunished by officials.

90+2: GOAL! Schade rounds off a brilliant performance with a clever chip to beat Lammens.

"Our support is unconditional to the players.

"Sometimes we have to feel pain. Now is the moment, from here, we must go up. That is the truth.

"The players feel, of course, the pressure and stress. Who take the responsibility? That's the difficult thing. We're here to do that.

"We have to know our reality. We are Manchester United but you cannot win with the history or the badge. We have to match the opponent."

Asked whether he believes the job to be tougher than expected, he replied: "Of course, yes."

"The key today was to block out the exterior noise and focus on us. Clearly there was a lot of noise because it was Mauricio's first home game. But I wanted to play with courage and personality.

"Once the boys relaxed into the first half, I thought we were really good. The development of this team has been around getting punched in the nose, getting up, and being able to go again.

"Not letting the emotions of this occasion affect us in any way was the most pleasing part today.

"This place has produced ridiculous games in years gone by and I was very keen for it not to be a comeback story. I was keen for us to push and fight with bravery. We managed the second half really well."

The Brazilian forward admits he didn't particularly want to leave Stamford Bridge but that Arsenal's offer was just too good to ignore

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Willian admits he was desperate to remain at Chelsea before a disagreement over the length of a new contract led him to join London rivals Arsenal in 2020.

The Brazilian had spent seven seasons at Stamford Bridge, winning two Premier League titles as well as the FA Cup and Europa League, and had become a popular figure among supporters.

But towards the end of his contract, Chelsea offered him a two-year extension and the winger, approaching his 32nd birthday, wanted the security of three - a request that Arsenal were prepared to meet.

Willian told FourFourTwo: “From the beginning after I arrived [at Chelsea], each year was better than the last.”

“There were several years of great joy – we won two Premier League titles together, the FA Cup and the Europa League. Of course, in football, we don't live only for victories.

There were defeats too. We lost league titles and cup finals; we reached the semi-finals of the Champions League and ended up losing that too.”

“But we had many achievements as well. The main thing is the connection I managed to create with the club, and with Chelsea fans, which is still very strong today.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“[But] look, at that moment, that decision had to be made. I was turning 32 and I had to think about the future.

“Chelsea wanted to offer me a two-year contract extension, and I wanted three years. We couldn't reach an agreement.”

Arsenal could offer the additional year he was seeking, as well as familiar faces from Brazil. The combination eventually persuaded Willian to leave.

Willian explained: Arsenal came along with a great project. Edu was there [as technical director] and David Luiz. I was offered a three-year contract and peace of mind.

"But it still wasn't an easy call. I really wanted to stay at Chelsea.”

In the end, though, it was largely immaterial: Willian ended up leaving Arsenal after just a single season. But that's another story...

#841. Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?

The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.

The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

The opening price valued the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Yet, after the first two days of trading, Anthropic stock closed Friday more than 20% below its opening price at $87.80, suggesting the hype had run ahead of what investors were willing to pay.

Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.

In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.

While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.

Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.

The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.

The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.

Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."

"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.

Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18, 19 and 20 to reflect the latest developments.

#840. Everton vs Liverpool: Prediction and betting tips

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Independent's journalism is supported by our readers. If you click links to other sites on this page, we will earn commission.

Follow our football betting tips as the first Merseyside derby of the season takes place at the Hill Dickinson Stadium

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andoni Iraola takes charge of his first Merseyside derby on Sunday when he takes his Liverpool side across the city to take on Everton at the Hill Dickinson Stadium (kick-off 12:00, live on TNT Sports and HBO Max).

The Reds go into the game on the back of three straight wins in all competitions, including last weekend’s controversial win over Manchester United.

They won 4-0 at Anfield, although the sending off of Leny Yoro, after just eight minutes, certainly helped their cause. That red card has now been rescinded, but the three points moved Liverpool up to fourth in the table, seven points behind the leaders, Arsenal.

Everton sit five points and five places below their neighbours, but David Moyes will be looking for a huge improvement on the performance at Brentford on Monday, when they were beaten 4-0 and had captain James Tarkowski sent off.

That defeat ended a run of three wins but was just their third defeat of the season after an impressive start to the campaign.

They have also picked out four wins and four draws so far, but they’ve not beaten Liverpool in the last four attempts.

Last season, Iraola’s side won both meetings 2-1, and football betting sites are offering 8/1 on a repeat result this time around.

The Blues have won just one of their last 10 Merseyside derbies, and that was in April 2024 when Jarrad Branthwaite and Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored in a 2-0 win at Goodison Park.

Other than that win, they have lost seven and drawn two, with both of those draws coming at home, and you can get 29/10 on a draw in this one.

With just two league defeats so far, against Manchester City and Arsenal, it’s easy to understand why Liverpool are the favourites at odds of 84/100 while Everton are 15/4 for the win.

With Tarkowski suspended too, things will be a lot harder up against a team that has scored 12 goals in their last four matches.

Everton vs Liverpool prediction 1: BTTS and Liverpool to win - 12/5 Bet365

Liverpool midfielder Florian Wirtz is finally showing the form that earned him a £116m move from Bayer Leverkusen, with three goals in his last three appearances.

Add his goals for Germany, and he’s scored six in his last five games, including a brace in the 5-0 win over the Netherlands.

As well as his two Premier League goals this season, he also has four assists and betting sites are offering 13/10 on him scoring or assisting at the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

FourFourTwo's dedicated FPL columnist, and one of the top players in the world, BigManBakar gives his captaincy verdict for GW12

I have changed my mind on the armband more times this week than I care to admit.

Usually one name stands out, but this time there are several players who could all justify the choice, and the one who normally walks in is the one I would most like to avoid.

Get this right and it could be worth serious ranking gains.

Erling Haaland: It's not often that Haaland is anything other than an automatic pick, but the trip to Arsenal makes me want to look elsewhere.

Arsenal have the strongest defence in the league by a distance, and their underlying numbers are the best for Expected Goals Conceded (xGC). Haaland can score against anyone, but I see his ceiling this week as a single goal. If there was ever a week to go different, this is it.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin: He is my favourite of the lot. Leeds host Coventry, probably the easiest fixture to call this weekend, and Daniel Farke's side will be full of confidence after that 4-1 win at Stamford Bridge.

Calvert-Lewin missed three big chances and hit the post in that game, which is not something he does often, so I wouldn't expect that sort of wastefulness to continue. The bookmakers project Leeds to score more than two goals and make him the most likely to score or assist.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Maxim De Cuyper: The next best option after Calvert-Lewin. It still sounds strange to say that the top scoring player in the game is a defender, but he leads all defenders for xG involvement and plays for the Brighton side with the most clean sheets.

He operates on the left-wing, out of position and shares some set pieces, so the Belgian offers real upside at both ends. Of the defensive captaincy punts, he is the one I prefer by some distance.

Bruno Fernandes: Probably the biggest differential on the list. He remains the most dependable Manchester United attacker and arrives off two attacking returns in the Champions League against Sporting. His underlying numbers are strong and he has penalties and set pieces to fall back on. The risk is that United blow hot and cold, so there is some volatility attached.

Nicolas Jackson: He has been consistent enough to be part of the conversation. Aston Villa face Ipswich, who are in the bottom three for xGC, and Jackson's goal involvements account for more than half of Villa's output while he is on the pitch.

Combined with a strong bonus profile, that matters for captaincy. Against that, Villa's attack has struggled in the last two games, he is not on penalties and could be taken off early. He is certainly viable, but the doubts are enough to push me elsewhere.

Pascal Gross: The highest scoring midfielder in the game by a distance, with set pieces and penalties and contributions at both ends of the pitch every week. He is a legitimate candidate in his own right. If I am going with a Brighton player though, I prefer De Cuyper because he has more explosive potential for a haul.

Cole Palmer: There are too many question marks to consider him, and his underlying data is poor.

Owners should probably keep him, since none of the premiums are performing and Nottingham Forest is a decent fixture where the odd penalty could help. As a captain, though, he is far too risky.

There is no obvious winner, but if I had to pick, Calvert-Lewin has the best mix of fixture, form and bookmaker backing. Take the shot if you can afford to be different.

#838. 90+9! Naderi scores late winner as Rangers move top

Rangers vs Falkirk. Scottish Premiership.

Ibrox StadiumAttendance: Attendance50,988.

Report as Rangers go top of the Premiership with a 2-1 win over Falkirk; Jacob Murrell put Falkirk in front before Kevin Kelsy came off the bench to head in a late Rangers equaliser; Ryan Naderi scored from the spot with a retaken penalty in added time to give Rangers an unlikely victory

Ryan Naderi's last-gasp penalty gave Rangers their 10th straight Premiership win as they stormed to the top of the table.

Jacob Murrell gave Falkirk a shock lead from the penalty spot after Tuur Rommens was penalised for appearing to tug back at Ethan Ross during a rare Falkirk first-half attack.

But Kevin Kelsy came off the bench to score a late equaliser before dramatic scenes deep into added time, after Ryan Naderi saw his penalty saved by Scott Bain, who was subsequently adjudged to have come off his line, meaning the penalty had to be retaken.

Naderi made no mistake at the second attempt as Rangers took all three points, giving them a two-point lead over Celtic, who are in action against Hearts on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

The home side dominated the first half with Naderi, Rommens, Findlay Curtis, Minsu Kim and Djeidi Gassama all going close in the first half hour.

Ivan Pandur was then forced into a brilliant point-blank save to deny Ross, but Rommens was adjudged to have fouled him, with the referee awarding a penalty after being advised to take a look at the challenge on the pitchside monitor.

Murrell made no mistake from the spot, calmly slotting in to give Falkirk the lead against the run of play.

Got Sky? Watch the Scottish Prem on your phone

Gassama and Minsu went close again either side of the break before Findlay Curtis thought he had got Rangers back on level terms just shy of the hour mark.

But VAR intervened, correctly ruling that Naderi had allowed the ball to run past the byline in the build-up to Curtis' strike.

Curtis then saw an effort deflected onto the crossbar, with Nico Raskin somehow managing to smash the ball over from all but four yards out in the ensuing goalmouth scramble.

Raskin missed two further chances before substitute Kelsy bagged a late equaliser for the home side.

Badredine Bouanani cut inside and whipped an inviting ball into the heart of the Falkirk box, and there was Kelsy to glance a header inside the far post to send Ibrox wild.

Rangers won a late penalty after Emmanuel Fernandez had his shirt tugged at a corner, but Naderi's spot-kick was brilliantly saved by Bain.

However, VAR intervened, with replays showing Bain had come off his line before Naderi struck the ball, giving the striker a chance to make amends.

And he did just that, rifling home from the spot on the second attempt as Rangers came from behind to win and extend their unbeaten run in all competitions to 15 matches.

"The game lasts 90-odd minutes for a reason and you've got to keep going. I'd like us to be winning games a lot more comfortably but as I've said before, I think there is a resilience to us.

"Nobody's playing their own game, nobody's playing for themselves, everybody's playing for each other. We're actually a really likeable bunch of boys.

"I don't need to like my players but I prefer to like them and I really love this team.

"I love how they are with each other and I actually feel that they all feel connected to getting the win. That is something that when the chips are down, you have to rely on that. It's not just your technique, it's not just your ability.

"The good thing for me, you see Ibrox absolutely full at the end. The fans believe it, I believe there are goals in us. The important thing for me is the players believe it."Falkirk boss John McGlynn:

"We ended up having to defend for pretty much the whole of the second half which wasn't in the plan.

"We held our own a bit in the first half but it's always difficult coming here. Given the circumstances coming here today, we didn't do as well as I would have liked.

"Then in the second half it was waves of attack. We had one really good chance, the only one we had and it was a really good chance which would have put us two goals up.

"I don't really have any issues with the scoreline as I think Rangers deserved to win the game and I haven't looked at any stats but they would heavily favour Rangers."

FourFourTwo tried out Be Your Best's state-of-the-art VR scanning technology - it was an illuminating experience into the mind of a top-level footballer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the basement of a central London WeWork this week, FourFourTwo slipped on a VR headset and stepped onto a virtual pitch.

It felt like living inside an interactively playable game of Football Manager - or recreating Guy Ritchie’s iconic late-2000s point-of-view Nike advert.

Within seconds the novelty wears off and the pressure is on. When a virtual teammate fizzes a pass toward your feet in the middle of a crowded midfield, you quickly realise just how hard it is to think like a top-level footballer.

Be Your Best (BYB) boast some of the most cutting-edge performance-enhancing technology on the market. Their virtual reality software is designed to train scanning, awareness and in-game intelligence.

Behind it lies nearly three decades of pioneering research by Norwegian sports psychologist Geir Jordet, who began logging how frequently players check their surroundings back in 1997 - armed with nothing more than a notebook and a VCR.

Scanning is the subtle, constant habit of taking mental snapshots of your environment before the ball arrives, and it's what separates good footballers from the greats.

Of the 117 players Jordet studied in his landmark research, the standout was Frank Lampard, who scanned an astonishing 6.2 times every 10 seconds before receiving possession. Lampard Snr. used to bark "Pictures! Pictures!" from the touchline during Frank Jnr.’s West Ham academy days, drilling into the future England international a habit that directly correlates with higher pass completion rates and a greater volume of forward passes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Timing, though, is everything. Scan at the wrong moment and you miss vital cues on the speed and direction of pressing defenders - FourFourTwo learned that the hard way, frequently dispossessed in traffic or making stray passes.

Inside the headset, BYB drop you directly into real on-field moments recreated from actual matches, complete with four distinct training modes and fresh scenarios released weekly.

Suddenly, you are in the boots of Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard - who famously asked developers to crank the simulation speed up to 120 per cent because standard 100 per cent match pace felt too easy. FFT was playing at 85 per cent. Show-off.

Built-in awareness tests freeze play, turning surrounding players into blank silhouettes, quizzing the user on which team each belongs to. When the ball finally arrives, you have a split second to pick out a pass or pull the trigger.

At the end of each round, the software delivers a brutally honest scorecard, at least that's how it felt to FFT. We were graded on our performance across the following metrics: BYB IQ, scan rate, scan timing, critical scans (checks made in the final moments before receiving the ball), decision-making and overall awareness.

Afterward, a bird’s-eye replay mode allows players and coaches to dissect every scenario from above, effectively handing professionals unlimited 'do-overs' to rehearse how they could have played a situation differently, all without physical fatigue or risking injury.

It is little wonder footballers have taken notice. In the past, Norwegian youth sides featuring Erling Haaland used the technology during their development, while Chelsea midfielder Romeo Lavia is an investor. On the consumer side, everyone from 10-year-old grassroots hopefuls practising in their living rooms to Real Madrid stars Endrick and Aurelien Tchouameni use BYB to sharpen their minds.

Meanwhile, clubs and federations, including Hoffenheim and the Portuguese FA, tap into BYB’s B2B side of things, which includes custom match-scenario builds for academies and Apollo, a separate analytical tool powered by synced 3D tracking and event data. Apollo lets club analysts step inside any player’s first-person POV to review flashpoints and decisions in full 3D.

After 30 minutes in Odegaard’s virtual boots, FFT had improved but we weren't quite at the level of a Xavi Hernandez with a head on a swivel - let's just say our BYB IQ left plenty to be desired.

Be Your Best is offering 30% off annual VR training subscriptions for Black Friday using promo code BF30.

#836. Relegation is coming for this embarrassment of a Manchester United team

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester United 0-4 Brentford: Mauricio Pochettino’s first home match in charge ended with a string of historic lows as the Bees won at Old Trafford for the first time since 1937

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Stretford End were just about to break into a chorus celebrating Michael Carrick, which probably was not how Mauricio Pochettino hoped his first game in charge of Manchester United at Old Trafford would end, when the Brentford fans produced their own taunt. It may have been more cutting than they realised.

“Four-nil again,” they chorused and, in different ways, it was. Erik ten Hag’s second game in charge of United brought a 4-0 defeat to the Bees. Keith Andrews’ side beat Everton 4-0 on Monday. More immediately, Pochettino has had two league games and they have ended in the same scoreline. First Liverpool, now Brentford. Four-nil again. “It doesn't look good when you lose 4-0 and 4-0,” admitted Pochettino. “We never expect this kind of result.”

There was a time when United dealt in 4-0 wins, not 4-0 losses. Not now. It was an embarrassment of a result for an embarrassment of a team. A half-empty Old Trafford booed the players off the pitch. New manager, same old rubbish, perhaps: although this was actually worse than Carrick’s last two games, which at least contained his comebacks against Roma and Aston Villa.

There was no new manager bounce; or if there was, it lasted for a first 11 minutes in which United played with ambition, attacked and had five shots. It instead became another record-breaking occasion. Brentford’s first victory at Old Trafford in 89 years was another historic low for United. It was the latest addition to a long list.

They can’t blame this one on the officials. Brentford were simply better: sharper in front of goal, quicker on the break and more resilient in defence. “We are a pretty special team,” said manager Keith Andrews. “It has been a special week.”

Not for United. The PA announcer, as is his wont, called United the greatest club in the world. They could be the last in the table on Sunday afternoon if Crystal Palace beat Hull at home. The ebullient Bees fans chorused about relegation. It feels ever more feasible.

This defence is not fit for purpose, as Pochettino is rapidly discovering. Harry Maguire was at least United’s greatest threat in attack, though that is an indictment of others.

Defensively, the dreadful statistics just mushroom, and not merely because United have now let in 40 goals this season. United have now conceded first in their last eight games. They have gone 2-0 down in seven of them. They became the first team in Premier League history to conceded two goals in six consecutive halves of football.

Then, ridiculously, they let in another two after the break. Make that seven. For the first time in 65 years, they have conceded at least four in three consecutive league games.

It was all the more damning as Brentford were without the suspended Igor Thiago. Instead, their second-choice striker was too much for United. Indeed, the 34-year-old Callum Wilson was even too quick for Leny Yoro; such were his struggles against the veteran, the Frenchman may wish his red card at Anfield was not rescinded.

After United’s deceptively good first 11 minutes, when Joshua Zirkzee was denied by Caoimhin Kelleher and Maguire headed on to the bar, Brentford started scoring the goals that means only Brighton have mustered more in the division this season and now, no one has conceded more than United.

First Wilson, picked up on a free transfer, twisted and turned away from Yoro and a backtracking Maguire. His shot went through Senne Lammens’ hands. Factor in Amad Diallo losing the ball and four United players were culpable, to various degrees. “We should not concede this goal,” said Pochettino.

United’s familiar vulnerabilities to the counter-attack were apparent in the second. Mikkel Damsgaard released Dango Ouattara, who was too quick for Lisandro Martinez. Yoro failed to track Wilson, who had a simple finish when the winger unselfishly squared the ball. “He took his goals brilliantly,” added Andrews. Wilson is up to 97 in his Premier League career, targeting 100.

United could cite their eventual tally of 25 shots in mitigation. In their frantic attempts to get back into the game, Kelleher denied Patrick Dorgu, though the Dane shot straight at him. Youri Tielemans curled a shot on to the bar. Keane Lewis-Potter cleared Maguire’s header off the line. Michael Kayode emulated him to deny Matheus Cunha. “I didn’t want it to be a comeback story,” said Andrews. It was not.

United were so open that they always looked liable to concede again. Kristoffer Ajer scored a third, poking home after United failed to concede a corner. Kevin Schade, who had missed a fine chance earlier, dinked in a shot after Kayode’s pass. “Four shots on target and we concede four goals,” lamented Pochettino. After Lammens’ mistakes in Lisbon, it got no better for him.

Nor did it for United. “It is so painful, the result,” said Pochettino. “We knew that this type of situation can happen when the confidence is low.” And that is the problem for United: the lows keep getting lower.

#835. An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

#834. Frick wins first match at Pittodrie as Aberdeen beat Dundee

Aberdeen vs Dundee. Scottish Premiership.

Pittodrie StadiumAttendance: Attendance15,334.

Report as new Aberdeen boss Mario Frick wins his first home game in charge; goals from Hicham Mahou and Kevin Nisbet give Aberdeen a 2-0 Scottish Premiership victory against Dundee

New Aberdeen boss Mario Frick made a winning Pittodrie debut as they beat Dundee 2-0 in an entertaining game played in awful conditions.

Hicham Mahou and Kevin Nisbet netted either side of the break as Aberdeen moved ahead of their visitors in the Scottish Premiership, while Nisbet also saw a first-half penalty saved.

Frick made two changes from the 3-2 defeat at Ibrox in midweek, the injured Nesta Guinness-Walker replaced by Mitchell Frame, while Mahou came in for Ayoub Mouloua.

Dundee also swapped out two men from their narrow defeat at Hibs, Idris Odutayo and Callum Jones replacing Matai Akinmboni and Joe Bevan.

A win for the visitors could, with results elsewhere, have moved Steven Pressley's side into the top six, and the visitors started well in horrendous conditions.

Joe Westley was slipped in by Jones as he seized on hesitation in the Aberdeen midfield, but Marius Muller pushed the low effort away strongly. The German goalkeeper denied the same player at the near post after just eight minutes, with Findlay Marshall testing Owen Goodman at the other end.

Aberdeen settled into the game and became more of a threat, and they should have been in front on 13 minutes when Marshall burst forward and slipped in Alexander Briedl, whose angled effort came back off the inside of the post.

Westley had another opportunity after slack play from Afeez Aremu, however the midfielder recovered well to spark a counter from which Brad Lyons' effort from distance was pushed away by a full-stretch Goodman.

Aberdeen were handed a golden opportunity to take the lead from the penalty spot midway through the first half. A VAR review concluded - perhaps somewhat harshly - Imari Samuels had handled in the area, and maybe there was a sense of justice done when Goodman denied the usually-reliable Nisbet.

The goalmouth action dried up for a while, but Aberdeen deservedly took the lead two minutes from the interval. A swift break forward saw Briedl pick out a slide-rule pass for Mahou, and the pacy Frenchman angled through Goodman's legs to open the scoring.

The lead was doubled early in the second half. Marshall was heavily involved, pulling back from the right for Nisbet who saw his shot spin away off a post. The play stayed alive and Briedl pulled back from the left for Marshall, who saw his effort parried away before Nisbet headed in from close range.

Dundee responded immediately and Samuels' strong run saw him go past Muller, but took him wide allowing Nicky Devlin to get back and clear off the line.

Just after the hour, Ashley Hay clashed with Jack Milne in the box - play initially went on before another VAR review confirmed no penalty to be awarded.

Milne was involved again a few minutes later, his wayward header from a Dundee corner being hooked away off the line by Frame.

Aberdeen were awarded a second penalty three minutes from time as Mouloua went down under what looked minimal contact at best from Joe Wright, but referee Ross Hardie was called over to review and overturned the on-field decision.

"It was very cold! I am very happy about the win, and the first clean sheet is very important because we said we want to improve our defending.

"I think it is a well-deserved win because we had a missed penalty and hit the post twice.

"I am very happy for the whole team, I think now it is turning also the confidence, but now we can enjoy the win.

"The boys defended with all they had so I am happy also for the back four. We conceded a lot of goals in the last games so it was very important and deserved our first clean sheet."

"I'm not going to sit here and try to pretend the results at present have been good enough. I accept that, but if I'm honest there was a lot out there that I really liked.

"I said on Tuesday that we restored some pride without being outstanding in any particular area, and I think we took another step forward today. I thought our energy and the intensity of our performance were good.

"Our confidence on the ball grew which is something we definitely need to improve on, but we created a lot of good moments against a very good Aberdeen team.

"I think we've played a lot worse than that and won games."

Former Liverpool centre-back Dejan Lovren has offered his thoughts on Virgil van Dijk's remaining time at Anfield

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Liverpool centre-back Dejan Lovren has admitted it will feel 'strange' when Virgil van Dijk eventually leaves Anfield, insisting the Dutchman deserves a fitting farewell whenever the time comes to part ways.

Lovren's role in the team was largely usurped by Van Dijk following the skipper's arrival on Merseyside in January 2018, who has since gone on to help the Reds lift both the Champions League and the Premier League title.

Speaking in an interview via Hajper, the Croatian international suggested that while Van Dijk could still earn a further 12-month contract extension if he maintains his current standards, both the club and player must ensure the timing of his eventual exit is right.

"It will be strange when Virgil van Dijk leaves Liverpool, but at some point it has to come to an end," Lovren said. "It’ll be important for him, the fans and the club that he leaves at the right time. If he stays at his level then you can see a one-year extension, but of course he’ll have to keep proving that on the pitch.

"But saying that, it’s so important that he gets a good farewell - he deserves it for what he has given to the club for so long, year after year. He has been at the very top.

"He is without doubt one of Liverpool’s greatest ever players. You just need to look at the stats. Look at what he achieved and what he won, it speaks for itself. How many times was he up for the Ballon d'Or or in the FIFPro World 11? It’s not just Liverpool, he's top of the tree."

Liverpool are already planning for life after their captain, and Lovren also weighed in on whether young defender Jeremy Jacquet has what it takes to fill Van Dijk's boots.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I hope Jacquet can be the next Van Dijk at Liverpool, but it's really important to realise why Van Dijk is at the top level, because of his consistency," Lovren added.

"It's as simple as that. If Jacquet is there for the next seven years, then we can talk about whether he deserves to stay there forever.

"But if he plays well this year and not well in the next six months, things will change. We know he has the ability, it's about consistency at the end. That's why top players are different from normal players."

Further up the pitch, Lovren is far more certain of Liverpool's long-term firepower, pointing to the chemistry between Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and his former Lyon teammate Bradley Barcola - as well as the eventual return of injured forward Hugo Ekitike.

"When Hugo Ekitike is back? These are beautiful problems, every coach wants that choice," Lovren added.

"Once he comes back alongside Isak, Wirtz, and Bradley, I believe they will have an amazing attack. Quality-wise, find me something better than what Liverpool have to offer."
