The former Arsenal striker believes it is time to cut ties with Renee Slegers with the Gunners lacking identity and leaders

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal would have already parted ways with Renee Slegers if this situation was happening with the men’s team, according to former Gunners striker Lianne Sanderson.

After 11 Women’s Super League games, Arsenal have just 15 points and sit sixth in the table, 12 points behind leaders Chelsea.

The Gunners’ latest setback came against West Ham, with a sixth home draw of the season, a result that left striker Alessia Russo in tears at the Emirates.

Sanderson was part of the Arsenal side that became European champions in 2007, with Slegers’ Arsenal side historically repeating the feat in May 2025.

The Dutch coach took charge on an interim basis following Jonas Eidevall’s departure, before being permanently appointed in January, becoming European champions four months later.

Following their triumph in Lisbon, they finished second in the league last campaign, four points off champions Manchester City.

“I've been a big advocate for Renee to stay in the job, but I feel like after the Lyon game [a 2-0 home defeat in the Champions League], I just felt this feeling in my stomach that it’s time [to part ways],” Sanderson told FourFourTwo.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“That was probably the most defeated I have felt. The players weren't fighting, they had just shown nothing, there was no identity.

“I love Renee, everyone loves Renee. But, I feel like if this was in the men's game, they'd have already cut ties.

“I actually feel gutted about the situation, because I have close ties and good relationships with everyone at Arsenal.

“The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.

“Six weeks ago, I believed she could turn it around. But the reality is, we are now in another international break and it’s the same story. To be drawing with teams like West Ham, Birmingham and Crystal Palace is not acceptable, that’s no disrespect to those teams.”

Arsenal made several additions to their squad including Lioness Georgia Stanway and World Cup and two-time Champions League winner Ona Batlle over the summer, but also lost a number of experienced players, including Katie McCabe and Beth Mead.

“There is something to be said about the types of personalities like Katie McCabe and Beth Mead,” Sanderson added. “Losing them is not the only reason Arsenal are struggling but Beth is a quiet type of leader and Katie is…you need a Katie in your team.

“Someone who is a nightmare to play against but will do anything it takes to win. You need those types of players. When I see Arsenal right now, I don’t see nastiness.

“My old captain, Jayne Ludlow, would do anything for us to win, putting your body on the line, and I'm not seeing that. Players have to take responsibility too.

“If Arsenal don't qualify for the Champions League, that will be a big, big, big blow.”

If Arsenal were to part ways with Slegers, Sanderson pointed to Nick Cushing as a potential option for a replacement manager, also saying she would love someone like Canada manager Casey Stoney to come in.

“Nick is the type of manager they need, someone with that personality,” she added. “I would welcome a personality like Nick Cushing, who knows what it takes to manage at the top and has good player management.”

With Arsenal all but out of the title race, Sanderson believes it will go down to the wire between Manchester City and Chelsea, tipping the Blues to win it.

While she can’t see third-placed London City Lionesses winning this year, she is impressed by their upward trajectory and believes the side who signed Alexia Putellas in the summer are ahead of where they are expected to be and could be contenders next season.

London City owner Michele Kang also owns NWSL side Washington Spirit, who lost the Championship to Kansas City Current, missing out in the final for a third year running, leading to the dismissal of head coach Adrián González.

“Michele Kang doesn't hang around,” Sanderson added. “Washington Spirit just lost at the weekend and the coach got fired the next day.

“The demand from her, it might be ruthless, but that's why she's successful. If Michele Kang was at Arsenal, this wouldn't be happening. That's the difference.”

Lianne Sanderson was speaking to FourFourTwo via polymarket promo code.

Ayisha Gulati is the women’s football writer at FourFourTwo. She covers the WSL, UWCL and international football, and has interviewed leading names including Alexia Putellas, Leah Williamson and Bunny Shaw. She enjoys telling stories that capture the personalities, passion and excitement of the women’s game, on and off the pitch.

#831. Mauricio Pochettino admits job ‘tougher than expected’ after Man United slump to historic low - reaction

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester United 0-4 Brentford: Callum Wilson’s double and late goals from Kristoffer Ajer and Kevin Schade deepens the misery at Old Trafford – and the hosts could finish the weekend bottom if Crystal Palace beat Hull

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino admitted his start to life at Manchester United had been tougher than he expected after his side were thrashed 4-0 in each of his first two Premier League games in charge.

Brentford’s first win at Old Trafford since 1937 followed Liverpool’s 4-0 victory over Pochettino’s United last week and left the Argentinian’s team languishing 19th in the table. United could even finish the weekend bottom – with eight points from 12 games – if Crystal Palace beat Hull tomorrow.

“We are disappointed and of course it's so painful, the result,” said Pochettino after Callum Wilson struck twice and Kristoffer Ajer and Kevin Schade added late goals. Remarkably, they have also become the first side to concede at least two goals in seven consecutive halves of Premier League football.

“Tough moment, of course. Maybe you say to me, ‘tougher than you expect?’ Of course, yes, because we never expect this type of result. But that is the reality and we need to accept the reality. We are here for that.”

Pochettino’s side had their chances and started the match on top, but they were punished for not taking their opportunities. United’s issues in defence were highlighted again as they conceded two goals or more for the eighth consecutive game, while extending their winless run in the Premier League to a 10th game.

Pochettino argued that he could not have been expected to have an immediate impact and that he has to carry on working with the same set of players, rather than getting rid of them all.

“Yesterday I was talking about being nice, being good, I don't know, or now it's about what the people expect from a coach that arrived ten days ago is to change twenty-five players, twenty-six players,” he said.

“Do you think that we are going to help Manchester United blaming the player because of that situation that we are now living? That circumstance, it's only players?”

Follow live updates from Man Utd v Brentford, below

Manchester United started well today and could have taken the lead. Mauricio Pochettino agrees it shows how low their confidence levels are that their heads dropped after Callum Wilson opened the scoring.

“The problem happened when we conceded,” Pochettino told Sky Sports. “And that is about building that trust and confidence in whether we can see it, but we need to keep playing in the same way. But that is normal because it's a situation that is affecting the emotional area - in psychology.”

Manchester United’s players were chants of “you’re not fit to wear the shirt” as they attempted to applaud the fans at full-time of the 4-0 defeat to Brentford.

In response to that criticism, Pochettino said the players have his support.

“We understand the fans. We understand, and the players, first, understand the fans. But we need to care,” Pochettino said.

"We need to stay all together. We need, you know, our fans being focused in help the player because the player need to perform and need to play.

“Of course, we are the first to understand. The player is the first to understand. We are all disappointed for different reasons. Everyone can have different opinions about why the situation is the situation that we are living in now.

“But the most important thing now is to put all our energy into improving things.”

Mauricio Pochettino admitted his start to life at Manchester United had been tougher than he expected after his side were thrashed 4-0 in each of his first two league games in charge.

Brentford’s first win at Old Trafford since 1937 followed Liverpool’s 4-0 victory over Pochettino’s United last week and left the Argentinian’s team languishing 19th in the Premier League.

Pochettino said: “Tough moment, of course. Maybe you say to me, ‘tougher than you expect?’ Of course, yes, because we never expect this type of result. But that is the reality and we need to accept the reality. We are here for that.”

There was a time when United dealt in 4-0 wins, not 4-0 losses. Not now. It was an embarrassment of a result for an embarrassment of a team. A half-empty Old Trafford booed the players off the pitch. New manager, same old rubbish, perhaps: although this was actually worse than Michael Carrick’s last two games, which at least contained his comebacks against Roma and Aston Villa.

There was no new manager bounce; or if there was, it lasted for a first 11 minutes in which United played with ambition, attacked and had five shots. It instead became another record-breaking occasion. Brentford’s first victory at Old Trafford in 89 years was another historic low for United. It was the latest addition to a long list.

Mauricio Pochettino is just the third Manchester United manager to lose his first two league matches in charge.

The other two were John Chapman in, in 1921, and Erik ten Hag, who also lost 4-0 to Brentford in 2022.

“I think now it's about to be calm. It's of course feeling the pain, the responsibility.

"But in the same time, that is a reality. We need to accept the reality and be aware of the reality and change.

“we need to be strong, stay strong, and like our coaching staff, we are going to push the player to keep improving.”

Brentford manager Keith Andrews, speaking to BBC Match of the Day after their first win at Old Trafford since 1937.

"Slightly surreal if I am honest. We have been keen to enjoy the journey. We want to be really ambitious but the level of humility of where we are. I think we can achieve special things because I think it is a special group. It has been a good week and the lads have been excellent."

Can Brentford now push and be in the hunt for the Champions League places?

Mauricio Pochettino, speaking to Sky Sports: “Well, I think it doesn't look good, no, when you lose 4-0 and 4-0 with the circumstances for the first game in Liverpool and today here at Old Trafford.

“We need to keep being united and we need to stay all together and we need to, you know, try to fix and improve. And we need improve. We need improve. That is our circumstance. It's our reality. There's nothing to say, nothing to justify, this type of situation.

“It's the situation that we knew when we arrived. And yes, it's only a matter of time.”

Manchester United play seven times in December. It’s Newcastle away on Wednesday, then Coventry at home next week. Will that become must-win if they can’t get three points at St James’ Park?

Brentford had lost all five trips to Old Trafford since returning to the English top-flight. On their sixth, they won at Manchester United for the first time since 1937.

They are fifth, and Keith Andrews’ side finally have an away win this season after four draws and a defeat from their first five games on the road this season.

It’s their first away win in the Premier League since winning at Burnley in February.

#830. Campbell gets hat-trick as St Johnstone rout Dundee Utd

Dundee United vs St Johnstone. Scottish Premiership.

CalForth Construction Arena at Tannadice ParkAttendance: Attendance9,186.

Josh Campbell claims hat-trick as St Johnstone trounce Dundee United 7-2; the visitors emphatically turned the game around to claim their record win at Tannadice, having gone a goal behind after just 10 minutes

St Johnstone ran riot against Dundee United, hitting a magnificent seven goals to set a new record for their highest-ever win at Tannadice.

Josh Campbell helped himself to a hat-trick as Saints netted further goals through Kai Fotheringham, Enes Alic, Joel Cotterill and Sam Stanton with Daniel Bennie and Josh Rawlins scoring for the hosts.

The result ended United's eight-game unbeaten run with Saints moving up to fifth in the table ahead of their Tayside rivals on goal difference.

The Terrors opened the scoring with their first meaningful attack of the game in the 10th minute. Skipper Dylan Tait delivered a superb, long pass into the feet of Jesse Randall who raced through on goal before cutting the ball back to Bennie who netted from close range.

However, Saints did not have to wait long for the equaliser in the 20th minute. Terrors centre-half Bert Esselink lunged in on Fotheringham inside the box with the Saints player crashing to the turf and referee Matthew MacDermid pointing to the spot.

Campbell stepped up and although United keeper Jack Walton dived the right way, the penalty flew into the bottom corner of the net for the on-loan Hibs player's fourth goal in five games.

And the match turned completely on its head just a minute later with Saints breaking up the park and Fotheringham producing a calm finish past Walton.

Got Sky? Watch the Scottish Prem on your phone

Fotheringham had another chance shortly after but Walton saved at his near post and then Bennie came close to adding his second, but Saints keeper Toby Steward produced a vital diving save.

However, St Johnstone added a third in the 35th minute when Alic cut in from the left and fired an unstoppable shot that flew past the helpless Walton.

Saints then netted their fourth goal in the 45th minute and it was the pick of the bunch so far, with Cotterill hitting a ferocious drive from all of 25 yards that seemed to deceive Walton before hitting the back of the net.

United would have been looking for a response after the break but instead it was St Johnstone who extended their lead. Esselink made a hash of a clearance at a corner with the ball falling to Stanton - another former United player - who sent a looping header past Walton.

The Terrors then pulled a goal back and it was another stunning strike from all of 30 yards by Rawlins that rocketed into the back of Steward's net.

However, St Johnstone hit their sixth in the 63rd minute with Fotheringham teeing up Campbell for an easy finish.

Campbell then completed his hat-trick in the 92nd minute with a clinical low shot past the shell-shocked Walton.

"Going 1-0 down away from home and not having a striker, it could have been a different story. I would have been sitting here answering questions like, 'How can you come here and not play a striker?'.

"My players know how we work and we have the profile of players to do it. We thought this was the best way to cause damage to them.

"In coaching we can only guess what will happen - today we guessed right. But whatever game plan you have, you have to totally invest in it. That's what we did.

"I could see the way the boys were competing with each other in training that we were on a high level. Josh was one of those boys - I'm so happy he got this hat-trick."Dundee United boss Jim Goodwin:

"I don't think anyone would have predicted that kind of scoreline. We had one defeat in 10 prior to this afternoon.

"It seemed as if every mistake we made was punished. Five of the seven goals we conceded were from our possession when we turned over the ball cheaply.

"They ran over the top of us at times, which I haven't had to say in recent weeks. It's a really humbling afternoon for us all and a major reality check."

"If you don't do the basics well enough, these are the kind of results that can come.

"It's a really difficult one to explain. It's an embarrassing defeat.

"We have to make sure we try and put this one behind us as quickly as we possibly can. We can all accept defeats but there is a certain manner to today's defeat that we can't accept."

A former US international has had his say on the Argentine's move to Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino has had a difficult start to his time at Manchester United, but some in the USA are questioning why he was allowed to join the club at all.

Pochettino followed up a 4-0 loss at Liverpool in his first game with the Red Devils with a Champions League draw at Sporting in midweek, having quit the US national team to move to Old Trafford.

The Argentine took charge of the USA for the final two times during the recent international break, guiding them to two wins over Haiti.

Pochettino was appointed as USA boss in 2024 after leaving Chelsea, then guided the Stars and Stripes to the last 16 of this summer’s World Cup.

His USA side started the tournament in scintillating fashion and won their group, although eventually succumbed to Belgium.

It had initially seemed like Pochettino would step down at the end of that tournament to pursue a return to club football, but instead he penned a new four-year deal in August, in theory taking him to the 2030 World Cup.

There was a catch, though – the contract contained a buyout clause, which Manchester United activated within only three months.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The insertion of that clause has since been the subject of some criticism Stateside, and former US goalkeeper Brad Friedel admits he is disappointed with how the last few months have unfolded.

“I think he did very well as US boss,” Friedel told FFT, speaking in association with APWin. “He’s a good manager, he’s incredible.

“I don’t understand the whole thing of US Soccer signing him again and giving him an out on a four-year contract. It leaves a huge gaping hole for the US.

“I think the US got themselves into a situation and here we are, now having to hire a new head coach going into a four-year cycle.”

There will be more from Friedel in FourFourTwo soon.

#828. Flying Leeds achieve five-year Premier League first with win over Coventry

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Leeds 3-0 Coventry: Sean Longstaff scored twice after Dominic Calvert-Lewin opened the scoring at Elland Road

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Sean Longstaff scored twice and created another as Leeds beat Coventry 3-0 at Elland Road to seal a third successive top-flight win for the first time in five years.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin celebrated signing his new contract this week by heading home the opening goal and Longstaff struck either side of the interval to keep Daniel Farke’s side on an upward curve after last week’s thumping win at Chelsea.

Leeds had not won three successive top-flight games since they ended the 2020-21 campaign under Marcelo Bielsa with a four-game winning run, while their fifth league win this season lifted them up to sixth in the table.

Ethan Ampadu and Jayden Bogle both fired off target from outside the penalty area, either side of a standing ovation for Gary Speed to mark the 15th anniversary of the former Whites midfielder’s death.

But Leeds were back-pedalling when Sidiki Cherif raced on to a long ball over the top, forcing Nico Elvedi into a superb last-ditch tackle.

Leeds then began to stretch Coventry’s defence. Noah Okafor fired wide and saw another shot blocked before Leeds forced a succession of corners without forcing Coventry goalkeeper Carl Rushworth into a save.

James Justin was crowded out and Ampadu lashed over the crossbar from in front of goal.

The home side’s pressure was rewarded though with two goals in four minutes just before half-time.

Longstaff’s excellent free-kick was met by Calvert-Lewin’s towering header – the striker’s sixth league goal of the season – and the former Newcastle midfielder’s shot took a big deflection off Tatsuhiro Sakamoto to wrong-foot Rushworth and put Leeds 2-0 up.

Leeds went close to increasing their lead early in the second period.

Calvert-Lewin was thwarted by Rushworth’s diving save, Okafor curled a right-footed shot inches wide and Ao Tanaka’s effort from the edge of the box span to safety after a deflection.

The third goal was brilliantly created by Gabriel Gudmundsson’s back-heeled pass inside the box for Longstaff to sweep home his second in the 66th minute.

Rushworth’s fine save with his legs denied Leeds a fourth after Calvert-Lewin’s clever pass sent Bogle in one-on-one.

Leeds’ rearguard had been rarely troubled by a Coventry side which had won four of their previous seven matches and Brandon Thomas-Asante’s shot on the turn, which was well blocked by Elvedi, offered only temporary respite.

Home substitute Harry Wilson went close to his first Leeds goal with a curling effort from 20 yards and Calvert-Lewin’s 77th-minute replacement Lukas Nmecha, saw his angled shot blocked by Stephen Mfuni.

#827. Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure

As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.

As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.

For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.

Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.

That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.

In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.

As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.

Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.

"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.

But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.

"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said.

That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.

In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.

As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.

"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.

This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.

That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.

Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.

Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.

But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.

A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.

Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation.

Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.

Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.

Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.

The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.

Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.

"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said.

Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.

For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.

Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.

#826. All Blacks bite back in Nations Championship dismantling of England

Tries: George (75) Penalties: Slade (3)

Tries: Sititi (17), Roigard (46) Conversions: Mo'unga (18,47) Penalties: Mo'unga (41,43,54,66)

England vs New Zealand Nations Championship 4:40pm Saturday 28th November

New Zealand bounced back from their record 25-point defeat to England to stun Steve Borthwick's charges a week on with a 26-8 Nations Championship victory at Allianz Stadium Twickenham.

England actually scored the opening points via a long-range Henry Slade penalty in the third minute, but did not trouble the scoreboard again in torrential Twickenham rain until the 75th minute - hooker Jamie George scoring a maul try.

The All Blacks scored tries in either half through No 8 Wallace Sititi and scrum-half Cam Roigard - the latter a stunning finish in the corner - as Dave Rennie's side produced a thorough dismantling of the hosts.

Fly-half Richie Mo'unga also kicked superbly for the visitors, landing both conversions and four penalties against an ill-disciplined England, who were shown yellow cards to lock Alex Coles (high tackle) and replacement back-row Henry Pollock (offside, repeat team penalties).

England - Tries: George (75). Pens: Slade (3).

New Zealand - Tries: Sititi (17), Roigard (46). Cons: Mo'unga (18,47). Pens: Mo'unga (41,43,54,66).

New Zealand lock Scott Barrett was also shown yellow late on for repeat team penalties, but by then the All Blacks were home and hosed as far as the result was concerned against a shocked England.

As if to sum up England's miserable day, Marcus Smith near comically ended up on his backside while attempting the straightforward conversion for George's late try, leaving England stuck in single digits for points for the first time in over three years (August 2023).

Less than a minute into the contest, New Zealand's starting scrum-half Cortez Ratima was penalised for failing to release in a jackal attempt on halfway, with England's Slade stepping up to notch three points off the tee from distance.

Two big chances then came and went for the hosts. First, a maul collapse handed England a lineout deep in the 22, only for Anton Segner to rise and steal it, before Coles then spilled the ball on the run within the 22 as a try looked likely.

The All Blacks made England pay for such profligacy, with Rieko Ioane and Ratima breaks paving the way for Sititi to finish strongly from close range in the 17th minute.

Mo'unga converted for the full haul, with England then suffering two further pointless visits to the New Zealand 22 - the second particularly costly as Slade kicked dead with a penalty kick from hand.

England were then reduced to 14 six minutes from half-time with Coles sin-binned for a head-on-head tackle on opposite number Fabian Holland.

Despite missing out via a five-metre lineout maul, New Zealand would stretch their lead to seven before the break, as Mo'unga struck over after Tommy Freeman had cheaply kicked the ball away to deny the visitors the chance to take a Roigard 50:22 quickly.

The second half started poorly for England from the off as they knocked on the restart, and though Freddie Steward produced a crunching tackle on Damian McKenzie, a breakdown penalty saw Mo'unga stretch the lead to 10 points.

Coles returned from his sin-bin shortly after to restore England to the full complement, but within moments the All Blacks blew out the score-board through Roigard's fabulous try after Ollie Chessum gave away a maul penalty.

Mo'unga added the difficult extras too for a 17-point lead, and though Borthwick made a raft of changes to attempt to alter things, Mo'unga added more points to the total with another penalty soon after as England kept infringing.

A remarkable piece of Scott Barrett defence held up Ben Curry to end a period of huge England pressure, while two very poor kicks out of hand followed from Marcus Smith, both too long and marked by New Zealand under little pressure, with the crowd booing in reply.

Instead, New Zealand would score again through the boot of Mo'unga next after the hosts were again reduced to 14 with Pollock shown yellow into the final quarter.

George added a try for England in what remained, but it was of scant consolation, while Slade knocked on in the corner as they sought a second in the final few moments.

"We just weren't good enough today, no excuses. As individuals, as a collective, we weren't good enough and the result reflected that.

"A lot of these things [differences in performance] come down to accuracy and execution. We put pressure on ourselves, gave away territory and put ourselves in trouble.

"We've done a lot of good stuff in this campaign. We were flying in the first three games, today was a bit trickier.

"We're not the finished article, we've always known that. We need to take our medicine today and come back stronger for the Six Nations."

England head coach Steve Borthwick told ITV:

"Full credit to New Zealand. The conditions were difficult and they played them better than we did.

"They were dominant in terms of territory, and that gave them scoring chances. They executed the kicking game much better than we did, we need to look very closely at that.

"You've got to take your chances, there were too many times when we had time in their 22 and didn't come away with points.

"There was a large swing of penalties against us that aided New Zealand, we need to get to the cause of why there were so many in a row."

New Zealand scrum-half and player of the match Cam Roigard told ITV:

"I'm a little speechless, it's awesome. We had a chance to bounce back from a very poor performance last week, and credit to everyone involved. There was a lot of pressure, we needed to respond and we did that, so we're really proud.

"We got the mindset right. Built belief through the week. Trained well and made sure we did everything right, so we were at our best mentally come kick-off. Credit to the coaching staff because a change to our structure in the week paid off.

"We've tested our depth a lot. I don't know how many injuries we've had. There are so many takeaways and learnings because there are so many things we did well throughout the year."

England are next in action during the 2027 Six Nations in February, when they start with a huge Test against Ireland in Dublin at the Aviva Stadium on Friday February 5 (8.10pm kick-off).

New Zealand now enter their offseason and are not in action again until April 25 2027 when they face Australia at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane.

Australia are hosting the 2027 Rugby World Cup between October 1-November 13.

#824. Rangers deny Falkirk at the death to replace Celtic at Premiership summit

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Rangers 2-1 Falkirk: Naderi’s retaken penalty finally ended the resistance of the in-form visitors

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ryan Naderi’s last-gasp penalty sent Rangers to the top of the Scottish Premiership after a remarkable late recovery edged out Falkirk 2-1 at Ibrox.

The hosts stretched their unbeaten run to 15 games but it was an afternoon of drama and frustration for the Light Blues, who had to fight back from Jacob Murrell’s first-half penalty.

Derek McInnes’ side now sit two points clear of Celtic, who have the chance to dislodge their rivals when they face Hearts on Sunday.

Deniss Melniks was first into the book for clattering into Nico Raskin before Scott Bain managed to push away a low shot from Tuur Rommens as Rangers turned the screw on the visitors. Findlay Curtis was next to try his luck with a curling strike which was deflected inches past the far post.

For all of that dominance, Ethan Ross found space to stab in a shot which required keeper Ivor Pandur to pull of a stunning stop to turn the winger’s effort past a post.

All eyes turned to referee Ryan Lee as VAR flagged up a pull of the jersey by Rommens on Murrell with the whistler pointing to the spot after a touchline check.

Murrell dispatched the kick and Rangers were shell-shocked as the striker made it eight goals in eight games.

Rangers looked to have levelled in the 57th minute as Curtis calmly slotted home Naderi’s cutback and Ibrox breathed a sigh of relief – only for VAR to conclude the ball had gone out of play in the build-up.

Curtis then cracked a shot against the bar before Naderi’s goalbound effort was clawed away by Bain as the hosts laid siege on Falkirk’s goal.

The contest should have been settled in the 69th minute when CJ Fodrey found himself free inside the box and, with only Pandur to beat, the striker tamely rolled his effort into the keeper’s arms.

The leveller arrived five minutes from time as Kevin Kelsy met a Badredine Bouanani cross to flick a header home and then the search began for the hosts in their bid for a winner.

It arrived from the spot in the fifth minute of added time as VAR once again spotted foul play and Naderi’s weak attempt was easily gathered by Bain.

His blushes were spared as he was allowed a second chance after Bain was off his line for the initial spot-kick, and the striker sparked wild celebrations with his winner.

#822. Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend

World No. 1 tennis player Alexander Zverev is facing a new lawsuit related to a domestic abuse trial. The lawyer for his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, told DW what the allegations are against the German player.

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."

Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."

Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

Bournemouth have won 10 on the bounce across all competitions for the first time in the club's history - their incredible form is proof they are the template for teams everywhere

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bournemouth's nine-game winning streak faced one of its sternest tests in Spain on Thursday night.

Marco Rose's men found themselves trailing to an Iago Aspas opener at Balaidos and reduced to 10 men following Bafode Diakite’s first-half dismissal, but refused to buckle.

Second-half strikes from Alvaro Rodríguez and Rayan sealed a remarkable Europa League comeback, extending a run of form that has seen the Cherries sweep aside AC Milan, Manchester United, Aston Villa and the like.

Away from the Vitality Stadium, Bournemouth’s form hasn't received the wider acclaim it warrants - perhaps because they aren't a 'big six' club.

Context makes this run all the more extraordinary because only 18 years ago, in the summer of 2008, Bournemouth were staring into the abyss at the bottom of League Two, slapped with a 17-point deduction after failing to exit administration. The club was fighting to remain in the Football League.

The Cherries of present day are a winning machine, domestically and on the continent, even after losing influential manager Andoni Iraola to Liverpool in the summer.

The success of their dugout transition comes down to decisive governance. When it became apparent that Iraola had outgrown the club, owner and chairman Bill Foley - the American businessman who bought 100 per cent of the club from Maxim Demin via Black Knight Football Club in December 2022 - and president of football operations Tiago Pinto moved early.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Rose’s appointment was rubber-stamped well before pre-season began, giving the former RB Leipzig and Borussia Dortmund boss a full summer to embed.

Under Foley and Pinto, Bournemouth’s recruitment machine has become the envy of most Premier League peers. In recent windows, their scouting network has consistently uncovered high-upside talent capable of generating massive resale value, from Illia Zabarnyi and Dean Huijsen to Milos Kerkez, before reinvesting shrewdly to build a squad that is now brimming with depth.

Rose now presides over a balanced group with what feels like at least two Premier League-level options in every position. It blends seasoned Premier League campaigners like Lewis Cook, Ryan Christie and Tyler Adams with European pedigree in new centre-back Antonio Silva, plus young flair in Amine Adli and Rayan.

Perhaps most surprising of all, this record-breaking 10-game winning run has been achieved without talismanic forward Eli Junior Kroupi, which is a testament to the collective strength the club has forged.

Unlike Brighton’s Tony Bloom or Brentford’s Matthew Benham, Bournemouth have not relied on an owner with a background in professional gambling, analytics and mathematical models. Foley’s multi-club network and Pinto’s acumen as a top football executive has combined traditional scouting, a bit of data analytics, but most importantly decisive succession planning and smart squad-building.

For clubs up and down the English league pyramid, Bournemouth are proof that you don't need state-backed billions or algorithms to punch above your weight. With coherent leadership, aligned recruitment and an acknowledgement of the need to plan two steps ahead, even a club once deducted 17 points in the fourth tier looks on course to maybe even conquer Europe.

#820. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

#819. 'Nothing will change at Manchester United until owners leave' Lianne Sanderson on the Glazers at Old Trafford

The former England international believes Manchester United's problems go far beyond what any new manager can fix

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United's problems will not be solved until the Glazers leave the club, according to former England international Lianne Sanderson.

Despite feeling optimistic about Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment, Sanderson believes the ownership situation leaves a big obstacle for managers to have success at Old Trafford.

Manchester United currently sit 19th in the Premier League table with just eight points from 11 games, and the club's struggles have left lifelong supporter Sanderson feeling increasingly disconnected from a team she has followed since childhood.

With Manchester United languishing in the relegation zone, Sanderson believes the problems run much deeper than the performances on the pitch.

Since Sir Alex Ferguson left in 2013, Manchester United have had 12 different managers. Michael Carrick’s departure earlier this month was followed by the appointment of Mauricio Pochettino, someone who is a friend of Sanderson.

“Nothing is going to change until the ownership leave and that's the reality of the situation,” Sanderson said. “You can't blame the coach.

"It wasn't Michael Carrick's fault. I love Poch, he's a good friend of mine and I want him to succeed.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"But I don't think they fully realise how big of a job this is going to be. I think every new manager thinks they can come into Man United and be that saviour.

"But the ownership are the biggest problem. Since INEOS came in, there's not been progress. I felt excited when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came in as a minority owner, but the Glazers are the biggest problem.

"Until they go, Manchester United are going to be in this situation."

Sanderson's frustration is particularly personal given her lifelong connection to the club.

Despite being part of Arsenal’s Champions League winning team in 2007, the former striker has been a United fan since childhood and said she would have loved to finish her playing career at United, had the club established a women's team earlier.

“I feel really disassociated with Man United right now, I just feel so gutted with where our club is at,” Sanderson added.

“Manchester United is like my religion. I often go in the away end because I love the club and I love being with the fans, it’s more meaningful.

“When I was five and I saw Eric Cantona play, I fell in love with Man United. That's why I love the club.

"It would have been easier for me to support Arsenal, obviously. It's a bit awkward when I go in the away end at the Emirates and some of the stewards recognise me.

"It's funny that they've got my picture outside the Emirates and I'm walking into the away end!"

Despite her concerns, Sanderson remains hopeful that Pochettino can turn things around, although she believes significant recruitment will be required.

The former England international suggested there are only around four players in the current squad worthy of keeping.

"I hope Pochettino can be the one to change things, I'm optimistic,” she added. “It can't get any worse, but the team are fighting relegation and that's the reality.

"I saw someone the other day say: ‘Would you take relegation in order to get the ownership out?’ That’s how strongly the fanbase feel about this and I never thought I'd ever feel that way.

"But I hope Poch can turn it around. They need a big transfer window to do that."

#818. Kilmarnock ease fears with thumping win at fellow strugglers St Mirren

St Mirren vs Kilmarnock. Scottish Premiership.

The Marbill Coaches StadiumAttendance: Attendance6,482.

Report as Kilmarnock earn emphatic win against fellow strugglers St Mirren; Tyreece John-Jules scores twice with Joe Hugill and Cathal McCarthy also on target for Kilmarnock; Eseosa Sule scored for the home side

Kilmarnock eased their relegation fears with a big 4-1 win over fellow strugglers St Mirren in Paisley.

A double from Tyreece John-Jules and second-half goals from Joe Hugill and Cathal McCarthy secured a first victory for Neil McCann's side in six attempts.

Kilmarnock remain bottom of the Premiership but are now only two points behind St Mirren who had drawn level just before half-time through Eseosa Sule.

Saints had the first chance but Killian Phillips' weak header failed to trouble Nico Mantl. Killie were next to threaten but Hugill's long-range effort was gathered by Jacob Chapman during an uneventful opening period.

The visitors, though, did move in front after 25 minutes. Phillips conceded a soft corner and, from Greg Kiltie's delivery, John-Jules was unmarked to head past Chapman.

The away team then nearly repeated the trick, with Robbie Deas' header from Kiltie's corner saved on the line.Hugill had another chance to stretch Kilmarnock's lead but his effort was saved by Chapman.

St Mirren should have drawn level after 38 minutes. Ismeal Kabia's cutback picked out Phillips only for the Irishman to strike the crossbar. Samuel Ramos leapt to meet the bouncing ball but also headed against the frame of the goal.

Saints did finally break through shortly before half-time. Ramos laid the ball off to Sule who finished well.

The home side began the second half on the attack with Phillips again heading into Mantl's arms.

Killie threatened again with Kiltie's run and shot diverted wide by Phillips before Ryan Carr nodded George Stanger's header off the line.

The visitors, though, would not be denied and scored three times in just six minutes to make sure of the victory. The first went to John-Jules who applied a composed finish after the St Mirren defence had failed to deal with a ball into their box.

Barely a minute later and Kilmarnock found themselves 3-1 ahead when Hugill sprinted clear before executing a precise lob over the goalkeeper.

It was all Kilmarnock now and a fourth goal made sure of the win. St Mirren again failed to deal with a corner, and after John-Jules sent a header against the crossbar, McCarthy was able to nod in from close range.

"I'm really pleased for everybody. It has been a tough time. I've never shied away from that. I don't think we've got enough points that probably our players deserved at times but you need to stitch it together.

"I'm so happy for the guys because it's not easy playing under pressure. You've got to embrace it as a professional athlete because it's going to come.

"I've been steadfast, as we all have as a staff, that this sort of performance has been coming.

"We understand the nature of it and the gap that could have opened up between ourselves and St Mirren (to eight points). The reason why we're celebrating is because everybody worked so hard for that today."

"I feel their (the supporters) frustration and their anger.

"They're paying fans and they've got every right to vent that towards me. I understand that, but no one's hurting with it more than I am.

"I know what we've been doing right now hasn't been good enough and it's up to me to fix that. But I also understand how it works.

"I keep belief in my ability, what we can do and what we can bring to it. And the players are feeling the same.

"We know that that wasn't good enough. We have to rectify it but we have to do it quickly."

#817. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

#815. Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI

Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.

Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share.

The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

Arsenal legend Thierry Henry expects his former employers to become back-to-back Premier League champions this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal legend Thierry Henry claims his former club are the only side currently showing control in the Premier League title race, dismissing the hype around Liverpool while pointing to high-flying Brighton as an overlooked threat.

Mikel Arteta’s side sit clear at the summit heading into Sunday’s showdown against Manchester City at the Emirates Stadium, where a victory would hand the Gunners a sizeable cushion over one of their fiercest rivals.

While Liverpool’s 4-0 demolition of Manchester United last weekend, and Man City's faltering form, led some pundits to anoint Andoni Iraola’s Reds as Arsenal’s closest challengers, Henry believes the weekly narrative around title contenders has been too reactive.

Speaking this week, via Betway, the Frenchman argued that Arsenal’s consistency sets them apart from the chasing pack, even if he expects the picture to shift again before the end of the campaign.

"No disrespect to anybody, but the only team that looks somewhat in control of games is Arsenal," Henry said.

"Every month we talk about a new challenger. At the beginning of the season, everyone thought Arsenal had no challengers.

"Then Man City went on a run of winning seven in a row, and they were seen as the challengers. Now City don’t win in four, and Liverpool look like the challenger. Nobody seems to talk about Brighton, but they are there as well. We will see.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"We can mention the game against Brighton or 25 minutes in the second half against Newcastle, but Arsenal do look like the most consistent team. Challengers come and go, and who knows who will win the league at the end of the day? But Arsenal look solid at the moment."

Henry’s mention of Brighton highlights just how impressive the Seagulls have been so far, with Maxim De Cuyper and Pascal Gross inspiring a side boasting the league's best defensive record.

Arsenal's immediate focus is getting back to winning ways on Sunday afternoon after being held to a 2-2 draw by Newcastle last weekend. Having almost surrendered their advantage to City during last season’s run-in, Arteta’s men know better than anyone that early control counts for little unless they deliver when the biggest rivals come to town.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League.
