#802. What will returning Magill bring to Northern Ireland?

Simone Magill made her return to football as a late substitute for Birmingham City against Manchester United on Sunday

After 13 months away, Simone Magill made her return to football as a late substitute in Birmingham City's WSL defeat by Manchester United on Sunday.

It was a moment that had been a long time coming for the 31-year-old, who gave birth to her daughter, Skye, in May and has been building towards stepping back on the pitch.

Now, she will hope to make her international return with Northern Ireland in a friendly against Greece on Friday.

"It's been some time since I've been here in a playing capacity, so it's really nice just to be back in the mix again," NI captain Magill told BBC Sport NI.

"I officially made my comeback at the weekend and it was really nice to have done that. I'm really looking forward to doing that here at home in front of the fans and my family as well."

'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'

Greece friendlies an opportunity to build - Andrews

In an interview with BBC Sport in October, Magill spoke about how being both a mum and a footballer can "co-exist".

While she was not ready to play any role in the matches, Magill, Skye and her husband Mark were all in camp for the World Cup play-off with Portugal last month, all with an eye of integrating into international duty as a family.

Having played just a handful of minutes, Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle said that while he was "delighted" to have Magill back, how much she plays across the double-header would be in collaboration with Birmingham and his captain.

"With the circumstances around this one, I'm very mindful that I need to build accordingly and I really need to listen to myself as well," Magill added.

"To even be back in this capacity this soon after giving birth, for me, is just unbelievable.

"I have no major expectations. I'm just really happy to be here and be a part of it, and if I do come on, that'll be even better."

Watch live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport app and website

Friday's match against Greece will be Northern Ireland's first friendly in three years.

The sides will then play again on Tuesday at 16:00 GMT, and both matches can be streamed live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport app and website.

The matches will act as preparation for the Nations League campaign in February, when Northern Ireland face tricky tests in the form of Poland, Finland and Belarus.

McArdle is developing a young squad and Magill says she hopes to bring "leadership and experience to really help us all move forward".

"We've obviously had a transition in the last year whilst I've been out, it's been nice to come back in and just feel where we're at, get on the grass with the girls and see, 'how can I help, what can I bring?'," she added.

"I'm very much looking forward to just getting back in the mix and helping try to bring the young players forward, use that experience and let's hold on to the ball, let's get into the final third, let's have a go, be brave - all of the attributes that we're known for.

"We're an underdog nation, so it's getting that across to the younger members in the squad to say, 'let's have a go with these teams and not be afraid'."

Simone Magill (centre) is set to make her Northern Ireland return against Greece

In her absence over the past year, Northern Ireland have used a number of different options in the centre forward role.

Winger Lauren Wade has shown her versatility by playing centrally, while Kess Elmore and Cora Chambers have also played up top.

Along with Magill, Portsmouth striker Kerry Beattie is also back in the squad to bolster McArdle's striking options.

"We've loads of young ones snapping at my heels. It's great, that's what we want.

"I feel we're more competitive now than ever. You never know who's going to be coming into the squad. Certainly, in more recent years, you kind of knew the squad every single time, whereas that's not the case now.

"We've got some exciting youth coming through, so it's their time now to shine."

Magill added that Northern Ireland are "heading in a new direction" ahead of the Nations League campaign next year, and the friendlies with Greece give an opportunity for the team to grow in a pressure-free environment.

"We're coming into a brand new campaign and it's really nice that we have a friendly window just now.

"We haven't had one in a very, very long time, so this is a brilliant opportunity to get us all back together, get the new faces in, get some more experience, learn things, try things.

"I'm really excited about where we're going."

#801. Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

Elliot Yates is an intern on the Nature Careers and Supplements team.

Changes in cities’ ranks in the natural sciences are shown for 2016 to 2025, as measured by Share in the Nature Index. Beijing remained in first place, while five more Chinese cities entered the top ten during the period. Two US cities that were once in the top 10 have since fallen out of the top 20.

The leading cities for biological sciences in 2025 are shown alongside their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject. This is the most geographically diverse of the natural-sciences subjects, with four US, four Chinese and two European cities in the top 10.

Chinese cities take all top 10 places in the chemistry rankings for 2025, shown here with their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject. Beijing and Shanghai had the highest growth over the period among the top 50 cities in the subject, each increasing their chemistry adjusted Share by almost 900.

Beijing contributed 25% of China’s Earth and environmental sciences Share in 2025 — the highest percentage among the top-five cities in the natural-sciences and health-sciences subject areas. Among the top 10 cities in Earth and environmental sciences for 2025, Qingdao had the biggest percentage change in adjusted Share between 2016 and 2025, at 545.5%, and Beijing gained the most adjusted Share points, at 703.

#799. Germany's Freigang given 16-month ban over drugs test issues

Laura Freigang has scored 17 goals in 45 appearances for Germany

Germany international Laura Freigang has been suspended from football for 16 months over issues with three drugs tests.

The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 October 2027.

The 16-month suspension begins from the date of notification by the German Football Association (DFB), which took place in June.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the National Anti-Doping Agency (Nada), DFB and Freigang reached a dispute resolution agreement.

The dispute said Entracht Frankfurt forward Freigang committed three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026.

Freigang can return to training two months prior to the end of the suspension period but cannot play matches until after 7 October.

All personal records of appearances, goals, assists or other statistics from 23 February 2026 are nullified, though Frankfurt's results are unaffected.

This season Freigang has scored six goals and provided two assists in 11 starts in the Frauen-Bundesliga.

Since joining the club in 2020, the striker has scored 107 goals in 187 appearances and was in the Germany squad for October's friendly victories over Australia and Japan.

In a club statement, external, Franfurt said they will "begin discussions shortly to determine the terms of her future employment relationship".

Freigang's current contract is due to expire on 30 June 2027.

Frankfurt's director of women's football Katharina Kiel said: "The agreement now reached provides clarity and planning security in a process unprecedented for Eintracht Frankfurt - for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

"The way she and the team have handled the situation in recent months, and how Laura personally led by example with her performance on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the highest recognition.

"The identified shortcomings, despite the agreement to settle the dispute, have resulted in a suspension, which means the loss of a key player."

Legendary US goalkeeper is taking inspiration from some high-flying clubs as he takes on sporting director role in League Two

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Brad Friedel recently became Shrewsbury Town’s new sporting director, as part of a US consortium that have taken over the club – and he hopes to help the Shropshire side climb the leagues in years to come.

Shrewsbury have endured tough times in recent seasons as they waited for new investment, suffering relegation from League One in 2024, then finishing 19th in the fourth tier last term.

They sit mid-table in League Two this season, though, and had previously spent a decade in the third tier.

The Shrews are ambitious to improve on their current position, with the help of funding from their new owners and the expertise of their sporting director.

“We want to try to achieve a promotion to League One, and once we hopefully get there, we would like to try to achieve another promotion,” Friedel told FFT.

But it’s a lot of hard work. There are a lot of good clubs, a lot of good minds and a lot of great footballers out there, so it’s not easy, but we hope with hard work and perseverance, we can get there.”

A number of clubs have previously climbed from League Two to much loftier heights, with Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth among them. The trio are now all in the upper echelons of the Premier League.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Near neighbours Wrexham were similarly in the lower leagues very recently, but have climbed from the National League all the way to the Championship under the ownership of Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds.

Friedel, though, understandably insists he won’t be looking too closely towards the Welsh side for inspiration.

“Yeah, I don’t think that’s the club I want to talk about right now, with them being our rivals…” smiled Friedel, who was speaking in association with a licensed casino.

“But if you look back historically, I think about three clubs from when I played professionally over here.

“Bournemouth, Brentford and Brighton were nowhere near where they are now, and those are three just unbelievable success stories in football. So it can happen, but it doesn’t happen overnight, that’s for certain.”

There will be more from Friedel about his career in football in FourFourTwo soon.

#797. Ipswich Women sign Ademiluyi for record fee

Ademiluyi had been on loan at the Tractor Girls from NWSL side Gotham FC since February

Ipswich Town Women have confirmed the permanent signing of England youth international Princess Ademiluyi for an undisclosed club record fee.

The 20-year-old forward has been on loan at the Tractor Girls from NWSL side Gotham FC since February and has agreed a three-and-a-half year deal at the WSL2 side.

Ademiluyi has been capped by England at under-19 and under-20 level, and has been called up for the under-23 side for the first time ahead of their internationals against Belgium and Portugal next week., external

"I have really made a home for myself in Suffolk and I am so excited to continue building what has been a positive start to the season for us as a group," she told the club's website., external

"The players, staff and supporters have all been brilliant with me since I arrived and I can't wait to see where this club can go and to continue making more memories together."

Ipswich Town chairman Mark Ashton said: "Signing Princess on a permanent basis has been a real priority for us and completing such a significant deal as this highlights the club's ongoing commitment to reach the top level of the game.

"This is a statement signing for the club, with further announcements to come in due course as we reaffirm our commitment to our women's set-up in both the short and long-term."

Ademiluyi started her career at WSL side West Ham in 2023 before moving to US-based Gotham and is Ipswich's top scorer so far in 2026-27, with four goals.

The Tractor Girls finished ninth in WSL2 last season following promotion to the second tier in 2025, and were in the fourth tier as recently as 2021., external

Under the management of former men's team player David Wright, appointed to the role in April, the Blues are third after eight games this season, three points behind leaders Newcastle United.

Ipswich on 'inevitable' path to WSL - Boswell

Ademiluyi has played an important role in helping the Tractor Girls transform from relegation candidates to title contenders.

She made an immediate impact on joining in February, scoring goals against Durham and Birmingham City to help secure the team's survival in WSL2.

The forward has continued to find the net this season, and won the WSL2 player of the month award for October., external

There is a growing feeling within the women's game that the Blues will be playing at the highest level in the not too distant future and securing a proven goalscorer whose stock is also rising on the international stage will only strengthen that train of thought.

#796. From Gunnersaurus to a giant cucumber: FourFourTwo ranks the 30 greatest football mascots in the world

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

It's time to rate the finest Wombles, jalapeno peppers and chainsaw-wielding maniacs that football has to offer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Football mascots are a staple of the matchday experience.

They're there to entertain the fans, get the crowd going and indulge in a bit of pre-match banter. Yes, some will occasionally overstep the mark - naming no names, especially not a north London-dwelling hornet who liked to bother Wilfried Zaha - but ultimately, it's all a bit of fun.

From iconic World Cup characters to the most gloriously ridiculous club mascots on the planet, FourFourTwo counts down the 30 best – with some unlikely contenders for the top spot.

The people behind The Muppets devised the official 2006 World Cup mascot – an anthropomorphic lion, accompanied by sidekick Pille… a talking football.

CONTROVERSY: The non-native lion didn’t go down well with the German public, and not because he didn't wear anything on his bottom half. “We have eagles and gnomes and garden dwarves, but not lions,” huffed design expert Erik Spiekermann. “That’s English or French, or whatever.”

Fulham share their colours with the wood-dwelling mustelid, who replaced knight Sir Craven of Cottage and giant computer Terry Bytes in 2006. Likes to dress up as Dracula for Halloween.

WEIRDEST MOMENT: A February 2008 red card from Chris Foy after a half-time breakdancing routine against Aston Villa delayed the restart. Short-sighted and greying, Foy is now a retired referee.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Noted illustrator David Squires designed permanently surprised predecessor Herbie the Hammer – Hammerhead has more than an air of Iron Man about him.

BEST ATTRIBUTE: West Ham’s mascot has been likened to a couple of all-time club legends, thanks to claims that he’s “as fast as Billy Bonds and blessed with the goalscoring prowess of Vic Watson”. Where’s he been this season, then?

Fred’s early 1990s arrival coincided with a period of greatness at Manchester United – didn’t need Fergie after all, eh?

PREDECESSORS: When they weren’t just people donning costumes, the club’s mascots included Michael the Bank Street Canary (actually a goose), Major the Saint Bernard Dog (went missing) and, er, ‘Hoppy’ Thorne the One-Legged Wonder (a First World War veteran).

The World Cup’s first mascot was a lion in a Union Jack shirt. Fresh from roaring England to victory in 1966, Willie then resurfaced in unofficial marketing for the next tournament in Mexico four years later, wearing a sombrero. Ole!

DID YOU KNOW? Actor George Claydon, an Oompa Loompa in Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory, inhabited Willie in the FA’s real-life promotional material.

Not a Barcelona defender, but Mexico 86’s sombrero-wearing moustachioed jalapeno pepper that played on tired stereotypes. “It’s as if a group of gringos picked out a symbol to depict Mexico,” complained a government official.

DID YOU KNOW? Pique, Spanish for spicy, was a tenuous pun on ‘PK’ – and the host nation later got knocked out on penalties. By West Germany, obviously...

The streets around the Estadio Benito Villamarin are lined with palm trees, providing the inspiration when Real Betis sought a fresh figurehead for their 2007 centenary. The perennially happy Palmerin has rocked various hairstyles in his time, plus an almighty hairband.

DID YOU KNOW? Palmerin got the gig with 53 per cent of a fan vote, making him slightly more popular than Brexit.

The 2024 Copa America symbol could only be one thing – the national emblem of a country not in South America, of course. Well, they had already allowed the USA to host the thing, for reasons unclear [loads of money – Ed.], so might as well make the mascot an eagle, too.

PREDECESSORS: Past Copa mascots include a macaw, an Ecuadorian corn cob and tango singer Carlos Gardel.

FC Tokyo plumped for a raccoon dog as their new mascot in 2009. Their website later explained Dorompa is “universally recognised as a Tokyo supporter in the Japanese raccoon dog world” and earned his name “for inhabiting a nest very close to Tokyo Tower”. Sure, lads.

WEIRDEST MOMENT: Riding a unicycle, dressing up as Michael Jackson and doing a karate chop on pitchside tiles.

With a name like a somewhat dubious second-hand ticket website, Footix was selected as France’s 1998 World Cup mascot ahead of the intriguingly named Zimbo, Houpi, Gallik and Raffy.

BEST ATTRIBUTE: On official merch, the rooster wore a France shirt and held the ball in one hand, with a knowing grin on its face, predicting the Thierry Henry vs Ireland incident 11 years later.

No cuddly mascot for Italia 90 – instead, they plumped for a stick figure featuring a football for a head. Why not? Rejected names included Dribbly and Bimbo.

DID YOU KNOW? The competition to devise Ciao drew a hefty 50,000 entries, a £25,000 prize and the frank opinion of the Azzurri’s all-time leading scorer Gigi Riva, who personally told the winning designer he didn’t like it. Brutal, Gigi…

What could be more child-friendly than a chainsaw-wielding bloke in a hard hat? Portland Timbers’ mascot is the successor to Timber Jim, who started taking a chainsaw to matches back in the 1970s... without getting arrested.

BEST ATTRIBUTE: Every time Portland net, Joey cuts his way through a 12ft log (later presented to the goalscorer) behind the goal. “Er, thanks, I guess?”

Joey isn’t the only weaponised mascot – Sheffield United’s Captain Blade is a pot-bellied pirate armed with not one but two swords (and an eye patch, naturally).

DID YOU KNOW? As a club director, Sean Bean wasn’t keen. “At a meeting, he made a big show of wanting to make a very important point,” revealed Neil Warnock. “He said we should get rid of Captain Blade. Captain Fking Blade.”

Are there any aliens on the Moon? The truth is out there. Either way, Manchester City mascot Moonchester (a nod to the club’s Blue Moon anthem) resembles an extraterrestrial, rather than Buzz Aldrin.

DID YOU KNOW? Moonchester was on FFT’s front cover with Pep Guardiola & Co in 2016, steadfastly remaining mute throughout the entire photoshoot, as per the stipulations in his City contract.

As David Attenborough has no doubt always said, there aren’t many animals cooler than an armadillo, the inspiration for Brazil’s 2014 World Cup mascot.

DID YOU KNOW? The Brazilian three-banded armadillo is endangered and the idea was to promote environmentalism, though protesters claimed FIFA cashed in on the mascot’s profits without giving much to actually save the animal itself.

The official 1982 World Cup mascot’s name means ‘Little Orange’, despite being absolutely massive. Naranjito’s smile implied satisfaction, but the eyes suggested otherwise, as if he’d just foreseen Gerry Armstrong’s winner for Northern Ireland against hosts Spain.

DID YOU KNOW? Had its own cartoon series, plus a squeeze called Clementine. Gerry probably crushed her dreams, too.

Owing to legend that the locals once hanged a monkey, believing it to be a French spy (sounds pretty plausible), Hartlepool are the ‘Monkey Hangers’ – a mascot all but created from there.

CONTROVERSY: Cavorted with a sex doll at Blackpool, punched the head off Desmond the Dragon at Rochdale, then elected Mayor of Hartlepool after Peter Mandelson labelled him “a disgrace”.

Harrogate Town asked schoolchildren to create a mascot in 2018, and we applaud their decision to make it an alligator, purely to call it Harry Gator – a piece of wordplay right up there with Peterborough’s rabbit Peter Burrow.

DID YOU KNOW? Harry’s also a skilled drummer, recently reproducing that Cadbury advert where a gorilla plays along to Phil Collins’ In the Air Tonight.

When Club Tijuana decided to model their mascot on a native Mexican dog, they had options: the Chihuahua or the utterly terrifying Xoloitzcuintle, so intimidating even its name sounds like it’s hurling abuse at you. Choosing the latter, they put it in goalkeeper gloves.

WEIRDEST MOMENT: Wearing a skull mask for Day of the Dead, and riding a motorbike across the pitch. Alarming.

Nothing remotely subtle going on at Brazilian club Bahia. First they created blatant rip-off Super-Homem Tricolor, translating Superman into Portuguese and suffixing it with the club nickname. In 2018, they added Lindona, definitely not inspired by Wonder Woman at all.

DID YOU KNOW? City Football Group own Bahia – could we see Lindona at the Etihad when Moonchester’s past it?

Dutch outfit Willem II take their name from William II, king of the Netherlands from 1840-49, who died in the club’s home city of Tilburg – they followed suit with their mascot, a gormless lion.

BEST ATTRIBUTE: A robe and crown, for the full regal look. It makes you wonder why Hampton & Richmond haven’t got a Henry VIII mascot – a light beheading might increase the stakes somewhat.

AFC Wimbledon didn’t have to debate long for their mascot, either – the home of The Wombles, the rodent also took its moniker from the nearby Haydons Road rail station. It was either that or a giant tennis ball, a strawberry or something.

DID YOU KNOW? Haydon has been known to crowd surf and also wheel a bin around the ground, then slide on it like the skeleton at the Winter Olympics.

A giant cucumber wearing a Zorro-type mask and cape, Leganes’ Super Pepino is everything a club mascot should be. The Cucumber Growers – the phallic vegetable is Spanish slang for a great goal – unveiled their new hero marching to I Like To Move It by Reel 2 Real.

WEIRDEST MOMENT: Attempting to fire T-shirts into the crowd with a cannon, but hoying them right out of the ground.

Best known for a tremendous beef with Crystal Palace – theatrically throwing himself at Wilfried Zaha’s feet in 2018.

THEY SAID: “If you’re asking me if Harry the Hornet, who I’m assuming is the mascot, should dive in that way, I think it’s disgraceful” – then Eagles manager Roy Hodgson correctly identifies the bloke in the hornet suit as the mascot, rather than Watford’s new trequartista.

Everyone knows that a swan can break your arm – in Cyril’s case, that’s only the half of it. The Swansea mascot earned ’90s notoriety for a series of regrettable incidents, drop-kicking the head of Millwall’s Zampa the Lion and telling him, “Don’t fk with the Swans.” Yikes.

DID YOU KNOW? Cyril once appeared as the Emperor of China’s pet in pantomime Aladdin at Swansea’s Grand Theatre.

Wigan schoolkids don’t fear stereotypes – asked to come up with the Latics’ new mascot, more than half of the entries were pies. Crusty was born, although his early interviews were surprisingly deep. “I don’t want to think about dying,” he explained. Hey, keep it light, pie-face…

HE SAID: “I don’t watch films, just the FA Cup wins over Manchester City on repeat.” Er, Michael Owen, is that you?

FC Köln became the Billy Goats after a circus director gifted them one back in 1950, naming it after coach Hennes Weisweiler. They’ve since been through nine iterations – six years ago, Hennes IX replaced Hennes VIII, who the club once tried to register to play during an injury crisis. The GOAT is literally a goat.

DID YOU KNOW? Hennes VII starred as a murder victim in TV drama SK Kolsch.

A giant most associated with a now extinct era, Arsenal also have a dinosaur mascot called Gunnersaurus – devised by an 11-year-old supporter in 1993.

CONTROVERSY: Gunnersaurus was let go to cut costs during COVID, and later reinstated (with a new suit inhabitant). Piers Morgan was at the front of the queue to voice his disapproval, as was queue-jumper-in-chief Holly Willoughby.

Baggie Bird has been West Bromwich Albion’s main mascot for decades, but it was well and truly upstaged when Boiler Man arrived in 2018, as part of a sponsorship deal with Ideal Boilers. Kids just love a combi-boiler, after all.

CONTROVERSY: Last year, the Baggies were in hot water after the chap who played Boiler Man retired – “a decision not made by myself”. Mysterious.

Described as “Lisa Simpson on meth” and “a demented Sun God”, Partick Thistle’s new symbol was never going to go unnoticed when it replaced the brilliantly named but rather tamer Jaggy McBee in 2015. Petrifying stuff.

HE SAID: “I got to chill out with David Hasselhoff when he was in town doing panto,” said Kingsley. What the Hoff made of Kingsley is anybody’s guess.

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...

#795. Head coach Slegers leaves Arsenal 18 months after Champions League win

Renee Slegers initially joined Arsenal in 2023 as an assistant coach under Jonas Eidevall

Arsenal have parted company with head coach Renee Slegers by mutual consent after a disappointing start to the season.

Slegers, 37, was initially appointed on an interim basis in October 2024 before being handed the role permanently three months later.

The Dutchwoman led Arsenal to their second Women's Champions League title in May 2025 and the inaugural Fifa Women's Champions Cup in February 2026.

But she leaves with the team sixth in the Women's Super League after 11 matches - 12 points behind leaders Chelsea.

Assistant coach Aaron D'Antino has also left the club, with assistant Melissa Clarke-Reed placed in interim charge as they begin the search for a permanent replacement.

D'Antino had been part of Arsenal's coaching staff since August 2018.

Arsenal director of women's football Clare Wheatley said the decision had been "extremely difficult".

"In leading us to glory in the Champions League and the inaugural Fifa Champions Cup, Renee has made a significant and lasting contribution to the history of Arsenal Football Club, with close support from Aaron," she said.

"After careful reflection, it is clear that results have been below the expected level, and change is necessary."

Chief executive Richard Garlick paid tribute to both departing coaches, describing Slegers as "a wonderful person" who had played "an integral role in some of the most historic achievements in the club's history".

"Our ambition is to compete for and win major trophies consistently, and our recent results have led us to conclude that a change is necessary to give us the best opportunity to achieve those goals," he added.

Why Arsenal are behind in race for Champions League spots

Slegers' departure comes after weeks of pressure as Arsenal's WSL form continued to deteriorate.

While the Dutch coach delivered the Women's Champions League and Women's Champions Cup, results in the league have fallen below expectations this season.

Arsenal have endured a four-match winless run in the league and their struggles have been particularly stark at their own Emirates Stadium, where they have gone six matches without a victory.

For a side expected to challenge for major trophies every season, those dropped points are damaging as they have fallen well adrift of Chelsea and even eight points behind London City Lionesses, who are in the third Women's Champions League qualification spot.

A lack of goals has been central to Arsenal's struggles. They have scored just 11 times in 11 WSL matches this season - less than half the tally of Chelsea (29), second-placed Manchester City (28) and London City Lionesses (31).

Before Slegers' exit was confirmed on Friday, former Arsenal and England forward Lianne Sanderson had called for the manager to depart.

"I've been a big advocate for Renee to stay in the job, but after the Lyon game [a 2-0 home defeat in the Champions League], I felt this feeling in my stomach that it's time [to part ways]," Sanderson told FourFourTwo, external.

"That was probably the most defeated I have felt. The players weren't fighting, they had just shown nothing, there was no identity.

"The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results."

After Sunday's draw with West Ham, Slegers acknowledged performances and results had fallen short of expectations and made it clear she accepted responsibility.

"I love the club," she said. "We're going through a very, very difficult time, and I take my responsibilities, because the results haven't been good enough.

"In the second half we are chasing again, but we're not creating good enough chances to the final third, from all phases, and the way we get there, it's not the Arsenal standard and we need to do that better.

"But I take my responsibilities in my role."

We ask players for loyalty - but where's the loyalty from the clubs themselves?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Booing players used to be reserved for the traitors, the mercenaries and the Judases.

Now, it’s lost all meaning, as evidenced by Newcastle United fans booing their greatest servant post-Shearer for daring not to waste his peak punching a PSR ceiling, and instead, go and actually further his career. The nerve of Bruno Guimaraes, a man who grew up 6,000 miles from St. James' Park, to put his own feelings above those of 60,000 Geordies and ask his agent to find him a new employer.

Arsenal fans smirking right now: you’re no better if you booed Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain or Alexis Sanchez for jumping the sinking ship of post-Wenger malaise; worse still, if you gave Hale End youth product Omari Hutchinson stick upon his homecoming with Ipswich Town a couple of seasons ago (no, seriously, they did that).

Ah, the dreaded “going about it the wrong way”. Simply put, if a player was no longer wanted, he went about it “the right way”. Otherwise, they're fair game for jeers next time they come back to your patch – and your former faithful may well even suggest that “they're actually our rivals”, simply because there have been a few close scrapes between the two sides in recent years. Trent Alexander-Arnold, Declan Rice, Mason Mount, Jack Grealish, etc. etc. Modern f***ing football. Ultimately, we all like to pretend we’re different. That our fans are above that nonsense. Our club is better than that club over there. But we’re not. We’re all the same. Football fandom is a horoscope, assigning vague characteristics that define an entire section of society. Football clubs, we regret to tell you, are all the same.Ask Bayern Munich star, Jamal Musiala. You can wear the No.10 shirt for your country and the biggest club in that country. That still won’t be enough for anyone to show you the loyalty that fans deserve from you. He’s now suffered a hamstring tear, which he’s having to deal with alongside absence seizures, which began at the start of the season.

Musiala is also having to now defend himself from Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, a member of Bayern's supervisory board, claiming his contract is “with all due respect, not justifiable any longer”, following the very public reveal of this neurological condition. Usually the phrase “with all due respect” precedes something awful, doesn’t it? Bayern's honorary president Uli Hoeness, meanwhile, has stated the star may never “regain the performance level he once had” and suggested his contract should be reviewed. Die Roten captain Joshua Kimmich has been sufficiently appalled to speak out. It’s shameful. But let's be clear, without spouting whataboutery of other clubs' egregious acts: Bayern are not uniquely atrocious or especially despicable.

Football fandom is a horoscope, assigning vague characteristics that define an entire section of society

Every club would do what Bayern are doing – and no, that’s not a defence of their abominable treatment of a player they have a duty of care for. It’s a cold and ruthless industry in which sentiment is sorely lacking (unless there’s a nice photo opportunity). Football clubs will look to employ players that have been accused of sexual assault if it helps them on the pitch. They will sign sponsorship deals with arms manufacturers. They will ask players to revoke political comments if they don't align with their values. Why should looking after their players be any different?Has your club ever had a ‘bomb squad’? Case in point. Raheem Sterling was chastised by Liverpool fans for chasing the money and winding up at Manchester City: within a decade, he was being frozen out by the very same club that had given him a £300,000-a-week contract. Alejandro Garnacho had the world at his feet at one of the biggest clubs in the world: now, he’s a pawn in a contractual stalemate between Aston Villa and Chelsea, as neither wants him and neither are arsed that it’s affecting his livelihood. Harvey Elliott went through something similar.

Those are just three high-profile examples. These astronomical wages are often justified by the argument that a player could suffer a career-ending injury at any moment; that the money a player sacrificed their childhood and education for could stop in an instant, leaving them unemployable, often qualification-less. The vastness of that wealth is then used as a stick to beat a player with, if they choose to chase a couple more zeroes.But who could blame them, really? Who can blame JJ Gabriel for wanting to sign for the biggest club in the world? What if he does turn down the big move to Real Madrid, and never makes it anyway? And where's the loyalty being shown to dozens of his age-mates every year, who are released by Manchester United and other elite clubs? Footballers sign contracts and are asked for loyalty – often to clubs that they had no prior connection to before signing – yet there’s no loyalty to the players themselves. Musiala is proof that no footballer is safe. Every club will take advantage of them if given the choice, and it's time as fans that we wake up to that fact.

#792. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, he comes up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posts them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

This information is a guide and is constantly changing. Please check the National Careers Service website for the latest information and all the qualifications needed and the GOV.UK website for more on T-levels.

For careers advice in all parts of the UK visit: National Careers Service (England), nidirect (Northern Ireland), My World of Work (Scotland) and Careers Wales (Wales).

#791. Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

#790. Russell bounces back by beating Antonelli to Qatar GP pole

George Russell beats Kimi Antonelli to pole as Mercedes seal dominant one-two; Lando Norris ahead of Oscar Piastri on second row; Isack Hadjar beats Max Verstappen to fifth; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports F1 at 4pm on Sunday, with build-up from 2.30pm

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

George Russell produced a superb performance in Qatar Grand Prix Qualifying to beat his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli to pole position.

The reignition of Russell's feud with Max Verstappen at last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix had dominated the build-up to the penultimate race of the season, but the Brit produced the perfect response as he topped all three parts of qualifying.

That came as a surprise after Antonelli, who sealed the drivers' title with four rounds to spare, had topped all three practice sessions, but the Italian was unable to match Russell when it mattered most.

Antonelli was unhappy with Mercedes' run plan for their final Q3 efforts, with the Italian questioning over the radio why he, with Russell behind him, was sent out ahead of the other cars participating in the final part of the session.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McLaren found significant improvement on the final runs to move ahead of Red Bull as Mercedes' nearest challenger and lock out the second row, with Lando Norris ahead of Oscar Piastri as the best of the rest despite being marginally either side of half a second down on Russell.

Verstappen, who said after winning in Las Vegas last weekend that Russell is "far below" his level, was beaten to fifth by his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar.

Charles Leclerc took seventh but his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton was beaten to eighth by Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, with the latter's team-mate Liam Lawson completing the top ten.

The buccaneering right-back swapped Sheffield United for Leeds United in 2024

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During his eight years in senior football, Jayden Bogle has experienced a number of different managerial approaches.

After breaking into the Derby County first team under Frank Lampard, he would play under former Netherlands international Phillipe Cocu at Pride Park, before being signed by Chris Wilder at Sheffield United.

Wilder would prove to be one of the biggest influences on his career to date, with his performances in South Yorkshire paving the way for a move north to Elland Road, where Bogle has again kicked on under Leeds United boss Daniel Farke.

These managers have different approaches to the game and to their man management, which has seen Bogle benefit from being exposed to two contrasting philosophies.

“One thing I took from Chris Wilder was being more diligent without the ball, more aggressive, a bit more horrible to play against,” he continues. “Under Daniel Farke, it's just been seeing the game from probably a calmer point of view – being more composed with the ball.”

At Leeds, Bogle’s changed 12 months ago, when Farke opted to deploy the defender in a back five, enabling him to maraud forward and show off the attacking side of his game.

“I played in a five sometimes at Sheffield United, so I was familiar with it,” he adds.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“It's just getting the relationship with the players around you, understanding their strengths and how you can help them.

“It's nice being in a five, you get further forward sometimes, off the back of the striker as well.

"But also, if we go to a four, it's just switching the mindset back to being a bit more defensive, while still having the hunger to go forward and get involved in trying to create.”

Farke’s decision to change formation came with Leeds trailing 2-0 away to Manchester City last November, in a shift which has rejuvenated both player and club.

“The manager changed the system [at half-time vs Man City], and he just told us to go out there with confidence and make it difficult for them – whether that was being a bit more direct, or putting in a few big challenges.

“There weren't any harsh words flying about. It was just, ‘Prove that we belong here, play with more confidence.' You could feel the reaction in the stadium immediately after half-time. Although we didn't win, we definitely took a lot of confidence from the second half, knowing we did belong at this level.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#788. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

#787. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

Ever wondered who makes sure your video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

#784. Daily briefing: A guide to the Riemann hypothesis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

An analysis of protein-coding DNA from more than 1.4 million people has identified hundreds of genes that influence a person’s height. Researchers identified 207 genes that were linked to a height difference of two centimetres, on average. They also identified 17 rare variants that prevent proteins from functioning, which have more striking effects. These include one variant associated with a 17-centimetre reduction in height and another with an 11-centimetre increase. The findings might help with the development of treatments that mitigate height changes caused by some medical conditions.

The number of reported global cases of the viral disease dengue in 2024 — a 34-fold increase from the 430,000 reported in 1990. (Nature | 5 min read)

Reference: Research Square preprint (not peer reviewed)

Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel, are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities. Just eight institutions dominate these top economics awards: Harvard University; the University of Chicago; Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT); Stanford University; Princeton University; Yale University; the University of California, Berkeley; and Columbia University. On the other hand, prizes in the natural sciences, engineering and social sciences outside economics have become less concentrated to certain institutions over the past 70 years.

Reference: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper (not peer reviewed)

Four years after NASA’s DART Earth-defence test mission smashed into an asteroid and succeeded in altering the space rock’s movement, a follow-up mission has confirmed it on camera. The European Space Agency has released the first images from its Hera mission, which show detailed views of the asteroid’s new crater. “Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact,” says Patrick Michel, principal investigator of the Hera mission.

This clip shows the final five-and-a-half minutes of images leading up to the DART spacecraft's intentional collision with asteroid Dimorphos. This replay movie is 10 times faster than reality, except for the last six images, which are shown at the same rate that the spacecraft returned them. (NASA/Johns Hopkins APL)

Last week, the field of mathematics was rocked by two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis. The hypothesis is considered one of the most important open problems in maths. But if, like me, you have some trouble getting to grips with the famed conjecture — and what solving it could actually mean — Nature has you covered.

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves and, at its heart, it boils down to a statistical test. One that will be familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

“If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?” says Xin Zhang, one of five mathematicians who spoke to Nature in the aftermath of the proofs’ publication. His reaction was one of excitement, despite Anthropic’s use of artificial-intelligence to develop its proof. But his enthusiasm was by no means universal. The format of Anthropic’s proof — 17 million lines of code with no natural-language version for humans to work with — is “the worst-case scenario”, says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo. And the shift towards AI-use in maths is “a choice to disempower ourselves”, says Tasmin Chu.

Bashyal observes a species of Coelogyne orchid, often found in tropical lowland forests and mountainous regions.Credit: CJ Karki for Nature

Wildlife conservationist Reshu Bashyal works with people in Nepal to protect the more than 500 species of orchids that grow there. Prized for their ornamental value and uses in traditional medicine, hundreds of these flowering plants are illegally harvested and sold each year. But blanket bans on the orchid trade are unlikely to be effective, Bashyal says, so more innovative strategies are required. One of these is an ‘anti-poaching taskforce’ that can document illegal activity, conduct patrols and spread information about the importance of conservation. (Nature | Leisurely scroll)

A biomedical innovation model that utilizes scientists in industry with government as their main funder could accelerate the development of therapeutics for common diseases that industry considers too risky to invest in, argue physician Victor Dzau, health-policy advisor Emily Shambaugh and healthcare entrepreneur Will Ellaissi. This government funding could operate at a national level, or several countries could form a consortium. Such a model “moves beyond the market-determined trajectory of research translation and ensures the public’s role in shaping the future of health,” the authors write.

Commensality — the act of sitting down to eat a meal with other people — has myriad health and social benefits, such as protecting against cognitive decline and helping us build trust with others. The presence of other people might also increase the enjoyment we get from eating. In an increasingly digital world, it might seem that opportunities to dine with others are dwindling. But research suggests that people are much more open and willing to accept invitations than we think, and simply putting ourselves out there might be an easy way to a dinner date.

Evolutionary biologist Pamela Yeh shares advice on how to navigate grief in the demanding environment of academia. (Nature | 8 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03894-3

Today I’m appreciating the world in monochrome through the entries into this year’s Black and White Photo Awards. The overall winner, photographer Shengwai Dai’s Bishwa Ijtema, depicts a man’s leap of faith between the tops of two train cars — “a scene filled with energy, tension, and detail”, the competition’s judges said.

#783. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Yeremy Pino is the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow-card suspension

Crystal Palace's Yeremy Pino has become the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow card suspension after accumulating five bookings since the 2026-27 season began.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash were the first players to receive a ban for collecting five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 17 players sitting on four bookings after 11 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have received a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (five yellow cards)

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Chema Andres - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Yeremy Pino - Crytsal Palce (yellow card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

Costinha - Brighton & Hove Albion (red card suspension)

Leny Yoro - Manchester United (red card suspension)

James Tarkowski - Everton (red card suspension)

#781. Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports

According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.
