'Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner.''

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#750. Has AI just cracked Internet encryption? Rumoured ‘bombshell’ stuns scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty

Artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans. Now, a threat is emerging that is on a whole other scale.

Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote yesterday on his blog. The details are still hazy, added Aaronson, who is at the University of Texas at Austin. “Until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”

The algorithms are rumoured to target the information-scrambling system known as RSA, which relies on the mathematics of prime numbers, as well as more-advanced technologies.

While the rumours could not be confirmed, other breakthroughs announced by the AI companies this week make researchers cautiously optimistic that the mathematics of encryption could eventually come to help.

Nature examines the threat, and what can be done about it.

Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from banking apps to Internet browsers. It relies on mathematical problems that are considered practically impossible for computers to solve within a reasonable amount of time.

An algorithm that could solve these problems in polynomial time would change that. It means the time needed to solve a problem would increase relatively slowly as the problem gets larger. For example, a password of length n could be broken in a number of steps proportional to the square or cube of its size (n² or n³).

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers

Theoretical computer scientists tend to think of P problems as relatively easy to solve, especially compared with problems that require exponential time, where the number of steps might grow as 2n, for example. As n gets larger — or a password gets longer — the time required by an exponential algorithm quickly exceeds that of any polynomial one.

In practical terms, an algorithm that could break public-key cryptography in polynomial time could undermine much of the security on which the Internet relies.

It depends on which encryption systems they could crack, and how efficiently they could do so.

One of the most ubiquitous techniques for establishing public keys is to multiply two large prime numbers. This technique, called RSA, was long believed to be secure because ‘cracking the code’ requires factoring that product back into the original primes, a much slower process (at least, without a powerful quantum computer, which does not yet exist). One of the rumours now circulating is that the AI labs have found an algorithm that can do this.

But even though a polynomial-time algorithm could be very powerful on paper, it could still be impossible to use except for the shortest passwords. An algorithm requiring n10000steps, for example, be very impractical to apply.

However, proving that a problem is in ‘P’, even if the polynomial-time solution is practically useless, has usually been followed by improvements that have eventually led to efficient solutions. “The issue is that the idea that [the problem] was hard — because of needing exponential time — is dead,” Aaronson tells Nature.

Not necessarily. This type of worst-case scenario hinges on a long-standing open question known as ‘P = NP’: could every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time? If so, problems that underpin essentially all public-key cryptography could become much easier to crack.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security

But most researchers think that this is unlikely. In fact, some recent AI-aided results have made them cautiously optimistic. Earlier this week, both Anthropic and OpenAI announced results in theoretical computer science that suggest that many similar problems could be hard to solve. Before the recent explosion in AI-aided maths, each of those advances would have been hailed as the computer-science breakthrough of the decade, Aaronson says.

Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, agrees. “I am definitely blown away by the latest developments.” One especially interesting result, he says, shows that for a ubiquitous type of computation called matrix multiplication, the exponent in a polynomial-time algorithm cannot be too small. “Underneath the hood, it seems to provide a brand-new framework for proving limitations on efficient computation,” says Williams.

#748. Pete Davidson, Elsie Hewitt Show Co-Parenting Dynamic on Thanksgiving

Pete Davidson and ex Elsie Hewitt proved they are nailing co-parenting as Hewitt shared a cute glimpse into their Thanksgiving reunion alongside daughter Scottie, 11 months.

Pete Davidson and Elsie Hewitt had a stinking fun Thanksgiving.

The model gave fans a peek into her holiday reunion with the Saturday Night Live alum and their 11-month-old daughter Scottie as she documented the less than scent-sational smell they discovered.

“OK, we're driving through Jersey right now, and it smells so bad,” Hewitt told the camera in a Nov. 27 TikTok as she covered her face with a red scarf. She then turned to Davidson in the driver’s seat, asking him, “What did you have to say?”

To which he playfully responded, “You asked me if I farted. And I said, ‘No.’ And I know it’s not me because I don’t like it.”

The two burst out into a fit of laughter before Hewitt shut off the camera, captioning the video of the duo, “Coparenting.”

But their adventures were far from over that night as she also shared a look at her Christmas tree, which appeared to have sound activated lights.

In another video posted to TikTok, with the caption, “See what I did there,” the 30-year-old showed off her singing skills, doing her best version of the famous riff from Wicked’s “Defying Gravity,” as she attempted to get the tree to light up all the way.

She then panned the video to Davidson who quipped, “Go off, queen,” as Hewitt urged him to try lighting the tree with his own voice. And the 33-year-old was not messing about, as he came in with a deep, “Oh,” which made the tree almost fully light up.

Of course, this is hardly the first time the How to Rob a Bank star and Hewitt have proven that they’ve nailed co-parenting since their split in May, just months after welcoming Scottie in December.

In fact, Hewitt and Davidson also reunited for Halloween, as they dressed up Scottie as Tony Soprano from The Sopranos—a move that Davidson shared was all his ex.

“I’ve got to give Elsie credit, she did the whole wardrobe,” he raved on The Tonight Show Nov. 9. “She crushed it.”

“Before she was even born me and Elsie were like, ‘We gotta.’ Because her hair’s gonna grow. She’s got the perfect Tony hair, because she has no hair,” Davidson—a longtime fan of The Sopranos—joked. “It’s the only year we could.”

#747. Germany face Belgium in Nations League quarterfinals — Klopp plays down favorites tag

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.

Germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals — after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.

"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.

"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."

The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.

Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.

Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway, a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.

In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.

The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. #744. Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Rare Photos of Son Christopher on Thanksgiving

Billy Ray Cyrus celebrated Thanksgiving surrounded by family, including his rarely seen son Christopher Cody Cyrus, his wife Nicole and their baby Hudson.

Billy Ray Cyrus is celebrating in the heart of family.

The 65-year-old proved his heart is anything but achy breaky as he and partner Elizabethy Hurley enjoyed a blended Thanksgiving with their loved ones, including a rare appearance from Billy Ray’s son Christopher Cody Cyrus, whom the singer welcomed with ex-girlfriend Kristin Luckey.

“Happy Thanksgiving!” Billy Ray captioned his Nov. 26 Instagram carousel. “I am so thankful for this moment - grateful for this time with my incredible son Cody, his amazing wife Nicole and my beautiful grandson Hudson. Feeling truly blessed.”

In fact, Billy Ray was all smiles as he posed alongside Cody and the 34-year-old’s wife and baby in a restaurant. Also featured in the snaps were Elizabeth and her son Damian Charles Hurley, 24, the latter of whom cuddled baby Hudson close in one photo.

Damian, born in England to Elizabeth and American filmmaker Steve Bing, also leaned into the Turkey Day festivities, sharing Billy Ray’s post to his own Story and writing, “Happy Thanksgiving!”

As for Cody, while he leads a far more private life then many of his Cyrus siblings—Billy Ray also adopted Tish Cyrus’ kids Brandi Cyrus, 39, and Trace Cyrus, 37, during their marriage, in addition to the pair welcoming Miley Cyrus, 34, Braison Cyrus, 32, and Noah Cyrus, 26—he did attend Miley’s nuptials to Maxx Morando on Nov. 21.

In fact, Cody was among the Cyrus family members featured in Billy Ray’s photo carousel from the wedding, with the country singer raving over the family affair.

“My little girl married the love of her life! I can’t describe how beautiful it felt to have all my family together in one room, united by love,” he captioned his Nov. 24 post. “@miley words can’t begin to express how proud you make me every day… I’m the proudest dad alive!!”

The Hannah Montana alum also reserved some special words for his now son-in-law.

“@mmaxxm I’m so honored to welcome you to the family,” Billy Ray continued. “The two of you kids are a match made in heaven… Happy, happy birthday Miley - I can’t wait to keep celebrating you both today and forever!”

For a closer look at how Cody fits into the larger Cyrus family tree, read on.

Billy Ray Cyrus married Tish Cyrus (née Leticia Finley) on Dec. 28, 2003.

At the time they already shared 12-month-old daughter Destiny Hope Cyrus—you may know her as Miley Cyrus—and Tish was pregnant with their son Braison Cyrus, who was born May 9, 1994.

Seven months before Miley was born on Nov. 23, 1992, Billy Ray's ex-girlfriend Kristin Luckey gave birth to their son Christopher Cody Cyrus on April 8.

When the "Achy Breaky Heart" singer married Tish, he adopted her daughter Brandi Cyrus (born May 26, 1987) and son Trace Cyrus (Feb. 24, 1989), whose biological father is their mom's ex-husband Baxter Helson.

Tish and Billy Ray's youngest, daughter Noah Cyrus, was born Jan. 8, 2000.

From 2006 to 2010, Billy Ray played the father of Miley's normal-kid-who-moonlights-as-a-pop-star character in the Disney Channel sitcom Hannah Montana and a 2009 film adaptation.

While the Cyrus family was still based in Nashville, Billy Ray and Miley made the move to L.A. to jumpstart her own entertainment career.

Billy Ray and Tish announced in October 2010 that they were getting divorced, but by the following year were back together.

They filed for divorce again in June 2013 but reconsidered barely a month later, telling E! News at the time that they'd been to couple's counseling and it had done wonders for them.

But before they reconciled, when the news broke that her dad had made the first move in a Nashville court to end his marriage after 19 years, Miley tweeted, "@billyraycyrus since your text and email obviously aren't working would you like to talk like this?"

After starring in 2010's The Last Song together and dating off and on for a decade, Miley and Liam Hemsworth married in December 2018, not long after their Malibu home burned down.

The decision came "from a place of trauma and just trying to rebuild as quickly as we could," Miley recalled on her "Used to Be Young" TikTok series.

But Liam filed for divorce in August 2019 and they finalized the paperwork in January 2020.

"It's honestly very simple," a source told E! at the time. "They fell in love when they were young and they are just different people now."

Braison and his wife Stella Cyrus welcomed son Bear Chance Cyrus on June 8, 2021.

Tish filed for divorce fo a third time in April 2022, and this time it stuck.

Moreover, her petition citing "irreconcilable differences" noted that she and her husband of almost 30 years hadn't lived together since February 2020.

"It is after 30 years, five amazing children and a lifetime of memories, we have decided to go our separate ways—not with sadness, but with love in our hearts," Tish and Billy Ray told People in a statement. "We have grown up together, raised a family we can be so proud of, and it is now time to create our own paths."

The exes noted that they hadn't come to the decision to split up for good "lightly or quickly," adding, "We will always be family and look forward to a continued and loving shared experience as friends and parents."

Billy Ray quietly got engaged to Australian singer Firerose, who's 27 years his junior, in August 2022 but waited to confirm the news until that November.

"Growing up in Australia, my love of music was predominant over everything," Firerose told People. "I've known his music since forever."

What started as a friendship turned into more during the darkest days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

"All of the sudden, the life that I've always known as a touring artist didn't exist anymore," Billy Ray said. "A moment of so much change. And at the same time, Firerose, who had been such a light of positivity, such a best friend. And then when we began sharing the music, it just evolved more into, as musical soulmates, to soulmates, happy, pure love that to me, I didn't know could exist."

Around the time her ex-husband confirmed his engagment in November 2022, Tish went Instagram-official with Prison Break actor Dominic Purcell.

They got engaged in April 2023 and tied the knot that August in Malibu at sunset with Miley, Trace and Brandi all standing by their mom's side.

"Life is unpredictable & always full of changes," Trace captioned a photo of himself and two of his sibling with the bride. "I think the most important thing to do is cherish the past, look forward to the future, & always be happy in the present moment because that’s really all we have."

"To see my mom this happy and in love is very emotional for me," Miley told Vogue ahead of her mom's wedding. "Dom and my mom share the sweetest, most genuine love. It's almost like it's for the first time, which is so fitting for my mom who is such a young soul."

As for her dad's next chapter, however, a source close to Miley told E! News in October 2022 that she wasn't in love with it and didn't have a relationship with her future stepmom.

"The divorce between her parents put a strain on her relationship with her dad and it's been hard to connect with him in the last year," the source said. "She hopes they can eventually work on their relationship."

Billy Ray told People that November, however, that his family had "no hard feelings" about his engagement.

"Everybody's turning the page," he said. "It's been a lot, but everyone knew that it was time for a change."

He and Firerose got married on Oct. 10, 2023, calling it the "beautiful, joyous day that our two souls united as one in holy matrimony."

Only Some of Miley's Family Get Their Flowers

Whatever rift opened up between Miley and her dad apparently hadn't been repaired by the night of the 2024 Grammys on Feb. 4.

Tish and Brandi were there, as was Miley's boyfriend Maxx Morando, and they all got shout-outs when the "Flowers" singer won Record of the Year.

As Miley concluded her speech, "I don't think I forgot anyone."

None of the three officially confirmed or denied eyebrow-raising reports that Noah was involved with Dominic before her mother was, but the Grammy-nominated singer had some choice words for an Instagram commenter in April 2024 after the person crudely suggested that Noah and Tish both had "sexy time" with the actor.

"I'm so sorry but will you pleeeeeass just choke on the fattest c--k," Noah wrote in response. "Just for a lil bit. Great thanks."

Barely eight months after they tied the knot, Billy Ray filed to annul the union, alleging in court documents the marriage was "obtained by fraud."

He listed May 22, 2024, as their date of separation.

However, Billy Ray amended his plan and filed for divorce, which was settled that August.

"This has been absolutely the most crazy insane scam I have ever heard of," Billy Ray said in a statement to E! News. "Let alone the fact I'm right in the center and basically the target of the scheme. It's unfortunate it played out this way."

“Since my earliest memories all I can remember is being obsessed with you and thinking you were the coolest person ever," Trace began a Jan. 22, 2025, Instagram post directed at his father. "I wanted to be just like you. The day you adopted me was the happiest day of my life. Sadly the man that I wanted so desperately to be just like I barely recognize now."

Referring to his sisters, he continued, "Me and the girls have been genuinely worried about you for years but you’ve pushed all of us away."

Noah was especially hurt, according to Trace.

"Noah desperately has wanted you to be a part of her life and you haven't even been there for her," he wrote. "That’s your baby girl. She deserves better. Somehow just like me she still idolizes you though. We are all hanging on to memories of the man we once knew & hoping for the day he returns."

After his son Trace said he and his sisters—including Miley, Brandi and Noah—were worried about Billy Ray, the country music star wrote in the caption of a YouTube Shorts post on Jan. 26, 2025. “Praying for my family. For my children … sons and daughters…and their mother."

In March 2025, Billy Ray seemed to signal that his bond with his kids was improving as he shared a touching tribute to Miley and Noah in honor of their latest music projects.

“Flesh and blood … completely taking their art to a whole new level. Congratulations girls,” he wrote on Instagram at the time. “I’m so damn proud of both of you. I’m actually crying as I write this. Thank God you can’t see me.”

In May 2025, Billy Ray shared a photo of himself with Miley, her boyfriend Maxx Morando and his son Braison Cyrus at what appears to be the "Achy Breaky Heart" singer's farm in Tennessee. He captioned his Instagram post, “Happy Birthday Braison!!!!!"

One day later, Miley broke her silence about the family rift rumors, noting on Instamgram that she and her dad "have had our challenges over the years."

Miley continued, "Now, in my thirties, family is my priority above all else. I'm at peace knowing bridges have been built and time has done a lot of healing. Grateful for the good health and love that flows through my family."

#741. How dad's embarrassment was making of Gross at Brighton

Pascal Gross has eight goal contributions in 11 Premier League games this season

Many people will have parents to thank for shaping them into who they are today, but for Pascal Gross it was his dad's embarrassment when watching him play that turned out to be the making of him at Brighton.

It was not that Gross senior was not proud of his son, but he was unhappy with how he acted on the pitch in one of his first games with the Seagulls after signing for them in the summer of 2017.

"He went to the game. He went to every game," Gross said in The Football Interview.

"It was Leicester away and I was on the floor constantly like a little child crying for free-kicks and did nothing.

"I think my dad must've spoken to a couple fans. He said he was my dad and stuff. But then on the way back [from the game], he said he covered himself with the programme. He said it was embarrassing the way I played.

"He said 'if you keep playing like that, you will quite fast go back to Germany'.

Gross' dad urged his son to not look for free-kicks and instead play "faster" to adapt to the Premier League.

It was to prove important advice as Gross has become a hugely popular and influential player at Brighton.

Across his two spells at the club - having returned this summer following a two-year stint at Borussia Dortmund - Gross has contributed to 87 Premier League goals, scoring 35 times and providing 52 assists, the joint-highest total of goal involvements by a German player in the competition's history.

'I watched every Brighton game at Dortmund' - Gross

'Gross will be remembered as one of the best Albion players of the modern age'

Gross' dad was not just a parent keen to see his son make the best of his talent, but he had also been a respected football coach.

A former player, Stephan Gross built up decades of experience of coaching at youth level.

In the early 2000s he was youth team coach at VfL Neckarau, where he coached his son and helped him and several others develop impressively enough to catch the eye of professional clubs.

"He coached us from maybe from age 10 to 15," Gross said.

"But he prepared us for what it takes on a professional level - that the mental side is really important and you have to be resilient to pressure.

"Technical game, behaviour, all of those things I think he coached into not just me, but there's a lot of players [he coached] who also went on to play in the Bundesliga, or other levels."

Gross, Manuel Gulde, Robin Szarka and Marco Terrazzino all moved to TSG 1899 Hoffenheim as a result of Gross' coaching.

As is often the case, Gross has had to evolve as a player with age, and by his own admission he is a different type of player now than he was in his first stint at Brighton.

The 35-year-old is still chipping in with the goals and assists, with four of each in his 11 Premier League games so far, but now finds himself as much an on-field coach as a player.

"I try to put the gameplan on the pitch and try to drive and coach and improve my team-mates around me," he said.

"I see in other teams where players on the pitch organise the press and I think it's really important and I try to just put the gaffer's idea as a player on the pitch."

To still be going at the age he is and performing to the level he is, it is clear Gross loves football, despite having an issue that some might have thought would have curtailed his career early on - an allergy to grass.

"I have had this allergy since I was a child, but I can handle it. It's not that bad," he said.

"My mum always texts me [when there's a reaction]. She sees it straight away."

SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#739. How Cardiff are changing Swansea derby narrative

Brian Barry-Murphy will lean on the likes of Ollie Tanner, who scored in Cardiff's 2-0 win over Swansea in 2023, in his first south Wales derby

It can be difficult to change the narrative in sport. Take Cardiff City and their rivalry with Swansea City.

For years, a certain idea had taken hold, that the Swans - their players, staff, the club as a whole - had a better understanding of what the south Wales derby meant, and that innate grasp of its significance had given them the upper hand.

Results have supported the theory. Since a nine-year period at the start of this century where there were no derbies, Swansea have won 11 out of 21 and become the first team in the fixture's century-long history to do the double â that is, to win both league meetings in one season â before repeating the feat the following campaign.

Once a pattern is set in motion, it can take some stopping but, by winning their past two home derbies, Cardiff felt the tide might have been turning.

Granted, the most recent of those triumphs still ended with their relegation to League One two seasons ago, but there was at least a feeling that the hoodoo had been lifted.

Nearly two years have passed since the last south Wales derby. In that time, Cardiff have made an instant return to the Championship under head coach Brian Barry-Murphy, who has introduced a refreshingly bold and attacking style of play, built around a core of young local players.

They are still behind their neighbours, though.

Cardiff travel to Swansea on Sunday 17th in the table, nine places and nine points adrift of their opponents.

The Bluebirds have caught the eye with their performances this season but, for all their ambition and stylish dominance of possession, the defensive risks that come attached mean that they are still searching for a first away win of the campaign.

Does another derby moment beckon for Williams?

The local boy aiming to be at the heart of Cardiff's derby aims

Latest Cardiff City news, analysis and fan views

You have to go back nine derbies for the last time Cardiff won in Swansea, and a decade further back again for the last time they triumphed there with fans present.

What an opportunity this weekend's reunion presents, then, to shift another narrative.

"You have to accept it's a different game," says Barry-Murphy, preparing for his first south Wales derby.

"It's not a normal game, and I think if you try to make out as if it's just another game, you're preparing for something that's not going to happen.

"This is a totally different fixture for our players because the atmosphere is going to be totally different.

"We have to show that we have the characteristics and personality to perform the way we want to perform in that heat of battle and show who we want to be as a team.

"We're a very aggressive team and have a lot of daring players who play on the front foot. Our intention on Sunday, despite whatever the opposition do, is to show that version of ourselves."

Cardiff players will have 'edge' against Swansea

There will be a marked difference between this freewheeling Cardiff side and the previous, cagier iterations to make the short trip down the M4 to face Swansea, who have built their identity around a progressive football philosophy over the past 20 years.

If that represents a hint of convergence between the two rivals on the pitch, then one area where the clubs have certainly flipped the script is managerial upheaval.

For more than a decade, this fixture had symbolised the dysfunctional running of Cardiff; between 2011 and 2023, none of their managers had lasted long enough to oversee two derbies in one season.

Erol Bulut bucked that trend, only to get sacked less than a month after he was sent off during a 1-1 draw at the Swansea.com Stadium.

Now, Cardiff finally have the stability they have craved â and it is Swansea who have to contend with changes in the dugout.

The Swans are looking for a third permanent head coach since the Bluebirds appointed Barry-Murphy in the summer of 2025.

It is a far cry from the situation four years ago.

After the third of four successive wins over Cardiff, Swansea's head coach at the time, Russell Martin, said their greater stability was one of the reasons for their success against rivals who had a different man at the helm for each of those four defeats.

Former captain Ashley Williams is in charge of the Swans temporarily - assisted by fellow club greats Joe Allen, Leon Britton and Kristian O'Leary - while they look for a full-time successor to Vitor Matos.

Given the abrupt nature of Matos' departure and the ongoing search for his replacement, could this be a good time to face Swansea?

"Maybe, maybe not," says Cardiff vice-captain Rubin Colwill, who is almost certain to wear the armband on Sunday.

"I think the focus for us is us. We've worked really hard, we're really nailed on in what we're doing, and I think that's the most important thing, regardless of any situation that they're experiencing at the moment."

Colwill embodies Cardiff's new ethos: the creative heartbeat of the team and a young, maturing Welsh talent flourishing with the greater responsibility he has been given by Barry-Murphy.

Growing up as a Bluebirds fan in Neath, closer to Swansea than the Welsh capital, the 24-year-old also has a strong sense of what this rivalry means on both sides of the divide.

Colwill featured from the bench in Cardiff's thumping 3-0 win when the teams last met in January 2025, while he was an unused substitute when his side won in Swansea five years ago.

He has yet to start a south Wales derby but, as a leader of this new-look Cardiff, Colwill is bound to put that right on Sunday.

"We're all really comfortable with this style of play," he says.

"It's just fine-tuning that last little bit and we'll turn those dominant performances into big victories. Hopefully that will start on Sunday."

#738. Celtic defend head of security amid Green Brigade row

The Green Brigade occupy a standing section at Celtic Park

Celtic have defended their head of security and the action taken against the Green Brigade last season after the fan group declared four supporters had been cleared over the incident that sparked a lengthy ban.

Five men were arrested and subsequently charged following a disturbance reported during a game against Falkirk on 29 October last year.

The Scottish champions released footage at the time which they said showed "around 100" supporters verbally abusing and assaulting a steward and two police officers.

The alleged flashpoint came after a ticket inspection at the rail seating section of Celtic Park, the club explained, as they outlined a ban on about 250 supporters, which lasted nearly six months.

The Green Brigade released a statement claiming Celtic's "irresponsible and vindictive claim" was intended to "smear", calling for suspensions on two supporters to be lifted while questioning the "credibility" of Celtic security chief Mark Hargreaves.

Celtic pointed out they play no part in criminal proceedings and added that they were not aware all had been completed.

The club said: "The conduct of the group witnessed that day was unsafe and completely unacceptable â it has no place at Celtic Park or anywhere in football. The club took reasonable and proportionate steps to deal with this conduct.

"Such was the seriousness of the incident that the club was called to attend a special meeting of the Safety Advisory Group of Glasgow City Council.

"Mark is a highly-qualified, dedicated professional who plays a crucial role at the club in ensuring the safety of our supporters."

When approached by BBC Sport Scotland, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Following a disturbance reported at Celtic Park, Glasgow, on Wednesday, 29 October, 2025, officers carried out enquiries and subsequently arrested and charged five men in connection.

"They were due to appear at Glasgow Sheriff Court and were reported to the Procurator Fiscal.

"The safety of all those working at or attending football matches remains a priority for Police Scotland."

#735. Man Utd trigger Fernandes' one-year contract extension

Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United in 2020

Manchester United have triggered their one-year option on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.

It is understood it was done relatively recently but both sides wanted to keep it private as negotiations around a new deal continued.

However, the Portugal international confirmed on Tuesday that those discussions had been paused. Sources say they will resume once United's league position has improved.

It is still uncertain whether an agreement can be reached. Marcus Rashford is currently United's highest-paid player following his return from Barcelona, but the club are reluctant to offer a comparable deal, which would be well in excess of Â£300,000-a-week.

Fernandes also remains ambitious and wants to challenge for major trophies, which seems unlikely at Old Trafford given the club's present predicament.

It leaves open the possibility of the 32-year-old leaving in January, or at the end of the season, although United would be entitled to a fee.

Fernandes has made 343 appearances for United, scoring 115 goals, since his Â£47m move from Sporting in January 2020.

Last season he broke the Premier League assists record and scooped all of the individual player of the year awards after an outstanding campaign as United finished third.

United had been open to selling Fernandes in the summer of 2025, with Saudi Pro-League club Al Hilal offering a huge deal.

After discussing the situation with his wife, Fernandes decided to stay, though he later said it "hurt" United were willing to sell him. He reiterated on Tuesday he was still ambitious to win the biggest honours in the game.

Fernandes is a doubt for Saturday's Premier League encounter with Brentford after returning from the Champions League trip to Sporting with a virus.

The playmaker, who scored both goals in the 2-2 draw with his former club, did not train on Friday.

It is anticipated Fernandes will declare himself fit to play, although the club's medical staff will have the final say and head coach Mauricio Pochettino said he would take a decision on his captain's fitness on Saturday morning.

"We are going to assess during the day and then tomorrow see how he is when he wakes up," said Pochettino. "We are not going to take any risks."

Pochettino is preparing for his first home game as Man Utd boss

Pochettino was criticised by former Liverpool and England midfielder Jamie Redknapp on The Overlap earlier this week.

Reference was made to the former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea coach high-fiving Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davidson after his side's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday as evidence Pochettino had lost his edge.

"When I saw Pochettino at Southampton and I saw him at Tottenham, he looked like he had that Argentinian dog in him," said Redknapp.

"I look at him now and he's high-fiving everyone, he's got the bracelets on, he's got the barnet. I think he's gone too nice."

It seems someone had mentioned the observation to Pochettino as he went off on a tangent at his Friday news conference when asked about a "crazy" first week that included red cards, refereeing errors, disallowed goals and a drone filming training.

"What are we going to do? Start to cry?" he asked. "No. We have to be strong, believe and keep going. I cannot judge the past. Who am I to do that? I was in Cincinnati. I was outside. I need to shut my mouth, say nothing and start from now.

"Sometimes we are so confusing two words that means something similar; nice and good. I am not nice. We have to be good. It is a different thing. We know when we need to push, when we need to be strong, and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything.

Pochettino also confirmed Â£70m midfielder Carlos Baleba is expected to be out until the last week in January with the hamstring injury he sustained against Roma on 3 November.

Forward Rashford had begun to do individual work outside as he tries to recover from a hip problem that has kept him out since 13 October.

#734. Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But the country could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years ago.

Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:

It has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

#731. Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Pamela Yeh is a professor of evolutionary biology at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Pamela Yeh with her mother in Los Angeles, California, in the late 1970s.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

There are few things in this world that are more universal than grief. And yet, each person’s own particular grief can feel as unique as the person they are grieving for. I have been in academia for decades, but have heard little about grief in that time, so I wanted to share a few tips that helped me get through the early stages of grief when my mother died last year.

My mother grew up in deep poverty in Taiwan and she worked relentlessly throughout her life to give me and my siblings many opportunities. She was the first in her family to go to college, and at 23 years old, she moved to Canada to work as a nurse. After a few years of enduring Canadian winters, she had had enough and moved to sunny California. She met my dad there, and a few years later she gave birth to my sister, then me and then my brother. She raised us while working several jobs as a nurse. She cheered the three of us on throughout our lives. That’s not to say that she ever fully understood my career: she once described my work (I am an evolutionary biologist, specializing in birds and bacteria, at the University of California, Los Angeles) as “counting birds”.

She was adventurous, but between her family and work responsibilities, she didn’t have much time to travel. So, once she retired, I took her on fieldwork and conference trips with me whenever I could — to China, the Netherlands, Italy, Mexico, Japan and throughout the United States.

When her grandchildren came along, she helped them to learn how to read, to do maths and to speak Chinese. In the last years of her life, I had a small house built for her in our back garden in Los Angeles, so she would always be close to me. When you lose someone who is extremely close to you, your world is never the same.

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

In the weeks and months after she died, I found myself in a fog of shock and grief. I felt the need to be moving constantly: running, walking the dog, cleaning the house. At times, I could not be certain of my ability to conduct the high-level abstract and conceptual thinking that academia often requires, so I turned to Trevor Price, my former PhD adviser at the University of California, San Diego (who is now at the University of Chicago, Illinois). I explained my brain fog and deep grief, and he read over my work and made sure that I didn’t miss any crucial scientific arguments in some of the papers I was writing. Although I graduated more than two decades ago, he did not hesitate for one second to help me.

People won’t know that you need help until you reach out. And the earlier you do it, the more time and energy you can give yourself and the easier it will be for others to help.

Here are some tips that helped me to navigate the academic world while grieving.

Ideally, you should determine what support is available before it is needed. Institutions often have all sorts of resources and benefits for people experiencing grief. These might include time off for a bereavement, leave for family care, counselling and a break from teaching classes. I never knew, until my mother passed away, that I could have taken paid leave to take care of her while she was unwell: she had a debilitating stroke five months before she died. Make sure you understand (and ask questions) about your work contract and what your employer offers.

Sometimes, a family member’s illness can occur suddenly, and other times it might start off as one condition and snowball into something else. Talk to the chair of your department and to your colleagues as early as possible about getting cover for your courses and committees. Be creative and brainstorm which other people — including your colleagues, former advisers and former students and postdocs — might be able to step in and give your conference talks, guest lecture for your classes and conduct other activities that you might need help with.

Pamela Yeh (centre) with her parents, husband, son and dog on the front steps of her home in Los Angeles, California, in 2014.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

I learnt this the hard way. I did not reach out to people early enough and was unrealistically optimistic about my mother’s health trajectory. While I waited for her to get better, I was so panicked about the thought of losing her that I became incapacitated. I couldn’t focus and, at times, I could barely do simple tasks such as answering e-mails, or making appointments for meetings. I told myself as soon as she was better, which would be any day now, I would catch up. And so, I didn’t have a realistic plan in place when she died.

You have to accept that you might not be at your best when it comes to research productivity, mentoring and teaching while you’re grieving. Ask someone to help with advising your students, and rely on colleagues or former students. You might have to reduce the frequency with which you meet your students, hold laboratory meetings and work with collaborators, and resort to advising through e-mail and video calls. And you might have to give less detailed comments on your students’ writing. I did all of the above during the first few weeks and months of grieving. I had an especially hard time giving advice to my graduate students who were doing field work. Ellie Diamant, a former PhD student of mine who is now a biologist at Bard College in Annandale-On-Hudson, New York, generously stepped in and met with many of my students. It took me a while to understand and accept that I simply wasn’t going to meet the normal standards I set for myself while going through this difficult time.

From the skyscrapers of New York to the ancient Parthenon in Athens, the Beaver Moon supermoon put on a spectacular show for skywatchers around the world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.

November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.

Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.

Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in New York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.

Hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of New York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon snapped a series of stunning photos from the International Space Station on Nov. 24, November full moon slipped out of view below Earth's horizon, while being gradually deformed by the warping effect of our planet's atmosphere. "Moonset today from space station - no edits to these photos from 400mm lens," Menon wrote in a post on X.

Heading back down to Earth Salih Zeki Fazlioglu took a colorful photo of the Beaver moon illuminating a thin veil of clouds above Istanbul, Turkiye, as reflected sunlight competed with the artificial glow of the city below for the viewer's attention.

This shot of the lunar disk looming over the Old Post Office Pavillion in Washington D.C. was captured by David Ake, with the pink sky complementing the orange and red leaves of autumn.

Our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.

"Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up."

This striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.

Allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.

"Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image."

Moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?

Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.

That Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.

Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

Feeling inspired to capture your own supermoon photos? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the moon and browse our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography because you don't have long to wait!

The final supermoon of 2026 rises in just a few short weeks on Dec. 23 and it just so happens to be the closest full moon of the year, passing just 221,668 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth at the point of maximum illumination.

So no excuses! We'd love to see your photo in our inbox next month.

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your full moon photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.
