#728. Sutton's predictions v Kings of Leon drummer Nathan Followill

Arsenal co-chairman Josh Kroenke should probably turn his phone off if the Gunners fall behind against Manchester City on Sunday.

Chris Sutton's predictions guest this week, Kings of Leon drummer and City fan Nathan Followill, is good friends with Kroenke - and says he will be in touch if the game is going City's way.

"I'm super excited for this weekend and I've got my smack talk ready for Josh already," Followill told BBC Sport.

"I've heard about the City fans with their inflatable bananas and I need to get myself one. My wife is going to be like 'er, an inflatable banana just arrived in the mail - do you know anything about that?'

"We are going to win 4-2 so I will be texting Josh throughout the game... and, after Erling Haaland's second goal, I will send him a picture of me kissing the banana!"

AI has also made its predictions, and you can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.

Followill got a behind the scenes tour of Etihad Stadium and City's training complex when Kings of Leon played next door at Co-op Live arena in 2024. "It's a beautiful stadium, and an amazing set-up," he said. "Their practice pitches are better than most college pitches in the US."

Followill has supported City for more than 20 years, external and his children have followed in his footsteps by becoming Blues, despite the best efforts of his next-door neighbour in Nashville, as well as Kroenke.

"When my kids were born, they both received a full Arsenal kit - head to toe - in the mail from Josh," he explained.

"Both times, they were returned to sender - instantly.

"My son and daughter are both City fans now, but my neighbour, Jeremy Connor, is Tottenham, and I mean flying the flag full on.

"When they lose, you can hear him screaming - and when they win, you can hear him screaming too.

"His son is trying to convert my son to Spurs and I am like 'that is never going to happen in this house!'"

Chris Sutton and Nathan Followill were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Followill says it was eye-opening to watch City's boys and girls' teams play when he visited their training campus. "I had no idea how much they put into developing kids from the youngest ages all the way up," he said. "That was probably the most impressive thing for me - to see how many young kids were out there, with the ultimate dream of pulling on that blue shirt one day."

Chelsea have scored and conceded 20 goals so far this season, which kind of sums up where they are at.

Xabi Alonso's side have also lost as many league games - five - as Manchester United, and United are in crisis.

Alonso is not under pressure, or anything like that, but if they lose this game too, you can imagine the mood of the club - and it won't be good.

Apparently their fans were singing 'you don't know what you're doing' at him after their defeat by Leeds - which is what they sang at me when I was there.

Alonso needs to decide on a shape and a way of playing, and stick with it.

Anything could happen here, because Nottingham Forest's form is hardly convincing either.

They tore Manchester City apart in their previous home game, before the international break, but can they really dig out another result like that here?

I think they will go about it in a similar way, and be aggressive and have a real go at Chelsea... and I don't see Chelsea's defence keeping them out.

Nathan's prediction: No-one thought Forest would beat us, and while Chelsea need a big result, I can see Forest getting a point here. 1-1

We talked about Leeds on the Monday Night Club and how they have upgraded their team with the players Daniel Farke bought over the summer.

Farke strengthened in the areas he needed to improve, but is still trusting some of the players who did well for him last season - the likes of Jayden Bogle and James Justin, who have been outstanding.

They are a really well-balanced team and they have good depth to their squad too. The only criticism would be that they are not usually free-scoring - they hit four against Chelsea but before then they had only managed 10 goals in their first 10 league games.

Leeds do not give much away at the back either, though, and I think that will be key in this game.

When I watch Coventry they are dynamic with their counter-attacks and I always fancy them to nick a goal like that.

Not this time, however. Leeds might take a while to break them down, but I think they will come out on top.

Nathan's prediction: Coventry play in sky blue too? Part of the reason I became a Manchester City fan was the kit, and I have always gravitated towards teams in light blue, so I am going to go with Coventry here. 0-1

I am at this game for 5 Live and I am not expecting much to change for Manchester United.

No-one thought it was going to be easy for Mauricio Pochettino to go in at United and turn things around. He has taken over a complete rabble.

United's draw in Lisbon on Wednesday was chaotic, but you also have to consider how Sporting have not got going in the Portuguese league or the Champions League this season.

That was not a great Sporting side. They are pretty average and Brentford will be a much bigger test.

The Bees are supremely well-organised and will be full of confidence, too, after putting four goals past Everton on Monday. They were against 10 men for the entire second half, but were 2-0 up by then anyway.

Pochettino needs something to cling to, but for him picking that backline must be like pinning the tail on the donkey. Whoever he picks, they are not very good.

I really want to be more positive about United, because I heard from quite a few of their fans last weekend, but this prediction is about as positive as I can be about them at the moment.

Nathan's prediction: It is tough for me to talk about United because in America we have a saying 'don't kick a man when he's down' and it's pretty rough for them right now... but I'm not going to lie, it is nice to see United this low in the table.

I don't think it is the manager that is the problem for United right now, so I don't think Pochettino coming in is going to be an instant fix. They've got some growing pains to get through, and I won't be disappointed to watch that.

When I watch the Premier League at home, Brentford always cracks me up because I am huge fan of The Office and I just imagine a bunch of David Brents out there, just running around the pitch, which is a very funny thing for me.

I know I just said don't kick a man when he's down, but I don't think United would be nice to us if we were down there... so, I think the David Brents are going to win. 1-2

I actually think Villa will win this game 2-1 but I want to make it clear the scoreline I have gone for is from my commentary colleague, Alistair Bruce-Ball, who is an Ipswich fan - a fake one, but still a fan.

I asked him about this game when we were in Belgium for Liverpool's Champions League game on Wednesday. He will be at Portman Road on Saturday for 5 Live and he is backing the Tractor Boys to get something, so I am doing the same out of respect for him.

Ipswich really need a result too. They have gone five league games without a win and, with Hull and Coventry both winning last week, they are the lowest placed of the promoted sides.

That is never a good thing, and it feels like Gary O'Neil's side are in a precarious position at the moment, where they are getting sucked towards the bottom three.

I've been surprised to see Villa hit a bit of a sticky patch too, with three successive league draws and no wins in six in all competitions, so it will be interesting to see if they are any better here.

Nathan's prediction: Villa have had some surprising results recently but I do think they will win this. 1-3

I was in Bruges to watch Liverpool in midweek and it was interesting to see two of their players who came in for some heavy flak last season, Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, both shine.

Isak is looking like the player who Liverpool thought they signed in 2025. He is finding his rhythm, and Wirtz also seems to be in a really good place confidence-wise. When I watch them now, it feels like something is going to happen.

There are other positives for Reds boss Andoni Iraola too. I know there will be a debate about Bradley Barcola's end-product but I love watching him in full flow when he is running past defenders - there is no better sight in football than moments like that.

Rio Ngumoha is exciting as well, and he has such a good football brain which makes him even more dangerous.

Everything points to a Liverpool win, but I am hesitant to just go with that because Everton are coming off the back of a drubbing by Brentford. You can imagine David Moyes giving his side a miserable old week and getting stuck into his players.

I didn't think James Tarkowski should have been sent off in that game, but he will be suspended here. It is his absence that swings it for me because he is a real leader for Everton.

Nathan's prediction: Everton are usually the underdogs in this game but both teams are pretty level at the moment. One of our record producers is a huge Liverpool fan so he won't be happy with me... but I am going to say Everton will take it. 2-1

I was at Newcastle's draw with Arsenal last week and, in fairness to Magpies boss Matthias Jaissle, he changed things around at half-time and got his reward.

Jaissle needed that half of football, because I don't think the Newcastle fans have been too convinced by his approach, but this is another very tough game for him.

Brighton probably still can't believe they lost to Hull last week - but lightning is not going to strike twice.

Nathan's prediction: I have to give a shout out to my statistician Lucy here, because there were a couple of teams I didn't know a lot about and she gave me some good insight. So, Brighton have scored a lot of goals this season and I think they will get more here. 3-1

Thomas Frank has got a huge task at Crystal Palace. They are conceding so many goals.

Losing Maxence Lacroix and Marc Guehi from their defence was like Robbie Williams and Jason Orange leaving Take That, because they were never going to be the same without them.

I still think Frank has got some decent attacking players, however.

The Hull keeper, Konstantinos Tzolakis, looks like a great signing. I don't know how he made some of his saves against Brighton and he probably doesn't know himself either.

Brighton should have buried them and I think Palace will get plenty of chances too.

Fair play to Hull for their spirit and the way they scrap for each other, but I still think they are going to go down.

Hull fans are probably wondering if I am ever going to predict they will win a game... the answer is no, at least not this week anyway.

Nathan's prediction: Palace have given up 27 goals in 11 games which is a lot. Hull have surprised a few people this season and I am backing them here. 0-2

Bournemouth are on a long winning run in the league but I've been impressed by Fulham whenever I've watched them.

Alvaro Arbeloa's side have not been great at home, with only one win at Craven Cottage so far, so I am going with them to get another draw - which would be their fourth in a row.

Nathan's prediction: Both these teams have picked up a lot, so this is a tough one to call. 2-2

Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi must think a lot of 18-year-old midfielder Luca Williams-Barnett after picking him for their win over Ipswich.

I love to see managers trust young players like that, especially because Spurs have had such a tricky season so far.

It will be interesting to see whether De Zerbi picks him again here, but I feel like the outcome of this game is more dependent on which Sunderland we see.

They picked up a good point at Villa last time out, but they never seem to be quite the same after they have played in Europe, like they are doing this week.

The Black Cats will be without injured duo Brian Brobbey and Granit Xhaka for this game too, so I don't think they will have enough to win it.

Nathan's prediction: Dave Stewart from Eurythmics lives in Nashville too and is a good buddy of mine - and he is Sunderland until death! He is such a die-hard fan that every time we have dinner, we will sit there and talk about 'Haway the Lads' and just shoot the breeze about Sunderland.

So I am going to back them in this one, because of Dave and also because of my neighbour Jeremy, who I mentioned earlier.

Jeremy was especially cocky when they had Harry Kane and he would just talk so much smack - I always knew if they were doing good because I'd get a text from him. So, because Jeremy is such a cocky little Spurs fan, I am saying Sunderland will win. 2-1

I always enjoy this game because of Gabriel's battle with Erling Haaland, but it is in midfield where I think it will be decided.

Manchester City have spent a lot of money on players in that part of the pitch but Enzo Maresca has not found the right combination yet.

Somehow Maresca has got to find a way of nullifying Declan Rice, but that will be very difficult because Rice is just an absolute machine.

You can never rule City out because of Haaland's ability to score goals but the only result I see here is an Arsenal win, and I am going for a classic Gunners scoreline.

Nathan's prediction: This is the big one! It's huge. I feel really good about it, too. Arsenal are riding so high at the moment, I feel like we might catch them snoozing.

I predict Haaland will get two goals, Phil Foden will get one too and we will end up with four. 2-4

After drawing a blank since week two, Chris finally picked up another win in week 11 - and it was his spot-on prediction for Liverpool to thump Manchester United 4-0 that sealed the deal.

That meant he got three correct results, including two exact scores - at Anfield, and Tottenham's 2-0 win over Ipswich - giving him a total of 90 points.

In a tricky week for predictions, where Liverpool were the only team to start the weekend in the Premier League's top six who won, it was those exact scores that made all the difference.

Chris' guest, undisputed world champion boxer Lauren Price, the BBC readers and AI also all got three correct results.

But the BBC readers were the only ones to also get an exact score - in the Spurs game - giving them 60 points.

Lauren and AI both ended up on 30 points - AI did call Newcastle's draw with Arsenal correctly, but it was wrong about Bournemouth's win over Nottingham Forest, which everyone else got right.

Not many of you got that Liverpool-United scoreline correct, either.

From around 27,000 predictions, the most popular scoreline picked was a 2-1 home win and only 570 of you went for 4-0.

"When has AI ever gone for a 4-0?" said Sutton. "That's what the crowd wants. The crowd don't want AI - who wants mathematics?

"The crowd want gut-feeling and instinct. I think I should get 1,000 points for that prediction, because I was brave enough to go for it."

For the first time this season, there were SIX games where no-one made a correct prediction - who thought it was easy?

The biggest shock of the week was Leeds' 4-1 victory at Stamford Bridge. Again from around 27,000 predictions, more than 3,600 (14%) of you did back Daniel Farke's side to win... but just 11 of you saw that scoreline coming.

#727. How JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes’ Romance Unraveled After 1.5 Years

After JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes fell in love on Celebrity Big Brother, their relationship was unable to stand the test of time, ending a year and a half later.

JoJo Siwa has long danced to the beat of her own drum, and she’s back to doing it alone.

While Siwa came out as a lesbian in 2023 after previously describing herself as pansexual, the Dance Moms alum proved sexuality can be an ever-evolving spectrum when she revealed she and British reality star Chris Hughes had fallen in love.

What began as a close bond while filming Celebrity Big Brother in the UK soon turned into something more after the season wrapped in the spring of 2025, as the pair confirmed their romance that May.

In the time since, Siwa reflected on how meeting Hughes changed what she thought she’d understood about her sexuality, having “always been grossed out by dudes.”

“Chris is a very conventionally hot dude,” she explained on the Wildmen podcast in September. “[But] I thought [he] was just another friend. Once I realized that I wasn't grossed out by the thought of him being a boy, I was like, ‘Whoa.’ It was weird because I'd never thought that before.”

In fact, as she’d never felt a spark for her “conventionally hot” male friends, Siwa was taken aback when her feelings for Hughes began to trend towards the romantic in the Big Brother house, admitting, “I just never thought it was possible.”

And though she also noted Hughes was “very much so the special dude” that could break her previous assumptions about her sexuality, Siwa has also been candid about how previously labeling herself as lesbian never quite felt right.

"I did that because of the pressure," Siwa—who dated Kylie Prew, Avery Cyrus and Kath Ebbs prior to Hughes—told the Daily Mail in 2025. “You just get put in this world where you feel like, because you now have said, 'Oh, I'm a lesbian,' you have to be a lesbian."

But everything changed after meeting Hughes, with the pair both raving about their connection.

“I feel so relaxed and at ease with where I'm at,” Siwa told E! News in July 2025. “I feel so happy and peaceful that the love that I feel is so real. You can't really help who you fall in love with.”

And the feeling was more than mutual, with Hughes telling E! that same month, “She's literally the love of my life, but she's also my best friend. Like, we sit and do nothing together."

And with hopes expressed for future babies and rings given at Christmastime in the months after, it seemed like Siwa and Hughes were in it for the long haul.

That is until Nov. 2026, when their breakup was confirmed by multiple outlets.

Though neither Hughes nor Siwa shared additional insight into their split in the immediate wake of the news, the breakup came as a shock to fans.

After all, just days earlier Siwa confirmed “having a baby” was at the top of her personal agenda during an appearance on the Petticoats Revolution podcast.

“Obviously that's not a career thing,” she continued, “but like a life thing.”

Now, however, it would appear Siwa will need to look elsewhere to start that next chapter.

For a complete look back at Siwa and Hughes’ road to romance, and their abrupt end, read on.

The couple's whirlwind romance unfolded for the whole world to see during their appearance on Celebrity Big Brother.

A year later, Siwa—who split from ex Kath Ebbs following her time on the U.K. the series—released the song "Serendipity" in honor of the now-couple's chance encounter.

"The only word to explain what happened on this day a year ago… Serendipity," Siwa wrote in an Instagram post. "Today, I’m reminded of the moment that quietly changed everything."

Less than a month after they put their bond on display in the Big Brother house and emphasizing they were just friends, Hughes and Siwa confirmed they were dating in late May 2025.

At the time, Siwa cheekily nodded at the romance during a cover of "Bette Davis Eyes" at one of her shows, in which she instead sang "Chris Hughes' eyes."

The Love Island alum joined Siwa at several stops of her Infinity Heart Tour, which spanned across Europe, the U.K. and the United States. In a sweet glimpse at their backstage moments, Siwa added of the tour in an Instagram post, "The show represents who I want to be as a person and the artist that I wanna be in this lifetime, and it’s translated so well to the crowd."

Siwa and Hughes stepped out for their first red carpet as a couple at the Dancers Against Cancer's 2025 Gala of the Stars in Beverly Hills, California.

Siwa shared a glimpse into the couple's favorite bonding activity: golfing in a sweet Instagram photo dump of her summertime adventures.

In September 2026, Hughes gave his followers a slice of life moment by filming Siwa arriving to his place in England—and naturally they shared a sweet embrace to boot.

October 2026: Coming Back Like a Boomerang

Siwa and Hughes turned the Gala of the Stars into a date night two years in a row by attending again in 2026.

Siwa proved her love for Hughes knows no bounds by teasing her next big step in life was to become a mom.

"That’s my next thing," Siwa teased during a Nov. 2026 appearance on the Petticoat Revolution podcast. "Career is doing her thing. She’s always there. She's been there for 15 years. She'll keep going, she'll keep being there.”

Just days after Siwa expressed her hopes for a baby, her breakup with Hughes was confirmed by multiple outlets, marking an end to their romance 1.5 years after it began.

The supermassive black hole, known as Dún Aonghasa, is unlike any other seen at a similar period of the early universe.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.

The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar.

The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun.

Quasars occur when supermassive black holes are surrounded by vast amounts of gas and dust on which they feed. The immense gravitational influence of the black hole causes this material, in the form of an accretion disk, to glow brightly and to blast out bright jets of plasma. That means quasars at the heart of galaxies in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs) like this one can often be brighter than the combined light of every star in the entire surrounding galaxy, but only briefly.

The newly discovered quasar, designated J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, is in this brief phase of its existence. It was discovered among millions of objects in 18 months of data from Euclid.

Euclid's initial observation of Dún Aonghasa was followed up by an array of ground-based and space-based telescopes, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). It was the JWST that determined the mass of this supermassive black hole.

What is interesting about Dún Aonghasa is that it is unlike other supermassive black holes seen at a similar period of the early universe. That's because this black hole is feeding relatively slowly. That means if it engaged in rapid feeding to reach its massive size, that period of gorging on gas and dust has either ended or it has paused.

That is something that further complicates our picture of supermassive black hole growth.

By staring back 13.1 billion years in time to see Dún Aonghasa, Euclid is also observing a crucial time in cosmic history when the first stars and galaxies were taking shape, and the clearing of cosmic gas was ending the dark ages of our universe by allowing light to travel freely.

Euclid's primary mission is improving our understanding of dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the expansion of the universe, and dark matter, the most mysterious "stuff" in the cosmos. Collectively, these aspects of the universe account for around 95% of its matter-energy budget and have come to be collectively referred to as the dark universe. Hence Euclid's nickname as the "dark universe detective."

This research, along with Euclid's discovery of at least 12 that date back around 13 billion years, shows that this pioneering space telescope launched in 2023 could also make a major contribution to our understanding of black holes and their growth.

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#725. Tom Brady Weighs In On Aaron Rodgers' Release From the Steelers

Tom Brady shared his thoughts on Aaron Rodgers being released from the Pittsburgh Steelers after Rodgers publicly criticized his coach Mike McCarthy.

Tom Brady is tackling his thoughts on Aaron Rodgers.

The retired NFL star shared his reaction to the quarterback’s release from the Pittsburgh Steelers, particularly after Rodgers made comments about Steelers coach Mike McCarthy sleeping during meetings.

“The sanctity of an NFL locker room is a very sacred place,” Brady told Fox Sports co-host Kevin Burkhardt during the Nov. 26 game between the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles. “And we shouldn't ever lose track of that as players.

“It’s a privilege to be in that locker room,” the 49-year-old continued. “You’re fighting with your teammates. You’re fighting with your coaches. You’re always acting as a team, together. [It] shouldn’t always be the place for private things to become public. That’s what I’ll say.”

The co-hosts also lamented the end of Rodgers’ previously illustrious career, with Burkhardt adding, “For the things that were said about Mike McCarthy and things from Aaron—who is the surefire Hall of Famer—if that's the last pass he throws, that's a really sad way to end.”

Brady agreed, noting that while Rodgers was a “tremendous” athlete, his behavior off the field “has nothing to do with his play style” on the field.

“I was fortunate to be around a lot of great teammates over the years, and what made a great teammate, to me, was you cared about your teammates and your coaches, and you cared about what the team was trying to accomplish,” the Super Bowl champ explained. “That supersedes any individual aspect of your game that you want to promote.”

“Again, I was very fortunate. I was in a great locker room. I played for my teammates. I played for my coaches,” he said. “There’s—nobody wins when the family feuds.”

For Brady, his relationships with his coaches and teammates mattered more than “winning a Super Bowl.” He noted that those bonds “transcend anything you do on the field.”

“It’s just unfortunate,” he shared. “I hate it and I hate to be even talking about it. But I just think it's a privilege to be in the NFL. You want to inspire the next generation of athletes and you always want to do it the right way.”

Brady’s comments came just one day after Rodgers was abruptly cut from the Steelers on Nov. 25, who he’d signed with in June 2025. Just before the news, Rodgers spoke candidly about his difficult relationship with McCarthy, including claiming that the 63-year-old would often fall asleep during important team meetings.

"We were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down and within 10 minutes began snoring," the 42-year-old recounted on the Nov. 25 episode of The Pat McAfee Show. "Woke himself up, was rattling his papers. We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again, and less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room like nothing happened."

He also said that the NFL coach was "not coming to everything you should be coming to as a play caller,” adding that McCarthy even missed meetings ahead of game day.

For a look at what else Rodgers has shared about the difficult relationships in his life, keep reading.

After growing up "in a really conservative, small-town environment" in Chico, Calif., Aaron Rodgers said in the Netflix docuseries Aaron Rodgers: Enigma, transferring from Butte College to University of California, Berkeley, was admittedly an eye-opening experience for him. "So that was fun, to have my ideologies tested."

But, as he recalled, he was already traveling a path that was taking him further and further away from how he was raised by dad Ed Rodgers and mom Darla Rodgers.

The "white, dogmatic church" he grew up in "didn’t really serve me," Aaron said. "It was very rigid in structure. I'm not a rigid person. Shame, guilt, judgment—it was like, 'We have the truth, our way or the highway, our way is heaven, your way is hell.' Even talking to my parents, it was very black and white. Somebody has to be wrong, somebody has to be right. I just slowly uncoupled from that in high school."

So being in a city like Berkeley "that challenged my beliefs" (and where he was sleeping in on Sunday after games instead of going to church), he continued, "definitely helped me to begin to question more things."

Desperately Seeking Spiritual Enlightenment

After capping off the Green Bay Packers' 2011-12 NFL season with a Super Bowl victory—which, until then, Aaron thought was the holy grail he was seeking—he started to wonder what else was out there.

"I really just desperately wanted to be more than  a football player," he said in the series, "and so I started my spiritual journey."

Aaron got into the teachings of progressive spiritual leader Rob Bell, author of What Is the Bible? (which the athlete is seen reading in the series), and started reading more philosophy and self-help books.

Appreciating what he found to be Rob's inclusive, nonjudgmental approach to faith, "He was a big help for me to totally unravel the religion of my youth," Aaron said in Enigma.

Through his readings, "I found a courage to speak my feelings better," he continued. "So I started to stand up to institutions of my youth, and that was everything from organized religion, my parents, dogma, ideology. That definitely changed the dynamics of my family, because I was just questioning all of it."

Winning a Super Bowl vaulted Aaron to another tier of fame, the athlete recalling how during the summer of 2011 he was "paparazzi'd" for the first time during a trip to Hawaii.

"I was like, 'F--k, life's different now," he said. And after he was on TV more, he added, "my whole ability to move around with relative anonymity changed."

He added, "I didn't do myself any favors with some of the girls I dated after that, that were in the public eye. I definitely hated it at first. Like really despised it. I enjoyed my private life. I enjoyed being able to go places. But from Super Bowl MVP, [league] MVP, State Farm commercials, that got a little more difficult."

While the doc flashed to pictures of him with three famous exes, that was the entirety of what Aaron said about his high-profile relationships with Olivia Munn, Danica Patrick and Shailene Woodley (who, incidentally, he was engaged to and didn't just date).

Olivia, who dated Aaron from 2014 until 2017, denied rumors that she played a role in her ex's estrangement from his family, saying on Andy Cohen Live in 2018, "He hadn't spoken to the parents and one brother for, like, eight months before we started dating."

Aaron reiterated to biographer Ian O'Connor, author of 2024's Out of the Darkness: The Mystery of Aaron Rodgers, that his issues with his family were "deep rooted" and Olivia "has nothing to do with all the years" they haven't spoken.

"There was a lot of times, when I became real famous," Aaron said in Enigma, "where I heard from a lot of people, including family members, who where it was like, ‘Your life is too big, we need you to be smaller. Be smaller, don't talk about your life.'"

Feeling woefully misunderstood, he continued, "It always hurt me because I just feel like you don’t see me. This is not something I ever desired or wanted, other than playing on Sundays. It can definitely change the people around your circle, because it can be intoxicating, the fame and notoriety. So, definitely relationships changed after that. Friendships, family."

Aaron said that, pre-estrangement, he wasn't "super-duper close" with everybody in his family anyway.

"I was close with my little brother," he recalled, referring to younger sibling Jordan Rodgers. "But in actuality it goes back to stuff from high school that kind of made me feel distant. Stuff in college, stuff post-college. And I was quiet about it. 'Cause I thought the best way to do it was, just don’t talk about it publicly. And what do they do?"

In 2016, Jordan appeared on The Bachelorette—and, incidentally, he's been married to rose-bearer JoJo Fletcher since 2022.

When he brought JoJo home to meet his folks and eldest brother Luke Rodgers, there were two empty chairs at the dinner table—purportedly for Aaron and then-girlfriend Olivia—and all of a sudden millions of people found out the Packers QB was estranged from the rest of the family.

"We miss our brother," Luke said on The Bachelorette. "We just are trusting that God brings things full circle. And just wish that everything would just get back to us being a family."

"They go on a bulls--t show and leave two empty chairs," he said in Enigma. "They all agreed this was like a good thing to do, to leave two empty chairs at a stupid dating show that my brother just went on to get famous—his words, not mine—that he ended up winning."

Aaron reiterated in the series that he was never even invited to the dinner, which was held during the NFL season.

A dinner "I was never asked to go to," he said, "not that I would have gone."

E! News reached out to Jordan, Ed and Darla for comment on what Aaron had to say in Enigma but has not yet heard back.

Jordan told E! in 2016 after his hometown episode aired that he "made a commitment to go on there and be honest with JoJo and make sure that she knew everything" about where he was coming from.

Aaron has embraced taking ayahuasca—"It's the hardest medicine possible, that I've tried"—as an essential part of his journey, also touting its healing power for "mind, body, spirit."

"I was searching, for sure," he said in Enigma. "My life was through one lens, of organized religion. Where are people in life finding deep peace and centeredness and presence outside of what I knew?"

Speaking of the divide between him and his family, Aaron said he "found a lot of resistance" once he started researching other religions and plant medicine, "doing things that, compared to what I grew up in, would be considered an alternative lifestyle."

As for his family, he continued, "You know, they’re living as best they can. That is, still engulfed in organized religion, which works for them. That's great. So as much as they might not like what they see, love and respect and gratitude for how I was raised, because it wouldn’t have turned me into who I am today."

"People ask me, 'Is there hope for a reconciliation?'" Aaron said. "I say, 'Yeah, of course. Of course.'"

He added, "I don’t want them to fail, to struggle, to have any strife or issues. I don't wish any ill will on them at all. It's more like this: We're just different steps on the timeline of our own journeys."

#724. England call up Wubben-Moy for World Cup play-off

England beat Greece 8-1 on aggregate in the first round of World Cup play-offs in October

Arsenal defender Lotte Wubben-Moy has been called up to the England squad for next month's Women's World Cup play-off ties against Ukraine.

The 27-year-old's inclusion follows the withdrawals of winger Lauren Hemp and defender Jess Carter.

Hemp is managing a minor injury sustained during Manchester City's defeat by Tottenham on Sunday.

Carter is unavailable for the two-legged play-off for family reasons.

Wubben-Moy has earned 19 caps since making her debut in February 2021.

Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses will travel to Spain to face Ukraine in the away leg on Tuesday, 1 December, with the second leg at Wembley on Saturday, 5 December.

#722. Work in progress but Liverpool find belief again with Iraola

Liverpool kept back-to-back clean sheets under Andoni Iraola for the first time this week

A year has passed, and there has been a world of change at Liverpool.

Thursday marked 12 months since the Reds lost 4-1 to PSV Eindhoven at Anfield in the Champions League, the culmination of their worst run of results in more than 70 years.

By the time the final whistle blew that night there were some boos, but Anfield was half empty and belief from the fanbase had evaporated as Liverpool lost for the ninth time in 12 games.

Arne Slot's side had won the Premier League title the season before, but that game against the Dutch side was arguably the nadir of his second campaign in charge. Steven Gerrard said that evening that Liverpool "just keep bleeding".

The bleeding did stop somewhat, and Liverpool qualified for the Champions League, but it was a campaign that left Slot wounded and, come the end of the campaign, he was sacked.

Everyone has moved on in one way or another. The PSV game is in the distant past now.

And after a dizzying few days where Liverpool have scored seven without reply across the Premier League and Champions League, beating Manchester United and Club Brugge, Andoni Iraola's side are giving fans reasons to start believing again.

That is just as well, because Sunday is derby day against Everton.

"You can really see this manager stamping his philosophy and his way of playing on the team," former Liverpool captain Gerrard said on BBC Radio 5 Live this week.

"They are playing a lot faster, a lot more intense, playing a lot more vertical and getting it forward a lot quicker.

"It's a lot more exciting to watch than it was at the back end of last season."

Everton and Liverpool fans debate Sunday's Merseyside derby

When Liverpool lost to Arsenal at the start of November, they were threatening in phases against the reigning champions but finished the game without a shot on target - despite starting with three attacking players who cost more than Â£100m each.

But they have now scored 10 goals in their past three games, with that trio of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola delivering 10 goal involvements between them.

Both Isak and Wirtz are in their best form since making the move to Liverpool in 2025 and both spoke in Bruges this week about how good they are feeling. Isak has four goals in his past four matches while Wirtz has scored in each of his past three.

"It's a dream situation for Wirtz now," said Gerrard.

"Under Iraola, he has given him more freedom, more licence to take risks and to be the difference maker."

Combined, Wirtz and Isak have surpassed their total goal involvements from last season and, alongside the likes of Barcola, Cody Gakpo, Victor Munoz, Rio Ngumoha and Hugo Ekitike - once he returns from injury in January - Liverpool have a youthful and vibrant attack that can rattle fear into defences across Europe.

"It's not just about those two [Isak and Wirtz]. If we play well, someone will score," said Iraola. "If we have more chances then the opposition, someone will score."

Iraola will also be pleased that his midfielders are getting high up the pitch and scoring too, with Alexis Mac Allister and Dominik Szoboszlai getting nine goals between them this season.

The challenge now is for the frontline to deliver consistently and crucially, in those games against the best opposition. In the Champions League, Liverpool have scored 17 times in five games, but it hasn't gone unnoticed that they failed to score once across 180 minutes against Manchester City and Arsenal.

Isak and Wirtz in a 'good place' - Iraola

Like he did against LASK, Iraola opted to rest Virgil van Dijk against Club Brugge and the centre-back duo of Jeremy Jacquet and Ronald Araujo helped to keep a clean sheet. From the eye test alone, Liverpool are looking more assured defensively and Araujo's ability to fill in across the backline is a big part of that.

Admittedly, they have failed to replace the attacking quality that Trent Alexander-Arnold provided, but Araujo is a trusted option and a fan favourite while left-back Milos Kerkez is finding his feet under Iraola after a difficult first campaign. Iraola said Wednesday's game against Brugge was Kerkez's best display of the season.

Van Dijk and Jacquet in particular have excelled, while Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni are on their way back from injuries.

Liverpool conceded 53 goals in the Premier League last season, their most in a 38-game campaign in the competition, and it looked like nothing had changed when they conceded twice against both Newcastle and Nottingham Forest in their first two games this season.

But since then they have kept clean sheets against Ipswich, Fulham, Bournemouth, high-scoring Brighton and Manchester United.

And it is worth noting that under the guidance of Tommy Elphick, one of Iraola's assistants responsible for defensive set-pieces, and Lewis Mahoney, the set-piece analyst, Liverpool are no longer conceding for fun.

It is still an area opposition teams are targeting, and they have conceded four non-penalty set-piece goals in the Champions League and EFL Cup, but their rate of 2.3 xG (expected goals) conceded per 100 opposition corners is the best in the Premier League.

It was quite the sight to see Iraola deliver Jurgen Klopp-style fist pumps with a smile in front of the Kop after Sunday's 4-0 win over Manchester United.

"It's not something that I normally do," he said. "But in that moment I felt like everyone was expecting, and I think we were all celebrating."

His side were rampant - albeit against a poor United side who were down to 10 men early on - and could easily have scored more if they were ruthless.

With the Merseyside derby next on Sunday and a chance to close the gap to four points on Arsenal, before the Gunners take on Manchester City later in the afternoon, Iraola will be keen to temper expectations.

Any talk of a title challenge seems premature, and Iraola is of the belief that you must wait until halfway through the campaign before "thinking and understanding" the table - but Liverpool are a side on the up.

From all of the managerial changes in the summer, Iraola has arguably had the strongest start, with his replacement at Bournemouth, Marco Rose, impressing too.

Fixtures come thick and fast now, with three games in the space of seven days coming up, starting with the short trip to Hill Dickinson Stadium. Liverpool host Sunderland on Wednesday before going to Chelsea next Saturday.

"To enjoy it, there is only one way: to win the game," Iraola said on Friday.

It is early doors, but the Anfield hierarchy wanted a fresh beginning when he was appointed and, after a stuttering start, confidence is rising under the Spaniard.

Win against their arch rivals on Sunday and that optimism will only grow.

'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith

#721. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

This article was originally published in German.

Hera is arriving to surveil the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission that slammed a kinetic impactor into a double asteroid system four years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After a two-year journey, the Hera spacecraft is arriving at the Didymos double asteroid system, and its first images are being released to the public today (Nov. 25).

The European Space Agency's (ESA's ) Hera probe launched atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 7, 2024. Its destination is the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos, a "rubble pile" asteroid, and its smaller moonlet Dimorphos. NASA slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in 2022 in the historic DART test, which confirmed that such an impact can alter the trajectory of an asteroid.

Hera arrives at Didymos today, and ESA is sharing the first close-up images from the mission in a free online livestream. ESA's livestream starts at 1:45 p.m. ET (1845 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 25). Watch it live here, courtesy of the European Space Agency.

At Dimorphos, Hera will inspect the wreckage caused by DART (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), humanity's first test of planetary defense. The test was designed to see if the orbit of a threatening asteroid could be altered, taking it off a potential crash course with Earth.

The DART mission succeeded, shortening Dimorphos' orbit by just over 30 minutes, showing that kinetic impacts can indeed alter the trajectories of asteroids.

Hera will now show up to the crash scene and study the impact crater left by DART and inspect any changes the collision caused. Scientists are thrilled by the prospects.

"ESA's Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know," the mission's principal investigator Patrick Michel said in an ESA statement. "How did the impact change Dimorphos? What is the mass of the asteroid and which of its properties explain its response to DART impact?

"Hera is carrying out a thorough investigation ever of a deflected asteroid, packed with scientific firsts, to give us a complete and unbiased picture of humankind's first planetary defense test."

ESA has already shared some of the remarkable images Hera has captured en route to Didymos, including a breathtaking image of both asteroids as Dimorphos cast its shadow on its larger companion in a deep-space double-asteroid solar eclipse.

Hera even stopped by Mars on its way to the asteroids, snapping pictures of its moon Deimos.

Hera will remain at the Didymos-Dimorphos system for months, deploying cubesats that will study the asteroids with visible and infrared light cameras and radar instruments.

Through Hera, scientists hope to refine planetary defense techniques so that, should the time ever come, humanity has options for defending itself against incoming space rocks like the one that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

"Through many years of hard work our international collaboration managed to do just that, and for the very highest of intentions: to help make Earth safer," said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli.

Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.

#719. Ranking the Premier League's ultimate free-kick specialists

Dip, swerve, curl, whip. Hours spent mastering the craft of a great free-kick ensure those that ripple the back of the net are particularly satisfying.

This week we are digging into the Premier League's all-time best takers.

The number of goals scored from direct free-kicks has gradually decreased over the past two decades (boo!) with a rising focus on generating higher-quality chances, rather than having a pop from range.

It is perhaps unsurprising then that James Maddison is the only current player in the competition's all-time top 25 free-kick scorers, after James Ward-Prowse returned to Championship side Southampton in the summer.

Dominik Szoboszlai, however, is bucking the trend with five since joining Liverpool from 32 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 15.6% and almost a third of his total Premier League goals.

He looks on course to become a free-kick great, already only one goal behind Trent Alexander-Arnold and Leighton Baines and just two off the likes of Matt le Tissier, Wayne Rooney and Steven Gerrard.

The majority of top scorers hail from the halcyon era of, essentially, having a dig.

Yaya Toure belongs in another category - he misses out on the top 10 below but could be deemed a 'one-season wonder' in this realm, despite having eight years at Manchester City.

His prolific spell in 2013-14 deserves recognition, scoring four of his seven free-kick attempts that term - a staggering 57.1% conversion rate and by far the Premier League's best since Opta began collecting such data in 2006.

There is also an honourable mention for Louis Saha, the only man in the Premier League era to score a free-kick with each foot - with his left for Manchester United against Southampton in January 2004, and with his right for Everton against Fulham seven years later.

And while we are here, these are the goalkeepers who least liked facing them.

What we are looking for, though, are the real free-kick specialists - those players whose names evoke memories of ball meeting top bins.

For that reason, despite sitting joint-third on the scorers list with 12, Cristiano Ronaldo and Thierry Henry do not make it. They just scored too many goals - and too many great ones - to be renowned specifically for their set-pieces.

Fewer than 7% of Henry's 175 Premier League goals were free-kicks, netting one on average every 21.5 games. Ronaldo, meanwhile, tried his luck 167 times, scoring one roughly every 14 attempts.

The first spot up for grabs could have gone several ways - Maddison, as mentioned, has a decent shout to be included, and likewise Christian Eriksen who netted eight in the Premier League and also laid on 13 free-kick assists.

Frank Lampard has nine goals but also the most attempts on record - and the data only accounts for half his Premier League career.

Ashley Young is the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick

OK, the case for Ashley Young is in his longevity - he curled in a free-kick during the play-offs to help Watford win promotion in 2006 and was still scoring them almost two decades later.

At 39 years and 148 days old, Young became the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick in Everton's win over Wolves in December 2024. His seventh successful free-kick strike in the competition and the final effort of his 50-goal top-flight haul.

Young holds a decent conversion rate, scoring with 10.3% of his 68 top-flight attempts, while also chipping in with nine free-kick assists - only a handful of players have more since 2003-04.

Young's set-piece duties also tend to bookend his career. A trusted specialist at Watford and Aston Villa, he fell behind Ronaldo, Rooney and co at United but still popped up with a memorable long-range free-kick against the Hornets, his boyhood club.

Nolberto Solano netted nine times from free-kicks in the Premier League - although that tally may have been higher had he not shared set-piece duties with Laurent Robert for a chunk of his Newcastle career, while Alan Shearer chipped in too.

In fact, including spells at Aston Villa and West Ham, the Peruvian scored 18% of his top-flight goals with free-kicks.

He had a decent conversion rate. Opta data only goes back to 2003-04, but since then Solano, who also played for Aston Villa and West Ham, netted 10% of all his free-kick attempts on goal.

Solano scored free-kicks throughout his career, including his last goal for League One Hartlepool in 2011

Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard reckons Juan Mata is the best free-kick taker in Premier League history and the only player who outshines current Anfield star Szoboszlai.

I disagree, hence ranking the Spaniard eighth, but Mata can claim to be the most ruthless - he's scored a higher percentage of free-kicks than any player to have had at least 20 attempts since the stat-counting began in 2003-04.

The World Cup winner, who recently retired, netted eight in the English top flight from 49 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 16.3%.

Morten Gamst Pedersen was plucked from the freezing fjords above the Arctic Circle to score bangers for Blackburn, a left foot as crisp as the icy waters surrounding his former home in Tromso.

The hair-gelled Norwegian netted 34 Premier League goals in eight seasons at Ewood Park, with just shy of 30% of those coming from free-kicks - the fifth-highest proportion in the competition's history.

It puts the winger eighth on the all-time list with 10 goals from 158 free-kick shots - only Lampard and Ronaldo have attempted more since 03-04.

The diminutive Italian announced himself to the Premier League as he meant to go on. In his fourth Chelsea appearance, Gianfranco Zola scored his first goal from a belting long-range free-kick against Everton.

It was the first of 12 in the competition.

What sets Zola apart is all of those came after turning 30, having been a phenomenal set-piece specialist back in Serie A - he remains sixth on the all-time list there with 20, one behind Roberto Baggio and Francesco Totti.

And Zola learned from the best. As a youngster at Napoli, he would seek advice from the legendary Diego Maradona.

"He was always fond of making suggestions and giving advice to young players," Zola said.

"We had a particularly good relationship and I used to stay a bit longer on the training ground with him trying free-kicks and playing small games."

Gianfranco Zola scored 59 goals for Chelsea in the Premier League, with just over 20% of those coming from free-kicks

Something of a rarity, a free-kick expert at full-back - the Drogheda Roberto Carlos, as they used to call him (they didn't).

Ian Harte has, however, previously suggested the Brazilian and David Beckham provided him with dead-ball inspiration, and reckons he has a better conversion rate than that pair.

Harte is joint-eighth on the list of all-time Premier League free-kick top scorers but leaps to fifth here for the specialist nature of his impressive resume. He scored 10 in nine seasons with Leeds, 35.7% of his total Premier League goals.

Fans at Elland Road would also point towards perhaps Harte's finest performance, though, the Champions League quarter-final first leg against Deportivo in 2001 - the Irishman crashed in a free-kick before claiming two assists.

Ian Harte scored 10 free-kicks for Leeds in the Premier League - though his most famous came against Deportivo in Europe

Sebastian Larsson scored 26 Premier League goals, 11 of them directly from free-kicks - the second-highest proportion in the competition's history.

Give away a foul within range and the Swede could be deadly, with an impressive ratio of scoring one from roughly every nine attempts in the top flight.

Indeed, the midfielder is the only player to score at least 30% of his free-kick shots in two separate seasons - 2007-08 with Birmingham and 2011-12 with Sunderland.

"Seb Larsson was a quality player and he had that ability to have a magic moment," fellow ex-Sunderland star Marco Gabbiadini told BBC Radio Newcastle. "When he connected correctly, they were lovely goals."

"I practise free-kicks for about half an hour after each training session. It's not just about mastering technique - it gives you confidence," Larsson told FourFourTwo.

"I visualise the ball going where I want it to go and I don't hold back."

One of Larsson's free-kick goals came against former club Arsenal

Left foot like a trebuchet. Laurent Robert loved nothing more than winding one up from 30-plus yards out, lashing goalwards and hoping the ball hit the back of the net.

And, in fairness, the Frenchman was very good at it. In four seasons with Newcastle, he scored 11 free-kicks, a remarkable 47.8% of his total 23 Premier League goals.

Robert boasts the competition's best free-kick goals-per-minute ratio, netting one every 994 minutes - he did have well over 100 attempts - and is also the only player alongside Beckham to score five in one season.

However, it was one missed free-kick, the story goes, that may have sealed his fate when on loan at Portsmouth. Robert fired wildly into the crowd when trailing 2-1, which was said to have left boss Harry Redknapp fuming. He signed for Benfica a few days later.

Eleven of Laurent Robert's 23 Premier League goals were direct free-kicks

James Ward-Prowse holds good company. According to Opta Analyst, he is one of only six players from Europe's top-five leagues since their data began to score at least 10% of free-kicks, having attempted more than 100. Ronaldinho is among the others.

Ward-Prowse is also second to only Beckham on the all-time Premier League free-kick goalscorers chart, netting 17 of his 141 attempts (12.1%), throughout spells with Southampton, West Ham, Nottingham Forest and Burnley.

A dream pick for Fantasy Premier League managers, there was a time when Ward-Prowse standing over a dead ball felt inevitable - he netted four of his 10 goals in 2021-22 from free-kicks, while another four were penalties.

The midfielder grabbed another three the following season, with his final two proving winners against Everton and Chelsea.

Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola was certainly a big fan, saying: "Southampton have the best free-kick taker I have ever seen, or at least in the world right now."

Overall, almost a third of Ward-Prowse's Premier League goals came from free-kicks, while he leads the way since 2003-04 with 31 dead-ball assists, a third of those from free-kicks.

A trait that transcended football. Beckham's free-kick prowess had Hollywood screenwriters scrambling and kids in classic Predators practising bendy run-ups on muddy weekend mornings.

Beckham has scored more free-kicks in the Premier League era than any other player, not to mention iconic strikes for his country and in the Champions League.

Eighteen of those came in the English top flight, accounting for 29% of his total 62 goals in the competition for Sir Alex Ferguson's Manchester United, and perhaps more impressively 27% of all the free-kicks United have netted in the competition.

Beckham got up and running on his 48th United appearance in October 1996, during a shock 6-3 defeat at Southampton.

That was the first of three set-piece strikes he would score against the Saints, with all of Beckham's free-kick goals coming in different matches, while he netted from a dead ball for the final time with United before his move to Real Madrid in a 2-1 win at Everton in May 2003.

Beckham was deadly when laying on goals for others, too. Of his 80 Premier League assists, more than a quarter came from set-pieces, with 11 of those from free-kicks.

David Beckham scored 18 goals from free-kicks in the Premier League

#717. Satellites watch volcanic eruptions add new beaches on Iwo Jima | Space photo of the day for Nov. 25, 2026

Iwo Jima looks remarkably different from space after a volcanic eruption created new land extending the Japanese island's beaches.

On Oct. 27, Japan's Meteorological Agency detected an underwater volcanic eruption off the shores of Iwo Jima. Soon after this initial detection of the "submarine" volcano, satellites orbiting our planet started taking a look, observing to see what havoc this eruption might wreak.

When you compare the satellite images above captured by the Landsat 9 satellite's Operational Land Imager (OLI), you can see the stark differences between the island on October 26 before the eruption and weeks later on November 11.

The island was also observed by NASA's NISAR spacecraft as well as the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors. Together, this imagery gave researchers a more complete picture of how the eruption continued and the effects it left behind.

And amazingly, with satellite imagery experts have been able to show that the eruption has actually added more land to the island's beaches.

On Nov. 16, Japan's Coast Guard confirmed in a statement that about 125 acres (50 hectares) of new land is now connected to the island's southeast beach following the recent volcanic eruption.

This is not the first time that a volcano has created new land. Lava and ash from a volcanic eruption can solidify and accumulate, adding land material around the volcano or to a nearby coast if it is located offshore or underwater, as we saw in this case.

But these new landforms aren't always permanent fixtures. This new addition to the island's beach could easily and quickly be washed away by the waves, which happened on Iwo Jima just a few years ago in 2023. And experts expect the same thing to happen with this new land.

"I imagine we'll see this new land wash away within a few months," Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center who has previously studied landforms created by volcanic eruptions, said in a statement. "But we'll have to wait and see."

#714. Chromosome ‘glue’ could boost fertility by stabilizing ageing eggs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chromosomes are held together with protein structures called cohesins, but these diminish with age.Credit: Power and Syred/SPL

Researchers have engineered a ‘molecular glue’ that can stabilize chromosomes in ageing mouse eggs1. They say their artificial cohesion system could pave the way for improved fertility treatments for women over the age of 35.

Chromosomes in animal eggs are held together by protein structures called cohesins. These help to ensure that chromosomes divide correctly during the process of cell division. But the level of cohesins declines as women age, which can cause chromosomes to separate early and be distributed incorrectly. The resulting eggs can have too many or too few chromosomes, a condition known as aneuploidy, which is a cause of infertility, failed in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments and early pregnancy loss, particularly in women who are older than 35 years.

To prevent this premature separation of chromosomes in eggs, Melina Schuh, a biochemist at Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, and her colleagues designed an artificial system called TALhesin. The system uses engineered proteins that attach to regions of the chromosome in which cohesin is usually present; these proteins then bind to one another.

Many groups are trying to understand cohesin because it diminishes as women age, affecting fertility, says Bettina Mihalas, a reproductive biologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, but this is the first approach to replace the protein’s function with an engineered system. “It’s a very creative, well-engineered and well-thought-out approach,” she says.

The findings were published in Science1 on 26 November.

The researchers injected messenger RNA that encoded the engineered proteins into immature mouse eggs. The mouse eggs then produced the proteins. Using fluorescence microscopy imaging, the researchers confirmed that the TALhesin proteins attached to chromosome regions in which natural cohesin is usually lost.

The artificial system reduced the frequency of early chromosome separation in older mice aged 13 months, 17 months and 20 months compared with untreated eggs. In 17-month-old mice, the proportion of eggs without any premature chromosome-separation errors increased from 46.7% to 74.1% in those treated with TALhesin, similar to what is observed in eggs from young mice.

Chromatids — the two identical halves formed by a replicating chromosome — must separate at the right time during cell division. To enable this, the researchers added a ‘molecular scissor’ into their artificial system. This switched off the artificial cohesion system at the appropriate time.

The team has adapted the system to deliver engineered proteins that attach to regions of human chromosomes in which cohesin is usually present.

Experiments in donated human eggs showed that the TALhesin proteins accumulated in these regions. The researchers also found that chromosomes with high levels of the engineered proteins tended to have smaller distances between chromatids. This demonstrates that the TALhesin system holds the chromosomes together.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03874-7

Webster, A. et al. Science 394, 982–989 (2026).

#713. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.
