NASA is sending research aircraft and using satellites as the Army prepares to detonate degrading explosives in Iowa.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has sent three different research aircraft and is using a satellite-based instrument to support the U.S. Army's detonation of degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, the agency announced yesterday (Nov. 24).

After a week-long delay caused by public concern over the event creating clouds of lead and toxic materials, today (Nov. 25) around 10 a.m. EDT (1400 GMT) the U.S. Army has planned to execute a controlled detonation of five tons of aging explosives at the ammunition plant. The detonation follows concerns that cooling winter temperatures or attempts to chemically neutralize the materials could lead to an unexpected, uncontrolled explosion.

"In challenging circumstances such as this, you want the nation's best on the field. That is precisely why you call on NASA, putting our airborne and space-based sensors and some of the brightest scientific minds in the country to work," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in an online statement.

To support this detonation, NASA deployed three research aircraft: a P-3 Orion, a Gulfstream III from NASA's Langley Research Center and a B200 from NASA Ames. The agency is also monitoring the situation using its TEMPO (Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution) instrument which is mounted and orbiting Earth on a commercial satellite.

"Working alongside our partners across the federal government, NASA is utilizing its advanced scientific instruments and expertise to collect environmental and atmospheric data to inform the broader federal response," NASA stated.

The environmental monitoring using TEMPO is especially important as the materials to be detonated include lead azide and other toxic components that are causing not just environmental worries, but significant local concern over possible health repercussions. This concern is severe enough that, following detonation, officials are encouraging local residents to stay indoors with the doors and windows closed for 24-28 hours.

In fact, the CDC has activated an emergency response "to provide accurate public health communication and technical assistance," the CDC stated online. They have also offered additional guidance for locals to try and mitigate as much exposure to toxic materials like lead dust as possible.

In the map below, which comes from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers using satellite data, the highlighted area shows where surface deposits of lead is expected to exceed the maximum allowable amounts on surfaces per the Environmental Protection Agency.

While this planned detonation has unsurprisingly caused concern among locals and nationwide, Isaacman has urged the public not to mischaracterize the event as something larger.

"Even if it's hyperbole, it is irresponsible to characterize this as a 'Chernobyl event,'" he said online in response to someone likening the event to the infamous nuclear accident.

"When there is no reactor and there are no fission products. This is a controlled detonation of aging explosive material and is being handled in the most responsible way possible."

#710. Gayle King’s Son-in-Law Virgil Miller Dead at 45 After Cancer Battle

Gayle King's son-in-law Virgil Miller, the husband of her daughter Kirby Bumpus, died at 45 after a battle with cancer, CBS Mornings' executive producer shared in a memo obtained by multiple outlets.

Gayle King and her family are mourning a tragic loss.

The CBS Mornings host’s son-in-law Virgil Miller—who married her daughter Kirby Bumpus in 2020 before welcoming two children together—died at the age of 45 following a battle with cancer, CBS Mornings executive producer Jon Tower told staff in a Nov. 27 internal memo obtained by multiple outlets.

He added that King would be taking a week off from CBS Mornings “to help with family matters,” noting the 71-year-old would return the week of Dec. 7.

Tower did not share additional insight into Miller’s health battle.

Miller married King and ex-husband William Bumpus’ daughter Bumpus in December 2020, almost two years after the couple had announced their engagement.

Bumpus, 40, shared the news on Instagram in February 2019, posting a photo of herself and Miller as she showed off her engagement ring with the caption, “Here. WE. Go!”

But the duo—who shared son Luca, 5, and daughter Grayson, 2—had quite a different wedding than they’d imagined, as they married at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic at her godmother Oprah Winfrey’s Santa Barbara home. As King shared, the guest list was very tiny, encompassing Winfrey, her partner Stedman Graham, King and her son William Bumpus Jr., who officiated the nuptials.

“Strict covid rules I couldn’t even hug her on her wedding day that was haaaaard!” King wrote on Instagram in February 2021. “Not the wedding we planned in 2020 but my favorite son @willgb3 performed the ceremony... the day was gorgeous and so was kirby!”

And through the years, the journalist had been effusive in her praise of Miller.

For his birthday in July 2022, King praised Miller as her “fav son-in-law,” and adding that he was a “great husband to fav daughter @kirbybump & best dad to fav grandson.”

#708. Guy Fieri Debuts Shocking Gray Hair Transformation

Guy Fieri’s new, naturally gray hair stole the show on Thanksgiving, leaving many fans stunned after he debuted the look on Instagram.

Guy Fieri served up a major makeover alongside his turkey.

While the Food Network chef’s spiked, bleach blonde hair and goatee have long been his signature look, Fieri shocked fans with naturally gray hair in a Thanksgiving photo carousel.

In fact, while the 58-year-old pointed to his plate full of delicious looking food in the first slide, it was his hair that truly gobbled up fans’ attention.

“Your hair looks so good grey!!!! Dont [sic] go back to blonde,” one user wrote in the comments, while another added, “PLEASE TELL ME YOU'RE KEEPING THE GRAY HAIR!!!!”

But though Fieri’s bleached locks are now a natural shade, a second photo showing the Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives star helping himself to food revealed that his signature spikes are still firmly intact.

As for his Turkey Day celebrations, Fieri was joined by his and wife Lori Fieri’s sons Hunter Fieri and Ryder Fieri, as well as a whole other host of loved ones as they dined together in a covered pergola outside.

“Hope you all had an amazing Thanksgiving!!” Fieri captioned his Nov. 26 post, encouraging fans to “leave a comment sharing something you’re thankful for.”

Of course, those who have been staying tuned in to the chef’s journey through Flavortown over the years will know this isn’t the first time Fieri has stunned fans by cooking up a completely new look.

Back in January, Fieri shared a video to Instagram in which he’d lost both his facial hair and his blonde locks, instead appearing cleanshaven with brown hair upon his head, hair that was styled into a much more classic look than his usual.

“Hey there,” Fieri said in the Jan. 22 video clip as he stood before a lit birthday cake. “After so many years of celebrating my birthday as Guy, I thought this year I’d celebrate it as ‘just a guy.’ Happy birthday to me.”

But while the video sent shockwaves throughout the internet—with many users decrying the clip as AI—it was later revealed to be part of Fieri’s Super Bowl partnership with Bosch.

"My commitment to doing this was, 'Okay, we're playing big ball. And I'll play,’" he told Entertainment Weekly of the transformation. "What it turned out to be, what people are going to see, I'm just gonna turn my phone off for about three weeks after this, because people are gonna hammer me."

Meanwhile, his family wanted front row seats to the transformation.

“My wife said to me, 'I gotta see this,’” Fieri revealed. “‘I gotta be there for this.’”

As for how other stars celebrated Thanksgiving this year, read on.

The Nobody Wants This star took advantage of Thanksgiving to reveal she and husband Tyson Mason to announce she's pregnant with their second baby.

The Witcher alum proved it's not only his acting that is super, but also his grilling skills.

The “Honey Bee” singer and “Hollaback Girl” hitmaker snuggled in close as they expressed gratitude for their fans. As Shelton wrote on Instagram Nov. 26, “Hoping everybody has a happy Thanksgiving!!! Thankful for y'all!!!!”

The supermodel and jiu jitsu instructor showed off their model life with their 21-month-old son.

“The amount of goodness we experience in life depends on our ability to notice it," Bündchen captioned her Nov. 26 Instagram post, which also featured pictures of her and ex-husband Tom Brady's kids Benjamin, 16, and Vivian, 13. "Gratitude is contagious, and the more we can appreciate the beauty around us, the more joy we bring into our lives and the lives of others."

She added, "May we always find something to be grateful for, not just today, but every day. Happy Thanksgiving! Sending you all so much love."

It was a celebration for the girls as Dunham marked her first Thanksgiving as a mom alongside husband Luis Felber.

As she captioned the Nov. 26 Instagram post as the family went on a stroll, "Thankful."

You oughta know how excited the country music star is about the holiday season.

“Time for a little more peace, love and cowboys,” she wrote on Instagram Nov. 26. “Let the holiday shenanigans begin happy Thanksgiving from my family to y’all’s!”

The Freaky Friday star got reflective this Thanksgiving as she shared an image of herself stretching while enjoying an ocean view.

"Going to turn off the noise for a moment," she wrote on Instagram Nov. 26. "To all out there in this vast environment that we opt into, that if you're lucky enough to have one, the Thanksgiving meal is not hard. It's a roasted bird and potatoes."

"What's hard are the people with their binary and rigid ideas and judgments and petty selfishness," she added. "Today let's all be like Dolly [Parton] and be welcoming and gentle and generous."

The Red Table Talk host showed off her family's extravagant Thanksgiving set-up.

"Preparing for Thanksgiving dinner at the family abode," she wrote on Instagram Nov. 26. "Happy Day of thanks to you all and may you, your families and loved ones continue to be lifted and showered by the gifts of grace from the Highest. They may not always show up how we want them to … but they are there."

The chef cooked up more than a Thanksgiving meal—he also debuted naturally gray hair.

The actor was grateful for some one-on-one time this Thanksgiving.

#707. Hera spacecraft gets 1st up-close look at stadium-sized hole punched in asteroid by NASA DART mission

"The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid’s entire width."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.

NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept. 26, 2022, when it slammed into Dimorphos, the small moonlet of the much larger asteroid Didymos. The mission tested if such an impact could be deployed to divert an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Scientists have known for some time that this deflection attempt was successful; the system's orbit around the sun was lengthened by 33 minutes, but the European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera mission launched in October 2024 to travel the 120 million miles (194 million kilometers) to the Didymos system to observe the effect of the DART impact in greater detail.

Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically. The impact also appears to have blasted out hundreds of previously unknown boulders that are now circling the binary asteroids.

"Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same," Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said in a statement.

"Much to our surprise, the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width."

Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, detailed some of the changes to the impacted moonlet seen by the spacecraft: "As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit.

"Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size."

It wasn't all change for Dimorphos. Hera discovered that the boulder fields covering the regions of the moonlet not impacted look just like they did when DART imaged it in 2022.

Hera isn't finished with Didymos and its moonlet. The ESA spacecraft is currently in a rectangular orbit around the asteroid binary system, using its thrusters to maintain a distance of around 18.6 miles (30 kilometers). This allows Hera to continue observing Didymos and Dimorphos.

Hera will soon come to within around 8 miles (13 km) of the asteroids, capturing even more detailed images of the space rocks. Following this, it will deploy two showbox-sized CubeSats, which will get even closer to the asteroids.

The CubeSat Juventas will use low-frequency radar to probe the interior of Dimorphos, the first time this has ever been done for an asteroid, and will eventually attempt to land on the moonlet to measure its gravity. Meanwhile, the Milani CubeSat will prospect asteroid materials and dust around the Didymos system.

Together, Hera and its CubeSats will more precisely determine the mass of Dimorphos, which, when combined with information about the orbital change of the system, will be crucial in planning missions to deflect threatening asteroids.

Hera's observations were revealed on Wednesday (Nov. 25) at the dinosaur hall of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, Germany. That location isn't a coincidence: It is a stark reminder of why this planetary defense mission is so important. Especially if humanity doesn't want to go the way of the dinosaurs, whose rule on Earth ended when an asteroid fell from the sky."Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth. Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli explained. "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. "By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet."

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#705. Will 2024 version of Palmer ever re-emerge for Chelsea?

Cole Palmer joined Chelsea from Man City for Â£42.5m in 2023

Cole Palmer left the City Ground without having a shot or a touch in the opposition box as Chelsea lost 3-2 at Nottingham Forest on Friday night.

The 24-year-old forward started the season by registering six goal involvements in his first six league games (two goals and four assists), but his penalty against Manchester United is now his only goal contribution in the past six matches.

Last weekend, after his side were booed off following the 4-1 defeat by Leeds United, Palmer appeared reluctant to take part in the customary post-match acknowledgement of the supporters.

On his way off the pitch, he appeared to ignore the club's player support and development officer Willie Isa, a former Wigan Warriors rugby league player, whose role includes helping to ensure that acknowledgement takes place regardless of the result.

Palmer was then seen in a heated exchange with injured striker Joao Pedro as he headed down the tunnel.

His visible frustration comes during a difficult period for Chelsea under new manager Xabi Alonso.

Chelsea have lost their past three games. They have conceded 23 goals in their opening 12 Premier League matches, their highest total at this stage since the 2015-16 season, with Alonso facing criticism for the leaky defence and constant line-up changes.

One positive had been the attack, with Chelsea scoring 18 times in six matches, largely because of the link-up play between Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro.

However, that has dropped off. Club-record signing Rogers, who cost Â£117m in the summer, has also become less effective, while Joao Pedro is sidelined for now by a groin injury.

Some observers argue Palmer needs to step up to help lift his team out of this difficult period.

It is nearly two years since he produced the form of his life, breaking Chelsea's Premier League record with 39 goal involvements (26 goals and 13 assists) in the 2024 calendar year.

Now many are asking whether he can return to that level.

There are no concerns about Palmer's attitude or behaviour internally at Chelsea.

Senior sources inside the club say he has been ultra-focused behind the scenes, doing extra sessions and he is described as a "leader" by Alonso.

Both Palmer and Chelsea seem fully committed to each other.

In mid-April, deep into a dismal campaign in which Chelsea finished 10th having had three different managers, rumours were rife he was pining for a return to Manchester, with United - a club he still supports - linked.

When speaking to the Guardian, he added: "All my family are there, but I don't miss it. Maybe I'll miss it if I don't go for three months or something. But then when I get home I think there's nothing there for me anyway. I've got no plans to move from Chelsea."

A move to United was never seriously explored by any of those involved and Palmer re-established his commitment to Chelsea by signing a lucrative deal until 2034.

It made him among the club's highest-paid players and followed similar deals for Reece James, Moises Caicedo and Joao Pedro.

Palmer's mother, father and girlfriend were all present in the directors' box against Bournemouth after he signed the new deal.

Like the others who have recently renewed, Palmer has been reassured by the sporting leadership team that Chelsea are ambitious, out to win trophies and have learned from past mistakes, hiring a high-calibre manager in Alonso and signing three over-30 players for the first time in four years to add experience to their squad.

That said, Palmer has not hit the heights of his first 18 months under former manager Mauricio Pochettino, now in charge of Manchester United, and then early into Enzo Maresca's reign.

Having been nicknamed "Cold" Palmer after his goal celebration, where he shrugs his shoulders and pretends to be cold, his decline began in early 2025.

A persistent groin problem affected his form as the goals and assists began to dry up. Even so, Palmer produced man-of-the-match displays in the Conference League and Club World Cup finals to maintain his reputation as a big-game player.

He did not fully overcome the injury heading into the following season and his return of 10 goals and one assist in 25 matches represented a significant drop in output.

In a candid pre-season interview, Palmer explained: "The first few months, with me being injured, I just wanted to go out and play, which I probably shouldn't have done.

"Obviously I couldn't play how I wanted to play. It was a bad season personally with injuries but I feel good now."

He added the impact on how he wanted to play affected his ability to move on the pitch and strike the ball with power.

Palmer has also found the situation with England unhelpful.

Over the summer, he was said by multiple sources close to him and inside Chelsea to have been bitterly disappointed to have missed out on the World Cup squad.

It has been further impacted by criticism from manager Thomas Tuchel, who said he "misses too many opportunities" to play for the Three Lions.

Sources at Stamford Bridge also reiterated Alonso's assertion that Palmer was unavailable throughout the extended England camp because of a muscle injury.

It was highlighted by the fact he did not take part in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Portsmouth towards the end of the break.

Palmer was then not selected for the following camp in November, but multiple sources say he remains fully committed to regaining his place in the national team.

Team-mate Rogers told BBC Sport it was "a lie" that Palmer does not want to play for England, while another of his best friends in football, Tosin Adarabioyo, called it "false, false, false".

Former Manchester City and Chelsea defender Tosin, now at Tottenham, is known to have called him a "little superstar", and Palmer has found fame difficult to cope with at times.

The Wythenshawe-born forward is mobbed whenever he leaves Stamford Bridge, while he has posted pictures going out in a balaclava to try to live as normal a life as possible.

Chelsea fan Savage Dan thinks Cole Palmer's inconsistency is 'an issue'

Lastly, there is the question of whether the Chelsea project itself could be impacting him.

The club's use of ultra-long contracts has attracted criticism from some commentators and external sources, who have questioned whether such deals can affect motivation once a player's future is secured.

Critics also argue such contracts may reduce a player's leverage if they later seek a move away.

There is little evidence to support that argument in individual cases, such as Palmer's, but contracts of that length remain rare elsewhere in English football.

Chelsea maintain their deals are heavily incentivised, with significant elements linked to individual and collective performance.

Ultimately, Palmer is one of many Chelsea players struggling, with teams adapting to deal with his threat and he has lost Joao Pedro, with whom he had a fantastic connection.

However, he has the influence to positively affect his team-mates as one of the poster boys for the club and carries the weight of helping his team arrest their downturn.

It now looks as though Palmer's success or failure is completely intertwined with Chelsea's fortunes, given he will likely remain at the club for a long time to come.

The Blues have shown belief in coaxing Palmer's extraordinary performances of 2024 back out of him and, should that be realised, it would go a long way towards reviving Alonso's side.

#704. COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

#703. The Challenge Alum Tyler Duckworth’s Cause of Death Revealed

Three months after MTV star Tyler Duckworth died at the age of 44 in his North Dakota apartment, his cause of death has been confirmed.

More information has come to light about Tyler Duckworth’s passing.

Three months after The Challenge winner died at the age of 44, his cause of death was confirmed as heart disease.

According to TMZ, citing the North Dakota State Forensic Examiner’s Office, Tyler died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease, which is when the heart and blood vessels become damaged due to long-term high blood pressure. His death, per the outlet, was confirmed to be of natural causes.

Tyler’s mother Joni Duckworth shared the news of her son’s passing in an Aug. 13 Facebook post, noting she’d share service details “as soon as his dad and I figure it out.”

At the time, the Grand Forks Police Department told E! News that Tyler was found in a bathroom in his North Dakota apartment. Though they were still waiting on toxicology results at the time, police noted there were no signs of foul play, nor did Tyler’s death appear suspicious.

Before his success on The Challenge, which he won twice, Tyler made his reality TV debut on Real World: Key West in 2006. Following his passing, many of Tyler’s former reality TV costars from both shows paid him tribute, including Johnny “Bananas” Devenanzio.

“You were more than a friend," Johnny shared in a video posted to Instagram Aug. 15. "More than a roommate. You were the brother I never had. Rest easy, Tyler. You’ll always be family.”

In fact, though they clashed on Real World, Tyler and Johnny’s bond was so close he also spoke at Tyler’s funeral.

“Lights will guide you home,” Johnny captioned a post from the ceremony. “And I hope wherever they lead you, you know how deeply you were loved, and how much of you we’ll carry with us forever. Rest easy, brother.”

Tyler’s funeral was also attended by Real World’s Jose Tapia, who honored his former costar with a moving tribute on social media.

“Tyler wasn’t just my castmate. He was my roommate and really my first friend in that house,” Jose wrote on Aug. 16. “Tyler was brilliant, incredibly witty, strong as a bull, and had an energy that could fill a room. If you knew him, you know.”

And after detailing some of the memories they shared, Jose concluded, “Rest easy, roommate. Love you, big bro.”

Tyler, however, isn’t the former MTV personality whose life was cut tragically short. Read on to remember more stars gone too soon.

Part of two winning Challenge teams—on Cutthroat in 2010 and Rivals in 2011—Duckworth reunited with fellow franchise alums at a Challenge Mania podcast event just weeks before his mother announced Aug. 13, 2026 that her son had passed away.

The 44-year-old was found dead at his North Dakota home, where police were responding to a request for a welfare check, according to the Grand Forks Police Department.

While he went on to work as a teacher, Duckworth told Entertainment Weekly in 2021 when he competed on The Challenge: All Stars 2, "I gave it my all. I don't know if this might be my last rodeo, so I'm going to give you guys a motherf---ing show."

The Road Rules: Extreme and The Gauntlet 2 alum was found dead in his Brooklyn apartment in June 2017.

The New York Medical Examiner's office later told E! News that the cause of his death was natural and there were no lethal drugs in him at the time, but that Dias had complications with chronic substance abuse.

Known for his larger-than-life personality and inseparable bond with professional skateboarder Rob Dyrdek, the Rob & Big star died from a heart attack at 45 years old in May 2017. Members of his MTV family paid tribute to the former bodyguard, remembering his unique sense of humor and family-first ideals.

The Newport Harbor: The Real Orange County star, 27, succumbed to a self-inflicted gunshot wound while on a desert trip with friends in March 2017. After the reality series end in 2007, Adler—who aspired to work in the entertainment industry—went on to book television roles on Make It Or Break It and The Fish Tank.

At only 23, the 16 and Pregnant alum was found dead of a presumed overdose in 2016. Fairman's years-long struggle with substance abuse was documented on her season, and in 2015 she was arrested on charges of prostitution. Valerie is survived by her 7-year-old daughter, Naveah.

Ryan Dunn, a stunt performer who plied his trade on Jackass and Viva La Bam, died in a 2011 car accident. He was 34.

Dubbed by friends as the "Random Hero," Hollywood mourned Dunn's sudden passing. Co-star Bam Margera told E! News at the time, "He was my best f--king friend in the world. It's been five days now and I can't stop crying man."

Diem Brown was 34 when she died of colon cancer in November 2014.

Former co-stars paid tribute to her after her death with an emotional MTV special, We Heart Diem, which highlighted her passion for life and dance.

The Real World: San Diego alum died at 25 in June 2007. She had long suffered from cystic fibrosis.

Her appearance on the MTV series raised awareness about the chronic lung disease, though she memorably left mid-season because, as she put it, "I guess I'm just a little too punk rock for this."

Pedro Zamora being part of the cast of The Real World: San Francisco in 1994 marked a pivotal moment in HIV/AIDS awareness and LGBTQ+ representation in pop culture and beyond.

The 22-year-old died from complications of AIDS on Nov. 11, 1994, hours after the season finale aired.

The 28-year-old star of The Real World: New Orleans and The Challenge was found dead from an accidental overdose at a residence in Wisconsin on Thanksgiving in 2014, two weeks after close friend Diem Brown's passing.

Knight's girlfriend and fellow Real World alum Jemmye Carroll penned an open letter paying tribute to her "soulmate."

Fans of The Real World will remember Sasser from his relationship with Pedro Zamora and their televised commitment ceremony on the series. He kept Zamora's legacy alive by continuing to bring awareness to AIDS up until losing his fight against mesothelioma, a rare cancer of the lungs, in 2013 at the age of 44.

A castmember of Buckwild, the 21-year-old and two others were found dead from accidental poisonous carbon monoxide fumes filling their in 2013. The Dallas Cowboys cheerleader turned flight attendant, who appeared on  Road Rules: Europe (a.k.a. season three) in 1997 and then competed on Extreme Challenge in 2001, died in a car crash along with her cousin Mandie Parma in October 2002. She was 27.

"Michelle had a spirit about her that just pulled you in," MTV producers Jonathan Murray and Mary-Ellis Bunim said in a statement at the time. "She was one of the nicest, most genuine people to ever be on one of our reality shows. We will all miss her terribly."

Sam Sarpong, who co-hosted Yo Momma with Wilmer Valderrama died by suicide at the age of 40 in 2015.

"Sam did it all, believed in dreaming bigger than anyone around him," Valderrama said in tribute. "We made memories together that will last us forever, thank you for sharing your talent with me and the world..."

The extreme sports star and frequent figure on Nitro Circus died at age 39 in 2015 after suffering injuries sustained in a freak skydiving accident. In Erik's mind, living any other way was a waste."

The Real World: Hollywood star left behind a young son and daughter after overdosing on opiates in 2012 at 29-years-old. More than 1,000 people gathered to mourn Joey's passing at a funeral in Illinois, where family and friends remembered him as a "loving father."

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and his Shenzhou-24 crewmates arrived at Tiangong at 1:35 a.m. ET today (Nov. 25).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time ever, a foreign astronaut has set foot inside China's Tiangong space station.

That pioneer is Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who arrived at Tiangong aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft early this morning (Nov. 25).

"The Chinese space station is always something to look forward to!" the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) wrote in an update today (in Mandarin; translation by Google). "China's 'Tiangong' welcomes partners from all over the world to visit!"

Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces, is a payload specialist on Shenzhou-24. He found his way onto the mission thanks to a space-cooperation agreement that China signed with Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025.

Ali and his two Shenzhou-24 crewmates — commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi — enjoyed a short and smooth ride to their orbital destination. They lifted off atop a Long March 2F rocket on Tuesday (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT on Nov. 25) and reached Tiangong a little over six hours later.

Tang and Wu will live aboard the outpost for the usual six-month stint. Ali, however, will come home in just a week, hitching a ride with two of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong in May.

Ali will be busy during his short space stay, conducting a set of joint Chinese-Pakistani experiments.

"Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, with Ali also scheduled to conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria," The Times of India wrote today.

The third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain on the station until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore set a Chinese record, becoming the first astronaut from his country to live in low Earth orbit for a full year.

Astronauts from the Soviet Union/Russia and the United States have already blazed this long-duration trail. The global record for longest continuous space stay is 437 days, set by cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov aboard the Mir space station from January 1994 to March 1995.

Ali is not the first person from Pakistan ever to reach space, by the way. That distinction belongs to adventurer Namira Salim, who traveled to suborbital space on a tourism flight with Virgin Galactic in October 2023.

Shenzhou-24 is the 12th crewed mission to Tiangong, a three-module, T-shaped outpost that China finished assembling in late 2022. Well, "finished" might not be the right term; China plans to expand Tiangong, which is currently about 20% as massive as the International Space Station.

#701. How a football team rebuilt after 19 players died in plane crash

How a football team rebuilt after 19 players died in plane crash

It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.

A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.

Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest game in their history.

It would later emerge the plane had run out of fuel and investigators would find the airline and pilot were to blame as the fuel load was insufficient for the flight on 28 November 2016.

But in the early hours, as Tozzo watched the TV news in the changing room at the club's stadium, his only thought was for the players who would not be coming back to this room.

When he sat alone in the club's boardroom after the funerals as the only director still alive, he cried.

That was the moment when Tozzo â who had changed his mind about travelling with the team because he had a sense of unease about the trip - decided he would lead Chapecoense to rise again.

Ivan Tozzo recalls the phone call he got after the crash: "It was our club secretary, Jorilda, who was desperate, screaming 'Ivan Ivan'."

Chapecoense had been travelling to Colombia to play Atletico Nacional of Medellin in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final, South America's second most prestigious club tournament.

It was a first continental final for the Brazilian team.

"The team was very motivated, knowing that we were engraving our names inside the history of the club," goalkeeper Jakson Follmann, one of the three surviving players, tells BBC Sport.

Aged 24 at the time, Follmann had also been looking forward to his imminent wedding, little knowing he would be spending two months in hospital instead.

"Everyone was completely proud of everything they were doing, both for the team and for the community of Chapeco and the region," Follmann says.

Commentator Rafael Henzel, who was one of six survivors of the crash but who died in 2019 following a heart attack, described the Copa Sudamericana as the team's "World Cup" and said in 2017 that "if anyone's ever died happy, it was the people on that plane".

Survivors Neto, Alan Ruschel, Follmann and Henzel (left to right) appeared together at a friendly between Brazil and Colombia two months after the crash

The LaMia 2933 flight from Santa Cruz in Bolivia to the Colombian city of Medellin had a journey distance similar to the plane's flying range, but it did not stop to refuel and crashed into a mountain just 18km from its intended destination.

The pilot, Miguel Quiroga, who was also a co-owner of the airline, died in the crash. In a leaked tape, he can be heard warning of a "total electric failure" and "lack of fuel". However, he did not make a formal distress call.

A Bolivian investigation concluded that the pilot and the airline were directly responsible for the crash, while a Colombian investigation said there was no technical failure and blamed the pilot, the airline and Bolivian regulators.

"I don't call it an accident, I say it was a crime that could have been avoided," says Follman, whose right leg had to be partially amputated to save his life.

"It's the crime of not stopping to refuel, the greed to think that he [the pilot] could get there... with the fuel practically finished."

To date, no-one has been found guilty in relation to the crash.

At the time, Bolivia did not have a system for prosecuting companies. Even when such a facility was introduced in 2021, it did not cover negligent homicide or causing an air disaster.

Charges were brought against individuals in LaMia's management - who denied wrongdoing - but in 2020 a trial was delayed by jurisdictional disputes and difficulties involving defendants who were abroad.

The plane was just 18km from its destination when it ran out of fuel

A number of key details about the disaster were established early on.

At 21:16 local time, the aircraft displayed a low fuel warning but flew on without the crew alerting local authorities.

Fourteen minutes later, the plane began its descent to Medellin airport but was put in a holding pattern.

At 21:49, the crew requested priority permission to land, vaguely citing "problems with fuel".

"I remember the lights went out suddenly; then I started praying, asking God to help us," recalled defender Neto, the last of the survivors to be found.

"But a lot of people thought the plane was just landing because it was not an abrupt fall."

Within five minutes, all the engines, drained of fuel, failed.

"Then, I couldn't hear the plane engine any more. It was just a wind. And then an alarm: beep beep beep," Neto told the BBC World Service in 2017.

Thousands of people gathered in the rain as the funeral cortege went past

Seven thousand kilometres away in the small southern Brazilian city of Chapeco, Tozzo watched the scale of the disaster unfold on TV screens at the stadium in the middle of the night.

"At five o'clock in the morning, the players' wives began to arrive. It was despair. People threw themselves on the ground and cried," says Tozzo, a local entrepreneur who was the club's vice-president at the time and had joined the club in 2009 when they were not even playing in Brazil's national football pyramid.

Two days earlier, Tozzo had suffered misgivings about the trip that were so strong that he had changed his mind about travelling to Medellin.

"It was a thing from God. It was not for me to go. I called [financial director] Decio, who organised all our trips, and I told him that I would not go," he says.

"He went crazy with me. 'Why? You agreed to go, now you do not want to go? You have to go.'

"My sister was next to me, saying, 'You need to go to this match, you worked so hard to get to this moment.' But in my head I said, 'No Ivan, I will not go', and I stayed at home."

After the crash, he had another strong feeling about his path.

"I think I had a mission here on Earth to continue Chapecoense after the accident," Tozzo says. "I was the only one of the directors left alive so I took over as [interim] president."

A sleepless week followed in which Tozzo arranged flights to Colombia for doctors, relatives and pastors to identify and recover the remains and be with the survivors.

A memorial service was organised and, in pouring rain, the coffins were brought into Chape's stadium, Arena Conda.

During the service came the news that Atletico Nacional had asked for the Copa Sudamericana trophy and winners' prize money to be awarded to Chapecoense.

Tozzo was determined Chapecoense would compete again, but none of the surviving players were in any shape to play and they only had two other squad members â who did not travel to Medellin because of injury â and a handful in the academy.

They called on Rui Costa, who had been sacked by Gremio as football director six months earlier and accepted the same role with Chapecoense, and appointed Vagner Mancini as coach.

In a matter of weeks, 22 new players were signed, most of them on loan.

Tozzo's message rang clear in the ears of the new players.

"Our fans were very sad, Chapecoense was very sad, and playing again with joy was not easy," he says.

"We explained very well the responsibility they would have."

Chapecoense's new players line up for their first match

Chapecoense's first match back â eight weeks after the crash â was a friendly against the last team the club had played, Palmeiras.

Before the game at the Arena Conda, Follmann â in a wheelchair â was joined by Neto and the other surviving player, Alan Ruschel, to receive the Copa Sudamericana trophy.

"It was the first time I had gone back to the arena, the first time I really had contact with people, because I was still hospitalised," says Follmann.

"When I received the trophy, a movie went through my head because our captain Cleber Santana should have been holding it surrounded by all of us, celebrating."

The friendly against Palmeiras was the first of 80 matches that Chapecoense played in 2017, only five of them friendlies.

There was an offer from the Brazilian Football Confederation to give the club immunity from relegation for three seasons, but Tozzo rejected it.

"How can you psych up the players to play their best if they know that their classification is guaranteed?" he asks.

As it turned out, Chapecoense stayed up on their own merits for precisely three seasons.

Chapecoense's new players faced Atletico Nacional in the South American Super Cup in 2017

In 2017, as Sudamericana champions, they once again had to face Atletico Nacional, the reigning Copa Libertadores winners, in the South American Super Cup.

It meant another flight to Medellin just months after the crash. This time Tozzo was on board.

"We went to see the exact location [of the crash]," he says. "I can't believe it was so close [to the airport]."

Chapecoense lost 6-3 on aggregate but later in the year won their state championship and finished as high as eighth in the national league in a demonstration of remarkable resilience.

The following year, in the second wave of new players, defender Bruno Pacheco was signed.

Pacheco, who has made nearly 150 appearances for the club in two spells, says: "Stepping on to the pitch at the arena was an emotional experience.

"I was representing those who are no longer with us, as well as the fans. I'm happy to be part of such an important chapter in the club's history."

After relegation from Serie A in 2019, Chapecoense won the Serie B title to earn promotion back to the top flight.

But that lasted just one season and they spent the next four terms in the second tier. They have spent this year in Serie A but will be relegated again.

Neto spoke at a ceremony in memory of the 71 passengers who died, marking the 10th anniversary of the tragedy

After the crash, Neto's only appearance for Chapecoense came as a substitute in a charity friendly in December 2017, when money was raised to support relatives of the victims.

He remained at the club as a player for two more years until being forced to retire by the pain of his crash-related injuries.

He became a Christian evangelist, and he speaks for the relatives of his former team-mates who are still seeking justice as some families pursue compensation and hold out hope for criminal convictions.

Left-back Ruschel, who suffered severe injuries and had spinal surgery, was the only player to continue his professional playing career meaningfully, returning to the game nine months after the crash and staying with Chapecoense until 2021.

He only retired this November, helping his side Juventude win promotion to Serie A in his final game, ironically to swap places with Chapecoense.

Neto presented him with a commemorative plaque at half-time in Chapecoense's game against Palmeiras at the Arena Conda on 24 November when both men held aloft a jersey bearing Follmann's name.

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video announcing his retirement, calling it "a day that changed my life forever".

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects," he said.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye."

Follmann's wedding - the one he had been preparing for before the crash - did happen and he became a father.

Despite having an offer to join Brazil's sitting volleyball team at the Paralympics, he turned to careers as a singer, motivational speaker and author, but with a new perspective.

"I observe everything around me. I observe life," he says.

"I have issues with making plans for the future, because life showed me that I only have today to live.

"I don't leave anything for tomorrow. I say everything today. I forgive today, I hug today."

Tozzo, the director who stayed at home, continues to live in Chapeco where he runs various businesses.

"I haven't talked about the accident for a long time," he says. "We keep remembering, and every time we talk, tears fall, but these are things in life that we have to face."

Additional reporting by Julia Dias Carneiro

#700. Whose Man Utd days look numbered? Player ratings

Callum Wilson gets behind Leny Yoro to put Brentford ahead at Manchester United

Manchester United were thrashed by Brentford at Old Trafford for the first time since 1937 as Mauricio Pochettino's first home game in charge ended in disappointed.

Senne Lammens: All the pressure on him but brilliant reaction save to deny Anthony. Could he have done better with the first goal? 5

Diogo Dalot: Picked out Bruno Fernandes with an excellent cross but Portugal team-mate couldn't convert. Did OK in a poor overall performance. 6

Leny Yoro: Wilson drifted off him for the opener. Didn't respond quickly enough to the danger for the second. 4

Harry Maguire: Early effort against the bar, then on-target header saved and another off the line. It's at the other end where the problems are. 5

Lisandro Martinez (off 46, Shaw): Played as left-back but didn't really work. Not strong enough defensively now either. Feels like end of his Man Utd career is looming. 4

Youri Tielemans (off 83, Mount): Did a lot of midfield scheming to try and create opportunities and hit the bar but midfield so easily bypassed by opposition. 6

Kobbie Mainoo: So much being asked of him in an under-performing side. Little wonder he is a long way off his best. 6

Amad Diallo (off 46, Mbeumo): A big threat on the right but home side couldn't make most of it. Surprise when taken off at half-time but Pochettino had to do something. 6

Bruno Fernandes: Recovered from virus to play. Usual invention and never stopped trying but you wonder how long he has left here. 6

Patrick Dorgu: Excellent opportunity at far post but headed wide. Passing not quick or clinical enough. Wasted another chance in second half. 5

Joshua Zirkzee (off 62, Cunha): Successive starts for the first time since December and brought early save out of Kelleher. Did a lot of running, but is he good enough? 6

Bryan Mbeumo (on 46, Amad): Free-kick into the wall but more expected against his old club. 5

Luke Shaw (on 46, Martinez): Return after seven-week absence and definitely improved home side's defending. 6

Matheus Cunha (on 62, Zirkzee): Didn't really get on the ball enough to make an impact. Had a late shot. 5

Shea Lacey (on 70, Dorgu): Crowd was willing him to do well and he forced Kelleher into a good save. 7

Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, De Ligt, Mount, Andrey Santos.

Man Utd still in drop zone after heavy Brentford defeat

Caoimhin Kelleher: Wasn't worked hard enough when the home side had the opportunity in first half, then reacted well to push away Dorgu effort. 6

Michael Kayode: Got in a tangle with Maguire at the far post at a corner but used strength legally. Sensational arcing run away from own box at start of second half. 7

Kristoffer Ajer: Solid and effective partnership in the middle with Ajer. Unfussy defending and home attack not good enough to exploit weaknesses. Late goal as well. 8

Sepp van den Berg: Helped out because home side didn't start with a conventional number nine but always seemed to be in control. 7

Keane Lewis-Potter: Solid in defence, lethal on the counter-attack. Very effective performance. 7

Mamadou Sangare: Returned to starting line-up and blazed early chance over but was a rare blemish on an otherwise excellent day. 8

Vitaly Janelt: Easy to go unnoticed but always seems to be in the right place, which keeps Brentford ticking over. 7

Dango Ouattara (off 87, Carvalho): Assist for the first and kept his cool for the second, cutting inside Martinez and pass through Maguire's legs for Wilson to score. 8

Mikkel Damsgaard: Had the vision to create the opener, via Ouattara's pass. Exceptional pass to release Ouattara for the second. Most effective creative player on the pitch. 9

Jaidon Anthony (off 87, Diouf): But for Lammens, would have put Brentford in front with instinctive overhead kick. Another effort flicked wide off Maguire. Big threat. 8

Callum Wilson: Clinical finish to put the visitors ahead. Tap-in for the second. Will hope second-half injury that forced him off is not serious. 8

Kevin Schade (on 52, Wilson): Tried to make inroads from the left. Completed the scoring with late finish. 6

Mathias Jensen (on 70, Damsgaard): Brought on to ensure victory and did his job. 6

Prime Video’s "Blade Runner 2099" has arrived with an 8-episode limited series revealing what the "Blade Runner" world looks like 50 years after the events of director Denis Villeneuve’s "Blade Runner 2049."

The most obvious change in this depressing dystopia is that replicants are running the LA show after some unmentionable ecological disaster and humans are now the ones relegated to underclass citizens.

Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.

We connected with three of the sci-fi show’s main co-stars, Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon"), Lewis Gribben ("T2 Trainspotting") and Dimitri Abold ("Love Addicts") to hear more about working with creator/showrunner Silka Louisa, and immersing themselves in "Blade Runner 2099's" vivid futuristic worldbuilding.

"For me it's a lot simpler than egos because he's such a goal-oriented person and all of his stuff has such a police procedural quality to it," Needham tells SPACE regarding his role as Yahya, an emotionless replicant who despises all humans.

"It was really fun to just follow what Silka [Louisa] did. She wrote this great, really exciting mystery thriller, and I just got to play in that.”

Scottish actor Gribben portrays Cora's ailing younger brother Elias, who has compromised mobility and a rocky relationship with his overprotective sister.

"I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television shows. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it."

As Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character.

"Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. "Starting out as someone who’s so hopeful and has to try and scrape up the last dregs of hope as things start falling apart. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for."

"Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations feature detailed production design that allowed the actors to experience a seamless transition into the complex shoot.

"For me and Dimitri, our first day was in Bebeto’s apartment, and it was all so well-realized,” Gribben recalls.

"You saw all the gadgets because obviously Bebeto was a bit of a tinkerer of a character and had lots of machinery and works and stuff. It took up about 70% of the acting, and we just had to come with compelling conviction. It made it so easy. When you audition for these things, you feel like you have to act more because you’re in a blue screen vacuum. But then you’re there, and it’s so visually well created like that, it made it so easy to be immersed in it."

"Blade Runner 2099" is currently airing all 8 episodes exclusively on Prime Video.

#696. From jeers to European dreams - how Farke transformed Leeds

Daniel Farke post-match interview - Leeds United v Coventry City

There is a song Leeds United supporters sing during games about passports and Daniel Farke.

It is about dreaming of a return to Europe and is usually heard when the German's side are winning.

At a rain-soaked Elland Road on Saturday, fans belted it out time and time again as their side turned on the style to dispose of Coventry City 3-0 and climb to sixth in the Premier League, having sealed a third-straight top-flight win for the first time since 2021.

Two goals from Sean Longstaff - after Dominic Calvert-Lewin had opened the scoring - secured the points and maintained Leeds' winning momentum after back-to-back victories over Tottenham and Chelsea.

The Whites have not competed in Europe since 2002, but Farke has got supporters believing a return to continental action might not be far away.

"They deserve to dream, think big," Farke told BBC Sport about fans' European dreams. "They should feel the joy."

However, the Leeds boss insisted he would not be allowing his players to get carried away - despite their impressive form.

"We are in our second season after promotion, second season is normally tough. We will stay focused and concentrated," Farke added.

Leeds' transformation over the past 12 months has been nothing short of remarkable.

They turned up at Manchester City on 29 November 2025 having lost five of their previous six league games, and lost again 3-2 at Etihad Stadium to remain stuck in the relegation zone.

However, Farke changed the shape of the team at half-time - switching to a three-man central defence - and an improved second-half performance in Manchester bought the under-pressure manager some time.

Since then Leeds have gone from strength to strength - and return to Etihad Stadium on Wednesday having picked up 56 points from the past 37 games.

"Leeds have been phenomenal - they are so aggressive and so difficult to beat," former Leeds keeper Kasper Schmeichel, who watched the Coventry game for BBC Sport, said.

"Daniel Farke's side just do the basics really well and have been relentless."

Since Farke switched to that three-man central defence, Leeds have reached an FA Cup semi-final, won 13 Premier League games, drawn 17 and lost just seven.

In the closing stages against Coventry, Farke's name echoed around Elland Road.

"The early days of Farke were functional and he felt like someone who would get us out of the Championship and maybe no further," said Michael Normanton, from the Square Ball Leeds United fan podcast.

"But the way it has gone over the last 12 months, I think maybe now there's still a chance of us moving beyond that."

Another reason for Leeds' upturn in fortunes has been the form of Calvert-Lewin, who celebrated his new contract by heading the opener against Coventry - his sixth league goal of the season.

It was his 20th in 47 Premier League games since the former Everton forward joined Leeds on a free transfer in August 2025. No other English player has scored more in the past 15 months in the top flight.

Leeds fans celebrated Calvert-Lewin's latest goal by chanting "England's number nine".

"I'm loving my football at the minute," Calvert-Lewin, who featured in England's 3-2 Nations League win over Spain in Madrid earlier this month, told BBC Final Score.

"The manager has been great with me. He gives me confidence and ownership when I go on the pitch. The people and the club and the culture, it's the perfect place for me and I love it."

Asked about Leeds' chances of qualifying for Europe, Calvert-Lewin added: "Who knows?

"I think the Premier League is the most competitive league in the world and you're only two or three match weeks away from being in a different position.

Sean Longstaff became the first Leeds player to both score and assist in the first half of a Premier League match this season

Off the pitch a stadium expansion is taking place which will raise the capacity to 53,000.

Meanwhile, Farke is said to be close to signing a new contract to add to the feel-good factor around the club.

On the pitch they have turned Elland Road into a fortress, with Leeds unbeaten in front of their own fans since 3 March.

However, caution remains the key word inside the dressing room.

"It's still far too early for that," Longstaff told BBC Sport when asked about the chances of Leeds playing in Europe next season.

"Three wins in a row is massive, it brings confidence and hopefully the sky is the limit. Hopefully it's a springboard for us.

"We're finding where we are as a team and it does not get any tougher than for the next match [at Manchester City on Wednesday]."

The difference this time is Leeds will make the midweek trip to Manchester City with confidence sky high - instead of trepidation.

#695. Brittany Mahomes Slams Call From Controversial Chiefs, Bills Game

Patrick Mahomes's wife Brittany Mahomes wasn't afraid to let her feelings known as she slammed a controversial call from Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills' Nov. 26 Thanksgiving game.

Brittany Mahomes is throwing a red flag at this call.

The wife of Patrick Mahomes made no secret of her thoughts on the Kansas City Chiefs’ loss to the Buffalo Bills during the Nov. 26 Thanksgiving game, sharing her frustration over an overturned call involving player Rashee Rice’s catch in the fourth quarter.

“HAHAHAHAHAHA WHAT A JOKE,” Brittany posted to her Instagram Stories Nov. 26. “Guess we can't even play football without getting it called against us.”

#694. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

#692. Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries."

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.
