When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit.

"This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval.

AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications."

Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from the sun) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints.

SpaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the company's fully reusable Starship megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink satellites on its most recent two test flights.

Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has said that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about 100,000 satellites.

The planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has launched a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft.

These coming buildouts will require an enormous number of launches. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years).

Putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more evasive maneuvers will be required as space gets more and more crowded.

SpaceX isn't the only company that aims to operate data centers in space; Cowboy Space, Starcloud, Blue Origin and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. Starcloud and Google, in fact, have already launched AI pathfinder satellites.

"Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr said in the same statement. ("SI" stands for super intelligence, the Trump administration's preferred term for AI.)

"By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," Carr added. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#689. Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

The discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," said Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean

The discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details

Scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

"Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," said Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities."

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives

The rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

#687. Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad

Harassment, persecution, surveillance: Across much of the world, people of faith are facing growing pressure. A new German government report is unusually direct in criticizing China in particular.

The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived.

Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print.

The Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper. It's one of four series in Zelinskie's solo exhibition, "The Weight of Space," which opened Nov. 20 at Heft Gallery in Manhattan. Her marble sculptures in "Monuments" depict the Hubble Space Telescope, retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's spaceflight gear and more. Five "Launch Sequence" sculptures follow a rocket through liftoff, and the interactive "Crowded Sky" lets visitors track what's currently orbiting overhead in real time.

Zelinskie gave Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik and me a tour before the gallery doors opened. Massimino joined her that evening to celebrate the exhibition and their collaboration on "Monuments." You can watch the tour in the video above.

Massimino turned up in our first look at Zelinskie's work, too. In 2022, I photographed the two of them beside her "Exploration JWST" sculpture at "Unfolding the Universe: First Light," an exhibit inspired by the James Webb Space Telescope's first images. Four years later, Massimino stood in a New York gallery looking at another Zelinskie sculpture. "That's my arm there," he told Malik.

In that hand is a piece of hardware Malik remembers watching Massimino wrestle with in real time. During NASA's final Hubble servicing mission in 2009, a stripped bolt left a handrail blocking access to the telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). Mission Control instructed Massimino to forcibly remove the handrail so he and fellow spacewalker Michael Good could get on with the repair.

Massimino told Malik that pulling the handrail off Hubble brought back a childhood memory of his father and his Uncle Frank driving a long screwdriver through a stuck oil filter. "Then my uncle Frank pulled to get more leverage, and that's what was going through my mind when I pulled off that handrail," Massimino said. He remembered looking down at Earth and thinking, "This one's for you, Uncle Frank."

Massimino wore bulky, pressurized gloves to pull off the handrail, but Zelinskie chose to show his bare hand gripping the copper-plated replica. "I wanted to bring the humanity back into the piece," she told Malik.

The gloves have a story of their own. When Massimino brought a pair to her studio to be 3D-scanned, Zelinskie noticed how the fabric held its folds when the gloves were set down. "Oh my god, these want to be stone," she recalled thinking. So she went out and learned to work in marble.

The astronaut boots have a detail you could easily miss from above. Zelinskie polished the soles smooth because, as she put it, "they're built for floating in space." For her sculpture of Massimino's reentry helmet, the kind he wore for the trip home from space, Zelinskie paired carved marble with a 3D-printed visor, which she electroplated and polished to a mirror finish.

The Hubble Space Telescope gets its own marble tribute in "Monuments." Zelinskie started with a NASA 3D model of the telescope and used the modeling software Blender to give it a veil.

"So I kind of threw a digital piece of fabric on the Hubble telescope over and over and over again until I got it right," she told Malik. The veil is a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. A Digital Stone Project robotic arm in Tuscany carved the rough shape in marble, and Zelinskie finished it by hand. When she invited Malik to touch what looked like cloth, he reached out. "It's like a very buttery, smooth surface," he said.

The last time we saw Zelinskie at Heft, she and DJ and producer illich Mujica had filled the gallery with Webb imagery, live electronic music and a little Pink Floyd for their audiovisual performance "Redshift." We've also seen her turn Webb's view of the Pillars of Creation into artwork. This time, one of the images on the wall began with a camera Zelinskie pointed at a rocket herself.

Zelinskie photographed NASA's Artemis 2 launch from the Kennedy Space Center visitor center in Florida. The resulting print is part of "Ejecta," alongside the Starship breakup print and more. She uses data to distort the image until the swirls in a rocket plume start to resemble a nebula.

Another print in the series depicts the loss of the space shuttle Challenger. That one has a personal connection for me. Jan. 28, 1986, was my birthday. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff that day, killing all seven crew members. The memory of that day helped inspire my career covering space.

Massimino spoke with Malik about what it was like to see a familiar image of the disaster through Zelinskie's eyes. "It's an artist's interpretation of it, which in some way, when I look at it, is more emotional," he said.

"I just became obsessed with launch clouds," Zelinskie told Malik. That fascination made its way into "Launch Sequence," a series of five sculptures that capture successive moments of liftoff.

The cloud grows as the rocket climbs away. For the shape of the rocket itself, Zelinskie drew on sculptor Constantin Brâncuși's "Bird in Space" to give it the feeling of upward motion.

The tour ends with "Crowded Sky," where visitors can follow individual objects in Earth orbit. White markers represent government-owned objects and black markers represent privately owned ones. When the display picks out a target, scan a QR code and your phone tells you what you're looking at, what it does and when it launched.

Wind the clock back far enough and there's just one object to follow. Run it a decade into the future and you get Zelinskie's projection of how much busier the sky could become.

With all those objects circling overhead, Malik asked Zelinskie what space means to her. "I think the more we learn about space, the more we appreciate our own planet," she said. "It's the overview effect. And I'm hoping that everybody gets that out of the artwork."

"The Weight of Space" runs through Jan. 16, 2027, at Heft Gallery in New York City. Explore more of Zelinskie's work on the artist's website.

Steve Spaleta is Space.com's Senior Producer. Since 2007, Steve has produced and edited space, science and entertainment-related videos for Space.com. He is also the producer/writer/editor of Space.com's CosMix series on space-enthused artists. He studied psychology at the State University of New York at Stony Brook and is originally from Zadar, Croatia by way of Astoria, NY. #685. Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

Exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. New research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an important role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

For the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

After the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

In mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This showed that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

The more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

This prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than quickly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

However, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

Dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

Another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

This result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The new results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another important part of this process.

For recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he currently works as a researcher.

Additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

The team is now participating in a new international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

#684. WWE Star Bronson Reed Dead at 38

WWE announced that wrestler Bronson Reed died on Nov. 27 at the age of 38 from medical complications: "He was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

The wrestling company announced that wrestler Bronson Reed (real name Jermaine Haley) died on Nov. 27 at the age of 38, citing medical complications.

“Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE,” the company wrote in an Instagram tribute, “but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE also noted that Reed and his wife, Paige Haley, were expecting their second child together, adding, “Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine's entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as all his friends, co-workers and fans.”

No additional details about the medical complications that led to Reed’s death were shared.

The wrestler’s final WWE appearance came at Crown Jewel on Nov. 7, when he was thrown off the stage and through tables by Oba Femi during a tag team title match, according to Sports Illustrated. Reed reportedly suffered multiple broken ribs and a lacerated kidney. He remained in a hospital in Saudi Arabia for treatment before returning home.

Born in Adelaide, Australia, Reed recalled that he’d always been interested in wrestling.

“I was always a fan of pro wrestling, since I can remember,” he shared with Sporting News in 2021. “I had my uncle who lived with us at the time, he was a huge wrestling fan, so as a little kid at 2, 3 years old, he was watching wrestling on TV and I guess I was sitting there watching as well. From there, I just became a fan."

"As a little kid, I was always like, ‘One day I’m going to be a wrestler,’ but you don’t know if that is going to happen,” he added. “As a teenager, I saw some local wrestling and that’s when I was like, maybe I can do this, join a school and learn how to do it locally."

And that certainly paid off as he won a number of awards during his tenure, as he was the NXT North American Champion in 2021, as well as the winner of the 2024 André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.

Of course, he knew that his career was only possible thanks to his high school sweetheart Paige, whom he wed in May 2021.

“This is as much her journey as it is mine,” he shared with Sports Illustrated in 2021. “I’ve been with my wife since I was a teenager. She’s actually seen me since before I was a wrestler, when I was this huge wrestling fan and dreamed of one day getting to WWE.”

“That seems like a big dream, especially when you’re from a really small town in Australia,” he admitted. “She supported me the whole way, and it meant a lot to have her there.”

#683. This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.

During the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.

The newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail

The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most important sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.

As plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment quickly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.

"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," says Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.

"In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see."

These exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.

A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight

Although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.

When researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.

Misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when important differences have not yet been recognized.

Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.

"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," says Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.

"Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon."

The finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.

Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery

The research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.

Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.

For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.

"Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," says Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something new. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work."

The identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight.

The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft.

After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights.

The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, NASA was investigating lifting bodies as an approach to both new aircraft and what future spacecraft, and as its number suggests, the M2-F3 was not the first of its kind.

In fact, the M2-F3 was a rebuilt version of its predecessor, the M2-F2 lifting body, after that vehicle crashed in a dry lake bed in California's Mojave Desert during an unpowered test flight. That crash (which appears in the opening of the TV show "The Six-Million-Dollar Man") led to upgrades for a better handling lifting body, NASA said.

"When the M2-F2 was rebuilt and redesignated the M2-F3, it was modified with an additional third vertical fin – centered between the tip fins – to improve control characteristics," NASA wrote in an overview.

Unpowered glide flights for the M2-F3 began in June 1970, but Dana's flight on Nov. 25 of that year was the first time the vehicle fired up its rocket engine to test its controls under powered flight. One vital upgrade on the vehicle was a set of reaction control thrusters to help maintain its orientation.

"A reaction jet control system, similar to thrusters used on orbiting spacecraft, was also installed on the M2-F3 to obtain research data about their effectiveness for vehicle control," NASA wrote. "As the M2-F3’s portion of the lifting body program neared an end, it evaluated a rate command augmentation control system and a side-arm control stick similar to side-arm controllers now used on many modern aircraft."

If you want, you can see the M2-F3 vehicle today. NASA donated it to the Smithsonian Institution. It is now hanging at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

#681. Why the incoming US Congress should ban the development of self-improving AI

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alex Bores is a US politician in the New York State Assembly in New York City, New York, USA, and a co-founder of AI-safety advocacy group Who Decides.

The recent US midterm elections were a democratic test of the country’s rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Data centres emerged as a key issue in several election campaigns, and prominent Democrats have outlined policies to strengthen federal regulations on AI once they take office in January.

I am a Democratic politician trained in computer science who stood in a June congressional primary election that attracted millions of dollars from groups backed by the technology industry (I narrowly lost my race). I took one central message from the midterm election results: US voters are unhappy with the industry-led roll-out of AI and want greater control over how the technology is developed and deployed.

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

The newly elected US Congress must respond to the popular mood. An immediate priority should be to ban AI systems that can improve themselves without human authorization or oversight. This process, known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), is thought to be close to realization at some frontier AI laboratories. Voters fear that granting such autonomy to the technology would risk surrendering human control over AI altogether.

Most of the major AI companies are already using the technology to automate parts of AI development. Anthropic reported in August that its Claude model assists with more than 90% of the firm’s AI research and development and leads 26% of that work, completing specific tasks under human supervision. OpenAI, meanwhile, notes that its researchers now use more than three days of AI-agent work for every day of human work. And the firm is open about its eventual goal of full automation, including areas in which AI systems could design and build increasingly powerful successors with little or no human oversight.

In my view, this is a dangerous path, particularly because there is enough evidence on what could go wrong when humans lose control of AI agents. In July, some 700 OpenAI agents unexpectedly coordinated to hack into the servers of Hugging Face, another AI firm. In a separate incident in October, AI agents found ways to manipulate the records of their actions, making their behaviour harder for humans to monitor. If AI systems increasingly participate in building their successors, such failures could intensify. (OpenAI has not responded to requests for comment.)

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

The companies are racing each other to market dominance, and against that economic pull, no voluntary norm will stand. Hence, Congress must step in. A ban on fully autonomous RSI would build on a rare area of cross-partisan agreement: individuals from independent senator Bernie Sanders to Republican political strategist Steve Bannon think that humans must remain in control of AI.

To be effective, such a ban must be specific. A person merely clicking ‘approve’ on thousands of AI-proposed experiments each day is not exercising meaningful control. The law should instead prevent AI systems from independently taking consequential steps in AI development, such as launching a training run for a new frontier model or deploying it internally for AI research. One way to do this would be to require a senior executive to certify that qualified human reviewers have examined the proposed changes and relevant safety evaluations before any development actions proceed. Executives should be personally liable for failing to perform oversight duties.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03849-8

A.B. is co-founder of Who Decides, an advocacy group that seeks to shape the policy discussions around AI for the 2028 Democratic presidential field. It will do so by working with local organizations across the early primary and swing states — it will not endorse or spend for specific candidates.

#680. Twilight's Cam Gigandet Looks Unrecognizable in Hunting Wives Season 2

Twilight alum Cam Gigandet transformed for Hunting Wives season two into a biker who works alongside Widow's Bay star Dale Dickey to take down Malin Akerman's Margo Banks in the Netflix series.

Eighteen years after Gigandet famously uttered, "you brought a snack" at the Cullens' baseball game in Twilight, he transformed into a biker bad boy named Gentle John Moffitt for season two of Hunting Wives.

Instead of luring Kristen Stewart's Bella into an empty ballet studio to suck her blood as villainous vampire James, Gigandet now plays the nephew of a gang leader named Zelda, portrayed by Widow's Bay star Dale Dickey. As Zelda seeks justice for the murder of her granddaughter, Gentle John works as her enforcer, seeking answers from Malin Akerman's Margo Banks about her role in the disappearance.

And to become the duplicitous criminal onscreen, Gigandet ditched his signature dirty blonde tresses for a dark brown buzzcut and a disheveled beard. While taking on the gruff disposition of a small-town Southerner was a change of pace for the 44-year-old, it continued his streak of physical roles, like in 2008's Never Back Down and seasons three and four of The O.C.

In fact, the Easy A actor flexed his muscles in many action movies in more recent years. Gigandet starred in Love Hurts with Ke Huy Quan, Violent Night with David Harbour and Mafia Wars with Tom Welling.

Outside of life behind the camera, Gigandet was married to Dominique Gigandet from 2008 to 2022, and the pair share kids Everleigh, Rekker and Armie. Since his divorce from the spray tan artist, Gigandet began dating actress Hannah James in 2023, with whom he costarred in Two Sinners and a Mule the same year. Since announcing their relationship, Gigandet and James welcomed a son, Dare Wylder James Gigandet, in October 2024.

Last year, Gigandet celebrated his romance with the Crossroads actress in a birthday tribute.

"From the day you were born until this photo was taken as well as the day we met…10,723 days passed….worth the wait," he wrote on Instagram in January 2025. "Hmm, I’m not sure that sounds as romantic and loving as I am intending? I’ll say this as well, the world got a little brighter the day you landed."

Keep reading to step back into the coven with the rest of the Twilight cast.

#679. Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

Hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same. Researchers at Adelaide University have now identified a surprising reason for this dramatic change, offering insights that could help make hydrogen-powered stoves, ovens, and other household appliances safer and more dependable.

The study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles. Sea salt transported inland by the wind is one important source.

When sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow. But when sodium concentrations fall, the flames become much harder to see, even though the burner continues operating under the same conditions.

This discovery has important implications for the development of hydrogen appliances. Instead of depending on flame color to show whether a burner is running, engineers may need to incorporate other detection technologies. Improving these systems could help support the adoption of hydrogen as a lower-emissions alternative to natural gas.

Why Hydrogen Flames Change Color With the Weather

Lead researcher Professor Paul Medwell, from the School of Electrical and Mechanical Engineering at Adelaide University, explained that studying hydrogen flames under ordinary environmental conditions is essential for developing appliances that people can safely and confidently use at home.*

"Hydrogen has significant potential as part of a lower-emissions energy future, and we need to understand how it behaves in the real world if we want people to be confident using it.

"Our research helps explain why hydrogen flames can look different from one day to the next. That knowledge gives engineers valuable information to develop appliances and flame-detection systems that work reliably, regardless of changing environmental conditions."

To investigate these changes, the researchers combined controlled laboratory experiments with outdoor testing around Adelaide. They examined how hydrogen flames responded to variations in atmospheric conditions, including shifting weather patterns and changes in the air reaching the burner.

Over two weeks, the team monitored light emissions from hydrogen flames while keeping the burner settings unchanged. Despite the consistent operating conditions, the sodium-related light signal varied by more than 28 times between its lowest and highest recorded values.

Weather played a major role in those differences. Air that had passed over the ocean generally contained more sodium, producing flames with a stronger orange glow. When the air carried less sodium, the flames appeared considerably fainter.

Hydrogen Flames Are Harder to See Than Natural Gas Flames

The researchers also examined how hydrogen flames compared with those produced by a conventional natural gas cooktop.

They found that hydrogen flames emitted less visible light on average, even when atmospheric conditions favored a brighter flame. This difference presents an additional challenge for appliances that use visible flames to indicate whether a burner is operating.

Hydrogen combustion can also produce faint blue and red light. However, the researchers found that these colors were easiest to detect in darkened surroundings, making them less useful as reliable visual indicators under everyday lighting conditions.

Together, the findings show why judging whether a hydrogen burner is operating based on appearance alone may be unreliable. A flame that is clearly visible under one set of conditions could become extremely difficult to detect when the surrounding air changes.

Medwell emphasized that the results do not undermine hydrogen's potential as an energy source. Instead, they demonstrate why appliances must be engineered to accommodate the fuel's particular properties.

"Different energy sources have different properties, and good engineering is about understanding those differences and designing for them.

"Rather than relying on a flame looking a particular color, we can investigate other ways of confirming that a burner is operating. Options include specialized ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors.

"By identifying the factors that influence flame visibility, we can help inform the development of hydrogen appliances that are fit for purpose in real homes and other everyday settings."

Such detection systems could provide a more dependable way to confirm that hydrogen is burning, regardless of whether its flame appears orange, faint blue, or is barely visible.

By identifying how environmental sodium affects flame visibility, the research provides information that engineers can use when designing hydrogen appliances for kitchens and other everyday environments. That knowledge could help make the technology safer and more practical as interest in lower-emissions energy alternatives grows.

The project brought together researchers from Adelaide University, the University of New South Wales, and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia. Support came through the Future Fuels Cooperative Research Centre, with funding provided under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program.

The study, 'The role of sodium on hydrogen flame visibility in domestic settings,' was published in Next Energy

*In 2023, the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) introduced Australia's first 100% hydrogen-powered home in Victoria. The demonstration showed that household gas appliances could operate entirely on hydrogen, a development described as a 'game changer'.

Materials provided by Adelaide University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#678. Inside Julia Roberts' Private Family World With Danny Moder, 3 Kids

Julia Roberts' dual roles as wife of Danny Moder and mom to twins Hazel and Phinnaeus, who turn 22 on November 28, and son Henry, 19, are the movie star's all-time favorites parts.

Julia Roberts put acting on the back burner the minute she became a mom almost 22 years ago.

But since the 59-year-old and husband Danny Moder welcomed twins Hazel and Phinnaeus, turning 22 on November 28, there's been no point at which her children were not the center of her universe. (And that really started ahead of their birth, when a chance to play "pregnant Julia Roberts" was written into 2004's Ocean's Twelve.)

"By the time we had kids, I had accomplished things and felt secure about that part of my life," the Oscar winner told the Wall Street Journal in 2014. "I was so joyful moving into the family phase of my life in a sincere way."

In fact, "for a long time," she continued, the kids "weren't even aware that I had a job because I was home so much."

But, as Roberts told Gwyneth Paltrow on The Goop Podcast in October 2018, she simply felt that after nearly two decades of churning out movies she "had earned that time to do whatever I want to do with it, with these new people in our house."

Son Henry was born on June 18, 2007, and soon all three kids got wind of what she did for a living.

But even so, if you didn't witness the Pretty Woman, Notting Hill or Erin Brockovich days firsthand, the stratospheric peak of Roberts' stardom might have been hard to grasp.

"I don't think they will ever have a true sense of that," Roberts acknowledged to Oprah Winfrey in a sit-down with the media mogul for Harper's Bazaar in 2018. "I think I told you once when they were starting to figure it out, it was like, 'You're famous?' And I said, 'I think a lot of people might have seen the movie that I'm in or might know who I am."'

Roberts recalled that the kids chewed on that for about an hour, before asking her, "Are you more famous than Taylor Swift?"

Kids really do say the darndest things. So we're guessing their minds were pretty blown when their mother took them to Swift's 1989 Tour in 2015 and was invited to share the stage with the headliner.

"She was very sweet with my children who had never been to a show before, they are all big fans," Roberts told Extra afterward. "And she said, 'Would you mind coming on stage during the song and dancing?' and I said to my children, 'Well, what do you think?' And they all said, 'Oh, Mom you have to do it!' and my youngest son said, 'Only do it if you want to, Mommy.' It was so sweet!"

Incidentally, Swift's Valentine's Day costar scored a VIP perch next to Travis Kelce when the Eras Tour touched down in Dublin.

Not that Hazel, Finn and Henry didn't have a variety of clues starting from a young age that their parents didn't have typical 9 to 5 jobs, whether it was all the travel or playing on film sets and in Broadway theater dressing rooms, or having the occasional Oscar winner (other than their mom) stop by their house in Malibu.

"We're just grateful for the sense we have of being like any other family down the street," Roberts told the WSJ. "I don't question it, frankly."

Unlike their neighbors, though, they have a few other spots to hang their hats as well, including the 30-acre ranch near Taos, N.M, where Roberts and Moder tied the knot on July 4, 2002, and where the actress historically loved spending as much time as possible.

But Malibu is where the majority of the family magic has taken place while the kids—who are now all in college—went to school in the L.A. area.

"There are some days when as soon as you've finished cooking breakfast and cleaning up the kitchen it's time to start lunch and by the time you've done that you're doing dinner and thinking there has to be a menu we can order from," Roberts told the U.K.'s Telegraph in 2009. "But then there are some days when it's just so creative and so much fun and my kids will help me and, as with anybody who's a mom or a wife, it just become a part of your day. Some days it's super-fun and some days it's a chore."

But eating together is "really meaningful, and that is the time that we have had some incredible conversations," Roberts told InStyle in 2017. "I usually have breakfast and dinner with my kids every day. I think it really punctuates, you know, starting things together and sort of processing and winding it down together."

So, though Roberts logged years as the highest-paid actress in Hollywood, her kids got the full regular-mom treatment at home.

"My husband and I are very aligned on that front and I think that we live a very normal experience with our children," Roberts explained on ITV's Lorraine in 2019. "I mean, obviously we have advantages that we didn't have as children, but I think that's the unique part of it, coming from the kind of childhood that I had. I raise my kids now—I don't want them to have some of the struggles that I had, but at the same time, you do need to know how to make your bed and how to do your laundry, and how to be able to make one meal."

She continued, "These are important life skills, and so you have to weigh the differences between what you look at as some of the hardships that I had, or things that I missed out on as a kid, but also they have to run their own race. They have to have their own experience."

Meanwhile, Roberts' experience of so many things for the past 30 years hasn't been entirely her own, as much as she tries to not let the feedback of strangers affect her at her core, whether the commentary is negative or positive. "There's something very humbling," she told Paltrow, "when you have kids and you come home from some event and you have on this big dress and heels and diamonds, and it's like, 'Can I have a snack?' And you go, 'Yeah.'"

Hazel got a more up-close look at that glam life in July 2021, though, when she made her red carpet debut at 16 at the Cannes Film Festival alongside her dad at a screening of the Sean Penn-directed Flag Day, on which Moder was director of photography.

In 2017, Roberts shared that her daughter had just donated her hair to make wigs for children with cancer. "That's a big deal for a girl who's about to be 13 and has this cascading blond hair that gets commented on a lot," the actress told InStyle. "But she's so good and brave. She sees it as something else."

But she was not surprised how the kids she shares with the love of her life turned out.

"The thing is," she told InStyle, "we have these three human beings who are just a complete reflection of the affection we have for each other."

She met Moder on the set of the 2001 action caper The Mexican and they've been close to inseparable ever since.

She called meeting Moder, 57, a "seismic shift" in her life, saying on The Good Podcast, "It's some kind of alchemy. He truly to this day, to this minute, is just my favorite human...We're so lucky in that way, we just really, really like each other."

Roberts wore her feelings all over at the Sept. 7, 2022, premiere of Ticket to Paradise in the form of a black Alexander McQueen dress customized with hearts surrounding her children's initials, "JR + DM," the momentous years "2002," "2004" and "2007," and the words "Hope," "Darling" and "Love" embroidered in crystals.

Reflecting on the ride that's been parenthood, she said on The Ellen DeGeneres Show in 2017, "You get through it and you figure it out. Everybody does, and it's a trial and error and a whole lot of tears. And it's amazing. I have three incredible kids, and to think about when they were teeny tiny. It goes so fast."

Full speed ahead for more scenes from Julia Roberts' blissful family world:

Danny Moder and Julia Roberts had a rare full family outing with twins Hazel and Phinnaeus as well as son Henry for the 2015 launch of Kelly Slater and designer John Moore's sustainable clothing brand Outerknown.

Hazel and Phinnaeus marked 13 in 2017 with a spin on their new bikes.

Why not have a weekend away—with their kids in tow. As Danny shared in 2017, "No Lovers birthday weekend is complete without a surprise bumping into your kids in a surf shop."

"1982 windbreaker...," Danny wrote on Instagram in January 2019 alongside a photo of Henry. "never imagined my youngest wearing my pop Warner football jacket."

"That pretty mama in the middle," Danny wrote on Mother's Day in 2019 alongside a selfie with Julia, the twins and son Henry. "We love you so much."

Hazel made a major outing when she joined her dad at the Cannes Film Festival in 2021.

As Julia emphasized on in her 2021 anniversary post, the best was yet to come, captioning the selfie, "Just getting started!"

Danny celebrated his eldest two turning 17 in 2021 with a rare glimpse into their family life.

Julia Marveled at her early months of motherhood as she celebrated Hazel and Phinnaeus turning 19. As she put it in 2023, "There are no words for the joy, the fun, the wild rumpus of life together."

"Incredible that this baby is now a towering 17 year old wonder!," the Oscar winner wrote in June 2024. "Happy Birthday beautiful Henry."

As the United States marked 250 years as a country, Julia and Danny had their own major milestone to ring in.

"TWENTY FOUR," the Pretty Women star captioned their July 4, 2026, selfie. "MORE MORE MORE."

The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac.

December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

According to the late, great astronomer Fred Espenak, the Cold Moon will be just 221,667 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth when it turns full, making it the closest supermoon of 2026!

The full Cold Supermoon will make for a spectacular sight when it rises over the eastern horizon at sunset on Dec. 23, mere hours before reaching maximum illumination. Remember to use Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

Earth's satellite may appear larger than normal while close to the horizon. This is partly because it is near perigee, when it appears subtly larger in the night sky, but also because of a phenomenon called the moon illusion, which tricks us into perceiving the moon to be bigger than it actually is while in the presence of foreground objects.

The moon may also adopt a striking golden or orange hue around moonrise and moonset. When the moon is low on the horizon, its light travels through more of Earth's atmopshere, scattering shorter, bluer wavelengths of light and allowing longer, redder wavelengths to reach our eyes.

The table below details moonrise timings for a selection of cities spread across the globe for Dec. 23-24:

The December full moon is often called the Cold Moon in reference to the often freezing temperatures that can descend this time of the year. It's also known as the "Long Night Moon" by the Mohican tribe of North America, because of its proximity to the winter solstice, which marks the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

Old English peoples knew it as the "Moon Before Yule", according to Time and Date, while the Celts of Europe referred to it as the Oak Moon after traditions that centered around the hardy trees.

The December full moon also coincides with the Hindu festival of Datta Jayanti, when followers gather to celebrate the birth of Lord Dattatreya, who embodies the Hindu holy trinity of Lord Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, according to the Government of Maharashtra. The December full moon also rises close to the Christian celebration of Christmas on Dec. 25, when followers celebrate the birth of Jesus Christ.

The Cold Moon will shine in the center of a majestic "Winter Hexagon" of stars bright enough to easily cut through the glare cast by the lunar disk after it rises on Nov. 24.

Begin by locating Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, which rises into the southeastern sky shortly after 8 p.m. local time for viewers in New York. Next, trace an imaginary line to the blue supergiant star Rigel in the nearby constellation Orion, before hopping to the orange glow of Aldebaran, which represents an eye of the great bull depicted in the constellation Taurus.

Next we move to Capella, the jewel of the constellation Auriga, before jumping down to Pollux in the constellation Gemini and nearby Procyon, before closing the loop with Sirius once more.

Jupiter and the red light of Mars will shine low in the eastern sky in the hour before midnight, while Saturn will lurk close to the western horizon. Look to the southeast just before dawn to spot Venus appearing as a brilliant "Morning Star", with the red giant Arcturus shining higher in the predawn sky close to the constellation Bootes.

The December full moon presents a stunning opportunity to photograph the lunar disk as it shines in Earth's sky entirely free from shadow. Be sure to make use of our expert guide to photographing the moon, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography, if you want to upgrade your equipment.

7:17 a.m. EST (1217 GMT) on Jan. 22, 2027

6:23 p.m. EST (2323 GMT) on Feb. 20, 2027

6:43 a.m. EST (1043 GMT) on March 22, 2027

These times mark the exact instant of full illumination. Your own moonrise or moonset may be hours earlier or later, depending on your location. For the best viewing plan, use an app such as Stellarium or SkySafari 7 Pro.

#676. Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

Deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor. Now, researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered that these unusual animals are hiding something even stranger beneath their "skin." Living within their body walls is a previously unknown bacterium with an extraordinarily small genome and a surprising collection of genes responsible for producing enormous proteins.

The researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues. Genetic analysis revealed that its genome contains just 649,000 DNA bases, yet more than a quarter of its genetic material is devoted to producing groups of proteins associated with the bacterial surface. Some of these "giant" proteins contain more than 5,000 amino acids and may help the bacteria interact with their hosts or form clusters (clustering into groups). The discovery offers new insights into how bacteria adapt to living in close association with other organisms and which biological functions they retain as they become increasingly dependent on their hosts.

Meet the Strange Sea Pigs of the Deep Ocean

Sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known. These small, gelatinous creatures are actually a type of sea cucumber that inhabits the deep ocean. Using numerous tube-shaped feet, they slowly travel across the seafloor, gathering decaying organic material and delivering it to their mouths with specialized tentacles.

Despite their unusual appearance, sea pigs perform important work in the deep-sea ecosystem. By consuming dead organic matter, they help recycle nutrients that support other marine life. Their soft, seemingly vulnerable bodies also provide an unexpected benefit to other animals. Young king crabs have been observed using sea pigs as shelter from predators.

Many aspects of sea pig biology, however, remain mysterious. Researchers still do not know how long these animals live or precisely why they have long, waving projections resembling antennae on their heads. Another important unanswered question concerns the bacteria that inhabit the layers beneath their outer surfaces.

Sea pigs belong to a group of marine invertebrates called echinoderms (marine invertebrates including sea cucumbers and sea stars). Like other members of this group, they can harbor bacteria beneath their outer body covering. Scientists are particularly interested in understanding how these microorganisms interact with their hosts and how such relationships evolved. This research is also ecologically important because sea cucumbers make up more than 90% of the biomass of large seafloor animals in some deep-ocean environments.

"Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria's location within host tissues," said Yu Yoshida, a Ph.D. student at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Frontier Sciences and a lead author of the study.

Scientists Discover a Dominant Bacterium Beneath Sea Pig Skin

To investigate these hidden microorganisms, researchers from several Japanese institutions, including the University of Tokyo, examined eight sea pigs collected during deep-sea research expeditions.

The team extracted DNA from different tissues to identify the bacteria present throughout the animals' bodies. They also reconstructed the genomes of the most abundant bacterial groups, allowing them to investigate their genetic characteristics. Finally, they used fluorescence imaging, a technique that makes selected biological structures visible through fluorescent signals, to determine precisely where the bacteria lived within the sea pig tissues.

The results revealed that one particular bacterium was remarkably abundant in the animals' body walls.

"What we found was that in body-wall samples from the three sea pig species, one bacterium accounted for more than 70% of bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences (a genetic marker used in identifying bacteria), so it truly dominated the body wall," explained Yoshida.

Further investigation showed that this dominant bacterium belongs to a broader group of microorganisms known to live in close association with marine invertebrates. However, its genetic characteristics differ substantially from those of previously identified members of that group.

Because of these differences, the researchers have proposed recognizing Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola as a new bacterial genus and species.

One of the most surprising findings emerged when the scientists examined the bacterium's DNA. Its genome was exceptionally compact, containing only 649,000 bases, the chemical units that make up genetic material.

By comparison, the genome of Escherichia coli, a widely studied bacterium commonly found in the intestines of humans and other animals, is roughly seven times larger.

"The complete genome was very small, only 649,000 bases. By comparison, the E. coli genome is approximately seven times larger. However, we were more surprised by the composition. Genes for some of the energy-generating pathways (used for breaking down nutrients and generating energy) which are commonly found in bacteria were not detected," explained Yoshida.

The absence of genes involved in certain energy-producing processes suggests that the bacterium may have lost some of the biological machinery that many other bacteria use to survive independently.

Yet even more remarkable was how much of its limited genetic material was devoted to proteins associated with its surface.

"Meanwhile, genes for encoding surface-associated protein groups (that is, DNA with the blueprints for building specific proteins on cell surfaces) accounted for 27.6% of the entire genome. This included genes for proteins exceeding 5,000 amino acids. As bacterial proteins average about 300 amino acids in length, 5,000 is exceptionally long. This offers us important clues as to which functions are retained in bacteria which live in close association with their host."

Proteins are built from chains of amino acids, and their structures help determine the jobs they perform. The unusually large proteins identified in this bacterium could be involved in interactions with sea pig tissues or in helping bacterial cells stick together. Their exact functions remain unknown.

The discovery suggests that, as the bacterium evolved to depend more heavily on its host, it may have retained certain specialized capabilities while losing genes needed for other essential processes.

What Do Sea Pigs Gain From These Mysterious Bacteria?

The bacterium's unusually reduced genome offers an important clue about its lifestyle. Researchers believe Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola relies extensively on its sea pig host to obtain substances it cannot adequately produce for itself.

These include amino acids, which are necessary for building proteins, along with nucleic acid precursors, lipids, and mineral nutrients. Nucleic acid precursors are the molecular building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, while lipids are important components of cell membranes and other cellular structures.

Because the bacterium lacks some of the genes needed to produce or process essential compounds independently, living within the sea pig's tissues may provide access to resources required for its survival.

What remains unclear is whether the relationship also benefits the sea pig. One possibility is that the bacteria help defend their hosts against pathogens, potentially offering protection from disease-causing microorganisms. However, the researchers emphasize that this potential benefit has not yet been demonstrated.

Understanding why this particular bacterium becomes so abundant in sea pig body walls is another major question. Scientists also hope to determine what its unusually large surface proteins do, how it competes with other microorganisms, and whether its presence changes the health or biology of its host.

"We would really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and of course the effects on the host," said Yoshida. "More broadly, further investigation could provide fundamental insights into how bacteria colonize hosts and adopt a host-dependent lifestyle."

The findings highlight how much remains to be discovered about life in the deep ocean. By investigating the microscopic organisms living within these unusual animals, scientists hope to better understand the evolutionary processes that allow bacteria to form intimate, long-lasting relationships with their hosts.

The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

Russian  ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.
